text: Crocodiles lie up in the flooded yard and mudcrabs thicken the shallows. The Lujei road above is the only safe approach.
Lujei salvagers strip its roof timbers and pull reed bundles from the flooded yards. Little is left to take.
The minder's platform is rotted, but Lujei's ferry families still drop a token of thread into the water here when they pass at dusk. The tree it served is the Blackrose tree.

Sheh-Ara fished the channel between Lujei and Blackrose. The Blackguards' heirs at the Rose raided it for boats and food until its families gave up and moved to Lujei, which pays the island core for shelter. The posts have since settled into the soft lake bed.

A ferryman's lost child's bead string is caught in the dead tree, and a Lujei elder wants the egg-stone from the minder's platform, the stone every Sheh-Ara hatchling was named over, carried to Lujei.
Black posts stand in a ring where a hall was, with a dead sapling tree on a mud spit and a rotting ladder going into the water. A ferry channel from Lujei runs close beside.
Sheh-Ara has two halls on leaning posts above a flooded yard, on the ferry channel south of Lujei. It stood outside the island core's protection, and the Rose's raiders emptied it.
Sheh-Ara has no residents. Lujei ferrymen cut across its channel, and a few salvagers sleep on the dry platform.
Two halls still stand on leaning posts above a flooded yard, and the tree-minder's platform has slipped to a lean toward the lake. Lujei boatmen pass without stopping.
Snake nests under the rotten platform and stinging midges at dusk, with silt that hides deep holes. A stranger is likelier to be hurt by the ground than by a person.
Farmers from Tei-Kur salvage planking and sow what rice will still take at the edges. Scavengers come for the old irrigation sluices.
The village tree-minder's platform has fallen in. Farmers from Tei-Kur leave a rice-sheaf at the dry corner after each harvest, a small courtesy to the people who first cleared the ground.
Oru-Neel grew rice for Lilmoth on the road between Tei-Kur and Reedfall. Its dyke failed over the years, salt water came into the paddies and its families moved to Tei-Kur.
A Tei-Kur farmer wants his grandmother's grave-stake pulled from the salt paddy and set again at Tei-Kur, and a half-buried granary may still hold sealed rice seed.
A ring of grey posts stands in an empty paddy, with a collapsed hall roof in the mud and sluice gates still hanging from the old dyke. Rice stalks come up wild around them.
Oru-Neel is a ring of grey posts in an empty paddy, with a tilted hall platform and sluice gates hanging from a broken dyke. Salt water stands where its rice grew.
Oru-Neel has no residents. Tei-Kur farmhands pass through to reach the far paddies, and none of them stays a night.
The raised platform of the hall is cracked and tilted, and brown water sits where the paddies were. Farm families from Reedfall use the dry corner to dry nets.
The smugglers fight anyone who comes near their stores, and the unstaked dead rise from the water under the walkways at night. Walkway planks give way into deep water where slaughterfish feed.
It was a fishing village that sent dried fish to Jarecai. Now it is a smugglers' store, and diggers come for the iron and the clan carvings left in the halls.
The village Hist stands grey and leafless in its root-hut, and no sap runs from it. The Mine-Burners say the dead without stakes cannot go to Sithis while the tree is sick.

Meris-Keth's Hist sickened within living memory, and its eggs stopped hatching. The families carried their last clutches to the Hist at Jarecai and did not come back, leaving the dead of that last sick year without grave-stakes.
Grave-stakes to carve for the unstaked dead, a clan's carved totem left behind in the headman's hall or the smugglers' store of moon sugar under the root-hut.
Grey timber halls lean on their stilts over black water, joined by sagging walkways. Vines hang from the roofs, and the leafless Hist stands in the middle.
A Mine-Burner village of tiered timber halls on stilts around a dying Hist. Its people left, Khajiit smugglers moved in and the dead its people never staked walk the walkways.
The village is uninhabited. Six or seven Khajiit smugglers stay in the two soundest halls, and the rest of the village belongs to the dead.
No tribe holds it. A crew of Khajiit smugglers who bring moon sugar up from the coast store it in the dry halls, and the Mine-Burners stay away from the sick tree.
Predators den under the empty halls. Scavengers sleep in the dry ones and are wary of strangers.
The village once housed the Old Goldseam crews and their families, and it fell with the mine after the uprisings; salvagers from Salaxul now pull timber from the empty halls.
The village's tree-minder is gone, and its shrine is a hollow stump with a ring of bird bones. Hunters from Salaxul touch it for luck.
Zeh-Orun was emptied after the 3E 427 uprisings, when the mine it served was burned and its families left.
The miners buried their gold under a hall floor when the tribes came in 3E 427, and it has never been dug up. A Salaxul hunter has seen a wamasu denning under the largest hall.
A ring of rotted halls stands among the trees on sagging stilts, with creepers climbing the old walls.
Zeh-Orun is a ring of rotted halls in the trees above Old Goldseam. It housed the mine's Argonian crews and their families until the tribes burned the concession in 3E 427.
Zeh-Orun has no residents. Hunters from the Salaxul road pass through, and Old Goldseam scavengers sleep in its dry halls.
Only rotted stilts remain, with the halls above them sagging and open to the weather.
Deep water hides the old lanes and house floors, and crocodiles lie among the roof peaks. Drowning is a greater danger than any person.
Mir-Xal salvagers wade in for roof timber and iron fittings, and eel-trappers set weirs between the posts. The salvage is nearly exhausted.
A fish-bone shrine to the Hist is set on the highest roof peak by Natai fishermen who still make the offering for luck at the trap lines. No minder tends it.

Zul-Etha carted ore and timber from the concession road to the south coast. When the tribes burned the mines in 3E 427 the carts stopped, its families moved to Mir-Xal and the washes covered the street.
A Natai fisherman's trap line snagged a carved grave-stake in the drowned street, and a Mir-Xal family wants its ancestor's stake raised before the eels have it.
Three roof peaks stand out of green water, with a leaning platform and a line of stumps showing the lost lanes. The drowned posts stand in a straight line along the old street.
Zul-Etha stood between Mir-Xal and Natai on the old cart road. Three roof peaks and a leaning platform now show above green water, and Natai fishermen call it the drowned place.
Zul-Etha has no residents. Natai trappers set lines among the posts by day and go home before dark.
The village has fallen into the water: three roof peaks and a bent tree-minder's platform are all that shows. Natai fishermen call it the drowned place.
Sea-drakes work the water off the village, wreckers lurk along the shore and hidden rocks off the landing tear the bottoms out of strange boats.
Acra-Tiin sends fish and salt in small boats across the water to the Soulrest port.

Acra-Tiin's Sithis shrine is a salt-white stone at the head of the landing, and the fishermen throw a fin or tail into the sea for it before a long set. The village sends its eggs the long way round the cape by boat to the Banujha tree, and presses a shell into the shrine's clay for each clutch that goes.
Acra-Tiin was settled as a shore landing for the Soulrest port across the water, and has kept that role since.
A smuggler uses the landing after dark. One of the village's boats has gone out and not come back.
Low stilt houses stand along the shore with drying racks beside them and a boat slip at the water's edge.
Acra-Tiin is a row of low stilt houses with drying racks and a boat slip. A reeve runs it for Soulrest's council.
Acra-Tiin's households are Argonian fishers and salters who work the south shore of the cape.
Run by a reeve for the council, with little oversight from the council.
Wildlife and the odd thief are the dangers of the ruin, which stands on high ground west of Loriasel.
Once a road post on the Gideon-Stormhold way, it is now stripped of anything of value and offers only shelter.
No Hist shoot grows at this Imperial post; only a worn plinth is left of its shrine.
An Imperial road post of the Third Empire, empty since the Legion left at the secession.
A smuggler's cache under the tower; a Khajiit runner who hid moon sugar in the wall and wants it back.
A broken stone wall, a stump of a tower and an archway half-buried in mud.

Agia Nero is a Third Empire road post on the high ground west of Loriasel, on the Gideon-Stormhold way. The Empire held that road with posts and forts until the secession; this one was never re-held, as the Archwardens keep only the forts on the trunk routes.
The ruin has no residents. Scavengers and smugglers shelter in the broken walls, with a scavenger camp in one corner of the yard.
Roofless walls, a tower stump and a yard of tall reeds; a scavenger camp in the corner.
Sea-drakes offshore, unlit coast at night, raiders from the delta channels.
Amalaja sells fish and swaps it for the delta's rice. It keeps small boats for the short runs to Lilmoth's coast.

Amalaja's minder looks east: eggs go with the salt-and-rice boats toward the delta trees, and drowned fishermen are given back to the sea at the point. The Hist is honoured in a small rice-straw shrine on the dune above the boats.
Settled from Blackrose in the generations after 4E 48, when the delta villages were cleared again and has leaned toward Lilmoth in trade since.
A rice-swap dispute, a lost boat or a message for Lilmoth's merchant council.
Reed houses on a sandy headland, rice sacks under tarps, a line of fishing boats on the beach.
A village on a headland at the sea edge, one of the stage points between the lake and the delta.
Amalaja's households are Argonian fishers on the headland, with a few families born in the delta who came to marry or trade.
Its elders pay little to the island core and trade freely with Lilmoth.
Bay pirates raid the lookout at night. The watchers fire on them without warning.
Customs on boats landing at Aphon, a signal fire and a fishing boat for supplies keep the watch going.
The watchers honour Sithis and keep a small Nine shrine left from the old Imperial retreat.
Built under the Empire as a retreat; the Imperial garrison left at the secession, and a Warden customs watch now keeps it.
A smuggler's name in the customs book that the captain wants answered for, a pilot who knows the reef channels for a price or a parley with the Khajiit crew at Kelp-Mouth Cave.
A white-washed house with a verandah on a hill, a signal-lantern and a stair of rough stone.
A belvedere built as a view-house for an Imperial governor; now a customs watch.
Argonian watchers of Archein families and a Bosmer pilot keep the lookout house on Aphon Isle.
Six watchers log ships in and out of Topal Bay and signal Soulrest.

Safe inside the walls; the harbour is policed and the water is a public road. Pickpockets, drunk sailors and smugglers working the lower wharves are the usual trouble. Outside, the beaches are mostly safe.

The legal trade of the south-east: cargo handling, pilotage, bonded storage, ship chandlery, customs and the chartered privateers who stand in for a navy. Rice and fish arrive from the bayou by lighter; clay and dye come down from Aroxhu.

Sithis and the Hist as everywhere, but the nearest Hist is a small landward tree that harbour families tend; Imperial-descended residents keep a little of the Nine. Sailors leave offerings at the water stairs for those lost at sea.

Founded as an Ayleid town by the Barsaebic exiles, on ground held earlier by the Lilmothiit and the Cantemiric Velothi. Its coast was full of pirates in the late First Era until General Lucinia Falco chartered them with letters of marque. The East Empire Company ran its wharves until the secession, and the Shadowscales kept a school here that closed in 4E 187. Umbriel in 4E 48 never reached it.

The sealed Shadowscale school, which the Dark Brotherhood wants reopened and the townspeople watch, with a very old ku-vastei living near it. A privateer crew whose prize the customs officers refuse to call lawful. Underwater games a visitor can join, which teach swimming.

A low harbour town of stone wharves and timber warehouses with Company brick at the waterfront, wooden stilt houses behind and taverns whose balconies overlook the bay. Boats and swimmers fill the water; the sea smells of tar, salt and rotting weed.

A major port city on the eastern coast, marsh to the north and beaches to the south, beside an estuary that leads inland. It is the province's principal legal port and the south-east end of the Archon, Lilmoth, Soulrest and Tear trade line. Anyone arriving by sea or by the bayou channels passes through its harbour.

About four in five are Argonians, with a sizeable Dunmer minority from Tear a short sail away, a few Imperials and Khajiit and a floating population of sailors. Pilots, wharfingers, ferrymen and the merchant council hold the real authority.

The harbour authority works from the old Company wharves, bonded sheds and warehouses, which still stand and which nobody owns by right. The Archwardens' customs officers keep a post on the quay beside it.
The village itself is safe, but swamp predators raid the paddies at night.
Red-clay pottery, saltrice and a toll-free rest-house for Soulrest caravans.
Dibella charms are pressed into the pots; Sithis is thanked at the kiln-opening.

Armanias is one of the clay villages Gideon has always drawn on: it digs the Onkobra delta's red clay that Gideon's pottery is known for. It lay south of the town, off Umbriel's path in 4E 48 and has kept its kilns lit since the Imperial years.
A missing kiln-master, a pot with a hidden message or a clay seam that should not be there.
Round clay kilns smoking along the road, red mud, drying pots on racks, stilt houses beyond.
A small village of kilns and rice paddies on the coast road between Gideon and Soulrest. Its pots are famous for the red clay of the Onkobra delta.
Lukiul potters and rice-growers, with an Argonian elder who keeps the kiln-fires.
About eleven people live in stilt-and-clay houses, fire their pots in the kilns by the road and send the best to Gideon's market.
Inside the village it is calm. On the shore road to the north, mudcrab swarms and giant snakes are the daily trouble and outlaws from Skeith Isle sometimes land in the dark to take boats.

Red clay, ochre and fired pots go out by boat; salt, dried fish and Thorn's saltrice come back. The tolls Arorha charges outsiders landing on its quay pay for the mound walls. Unfired clay is cheap here, finished glazed ware costs three times as much at Thorn.
The village's hatching-tree is at Aroxhu, three days' walk inland and its eggs go there. A small clay shrine on the quay holds votive pots to the dead; broken ones are left on the shore.

The mounds were raised by the village's founders, a generation or two after the Knahaten Flu (2E 560-603) emptied the coast of Cantemiric Velothi, over ground the Velothi had left fallow. Until the secession East Empire Company boatmen called here for clay; in 4E 201 the landing is the same and the buyers are Argonian.

The elder wants a lost kiln-load of ochre found: the boat that carried it was taken by Skeith smugglers. A broken Velothi ancestor-tablet from Virtluush has turned up in the clay-pits and an old Dunmer trader will pay to know where it came from.

A ring of low red mounds, each carrying two or three reed-thatched houses on stilts, stained rust-brown by the clay. Kilns smoke at the water's edge and the shore is crazed red mud. Gulls and swamp-herons crowd the quay at dawn.

Arorha is the north-eastern outlier of the Aroxhu clay-mound country, a village on the first raised ground south of Hatandros Bight where the road from Inoja meets the sea. It exists to move the confederacy's clay, dye and pottery onto coastal boats.

About eleven Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel, mostly clay-diggers, potters and boatmen. The elder is a pot-painter who knows every kiln and every flat boat by its maker. Two or three Dunmer traders from Thorn lodge here while they buy.

A working village with a short stone-free quay of piled mud-brick and wattle where flat boats unload. Elders from Arorha sit on the Aroxhu council. The warden post at Marshgate Watch to the north takes a toll on goods bound for Thorn, and Arorha pays it.
The town is safe; the elders keep a quiet watch of spear-bearers. The road to Inoja is mostly safe, but Sarpa and Paatru bands raid the outlying mounds.
Pottery, red clay, ochre and madder dye go down the rivers to Archon and Thorn; Aroxhu takes salt, fish, metal tools and coin. The clay trade is the confederacy's wealth, and the Archwardens envy it.

The Aroxhu Hist is a young tree grown on the central mound. The elders hold the hatching rite beneath it, and eggs are laid in warm clay-pits at its roots. The dead go into the mounds beneath their houses, with their stories carved on the stake.

Raised over generations on a clay ridge above the low ground; it never held a stone wall. The Arorha and Inoja families moved up to its mounds when raiders burned their lowland villages, and it became the confederacy's centre.
A kiln-master's secret madder red has been sold to a Thorn buyer, and the council wants the thief found. Two villages dispute a mound boundary and the speaker needs a neutral go-between.

A hill of terraced red mounds topped with a great gnarled Hist, reed-thatched houses on each terrace, kilns with long streamers of smoke, drying racks of cloth in madder red and ochre yellow and a clay-paved moot-ground at the foot of the tree.

The seat of the Oxhu-Teeleel confederacy, a mound-town of red clay with a Hist at its centre, nearly forty people, a small city by the standard of the interior. The confederacy was made from many interior tribes whose names outsiders do not know.

About thirty-eight Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel: a council of seven elders (each from one village, with a speaker chosen yearly), potters, dyers, mound-farmers and boatmen and a few visiting Agaceph traders.
A busy mound-town: the council meets each new moon under the Hist, the potters' kilns burn day and night and the Archwardens must bargain for any road or toll in Oxhu country.
Crocodiles prowl the river bank at Ayiin. The odd thief works the road toward Thorn.
Quarried stone and fish, sold to Thorn's builders; Ayiin buys grain and metal tools.
A cairn takes the place of a tree; the elder reports dreams to Tsonac.
Founded as the Stone-Sleepers took the quarries of the east mesa after the Archeins' time.
A quarry cart overturned in the ford with a locked chest under it, and an elder who wants to know who has been leaving shells at Balormaak's gate, since every family in Ayiin denies it.
Squared stone houses with reed roofs on a riverbank, a stone jetty, mesa cliffs behind.
The Stone-Sleepers' eastern hamlet stands on a river below the mesa where the Kalaxo Cut quarry works. The road from it runs a day north to Thorn.
Stone-Sleeper families, a gang of quarrymen and an elder who knows every carter on the Thorn road by name and by debt.
Eight live there, working the Kalaxo Cut quarry upstream and fishing the river.
Undead guardians in the arch and snakes in the reed edge. The lower rooms are flooded and the track below is the only safe ground.
It was a small Ayleid hall. Relic-hunters from Slough Point now come to it, with the odd Fort Rustmoth soldier looking for white stone.
A cracked Ayleid shrine-stone stands at the top of the mound with Veesa-Teeleel ward-stakes ringed at its foot, leaning in.
Orimel is a small Barsaebic Ayleid hall on high ground north-west of Slough Point, one of the settlements left by the Ayleids after 1E 198. Nobody living can say who built it or how it fell.
A Vel-Sapha hunter has a carved stone from the shrine he wants rid of, and a Fort Rustmoth sergeant wants to know who keeps re-setting the mound's ward-stakes.
White arches rise from the reeds on the high ground, with vines over the fallen columns and black water in the lower rooms. The Rustmoth track runs below.

Orimel is a small Barsaebic Ayleid hall on high ground north-west of Slough Point. Canon has the Barsaebics holding parts of Blackwood, so their halls reach this far west; the name is in the Ayleid manner.
Orimel has no residents. Hunters from Vel-Sapha Stand and the Fort Rustmoth garrison patrol the track below it. Neither side goes up.
The mound's lower rooms stand in black water; Vel-Sapha Stand's people watch it from the track and the Veesa-Teeleel call it sick ground.
Undead guardians and giant snakes make the flooded ruin dangerous.
Once an Ayleid hall, it now stands unused and half-flooded in the reeds.
Fragments of an Ayleid shrine lie among the fallen arches and the vines.
Barsaebic Ayleids reached Blackwood after 1E 198, and Anutasil is one of the halls they left in the western marsh.
Umpholo reed-cutters say a white light moves in the flooded hall at night, and a Welkynd stone lies on the stair below the water.
White arches stand half-covered in vine above black water in the western marsh.

Anutasil is a Barsaebic Ayleid hall in the western marsh, the furthest west of their halls in the province. Canon has the Barsaebics holding parts of Blackwood after 1E 198; the name is of Ayleid form.
Anutasil has no residents. Umpholo reed-cutters see its arches from their flats and keep clear, and the odd Meliton-bound traveller sleeps in its dry corner.
The ruin in the western marsh is half-flooded and avoided by everyone nearby.
Giant snakes in the reeds and undead guardians below the arch; the undercroft stairs go down under black water.
It was a minor hall of the Ayleid settlement. Scavengers and relic-hunters now come from Jal-Veesa by the Teel-Fen creek.
A worn Ayleid altar sits under a vine on the island's crown, ringed by Veesa-Teeleel ward-stakes set facing in.
Mirasel is a small Barsaebic Ayleid hall on a sedge island east of Loriasel, from the settlement that grew in the region after 1E 198. The weir-wardens say it fell with Loriasel.
A Jal-Veesa relic-seller will pay for the altar's Welkynd stone, and a Teel-Fen warden says a ward-stake on the west side has been pulled.
White arches stand in sedge with a fallen column lying across a black pool; the undercroft stairs go down into the water.
Mirasel is a Barsaebic Ayleid hall on a sedge island east of Loriasel, one of the small halls that ringed the Barsaebic citadel; its name is the Ayleid form of Loriasel's.
Mirasel has no residents. Weir-wardens from Reed-Sill and Teel-Fen see its white arches on their rounds and have never seen a visitor stay.
The island is half-flooded and the Veesa-Teeleel of Reed-Sill Weir, a few cells to the north-east, will not go onto it and tell visitors it is sick ground.
Slaughterfish swim in the inlet by the landing. The odd crocodile comes down to drink there.
Red-clay pottery, dyes and pigments, saltrice; carried down the river to Archon and Thorn.
They bury and hatch at Aroxhu's Hist; the villagers keep clay figures of ancestors on the mound crest.
Settled by mound-builders from the confederacy of Aroxhu, who found the clay banks of the inlet; the village's mounds lift it out of the wet ground.
A potter's master-glaze pot gone missing from the kiln; a dye vat spoiled by something in the water; a quarrel with Aroxhu over who digs the best clay bank.
A ring of raised red-clay mounds with thatched halls on top, kilns and clay pits, drying racks of dyed cloth and a landing on the inlet.
A village of the Clay-Mound people at the north edge of the Nushara Bayou, where the east road meets the Okuwun-Rahei clay country.
Oxhu-Teeleel Argonians, with Three Waters traders and Archon dye-buyers as visitors.
About twelve households farm the mound slopes, fire pots and dye cloth; a council of elders speaks to the Aroxhu elders and to Three Waters traders.
Ghosts and skeletons in the halls, cliff-nesting hackwings outside and a water-filled lowest hall where slaughterfish have been trapped.
Once a fortified holding that took tolls from coastal boats. Now it draws scavengers: Velothi bronze, ash-glass and carved ancestor tablets sell at Thorn to Dunmer buyers.

The Velothi who came south followed the Mephala-led exile and kept ancestor veneration. Tablets and altar niches remain in the upper halls; the Argonians who pass by say the place is sick and do not leave offerings.

Cantemiric Velothi, Dunmer dissidents who settled the eastern seaboard, held this coast until the Knahaten Flu (2E 560-603) killed them all. The hold has stood empty since. Chimeri myth says Mephala led a third of the Velothi into Black Marsh.

A Dunmer relic-seller in Thorn will pay for the ancestor tablet carved with the family sign of the holding's last lord. The door to the lowest hall is barred from within, and the lord's ghost carries the key.
Grey basalt and black volcanic stone in heavy, battered Velothi courses, crusted with barnacles and salt at the base. A broken tower stands on the rock at the end of a causeway of piled stone.
A ruined Velothi hold on the rock off the Thorn coast, the nearest of the Hatandros Bight ruins to the city.
No living inhabitants. Ancestor ghosts of the Velothi walk the halls, for the Velothi buried their dead beneath their houses and the flu killed whole families at once.

Empty except for the dead. Thorn's slavers, until the Red Year and later the Warden Marches' toll men both kept away from it. The coast Argonians call it sick ground. The lowest hall stands knee-deep in still black water.
Skeletons of the flu-dead walk the cellars under the vines. The open cellars hold standing water to the knee and skeevers in the silt.
Once a farming and stone town; now a store of old ironwork and clay goods for scavengers.
The Velothi followed Mephala; Ayiin's people call the ground sick and leave a shell at its gate.
A Velothi settlement dead of the Knahaten Flu in 2E 560-603; Ayiin's people use its dressed stone and tell children it is empty of ghosts.
An Ayiin child dropped her egg-charm, a carved shell on a cord, into a cellar while hiding from her brothers and a Velothi bronze bell lies in the fallen tower that a Thorn smith will pay well for.
Dunmer stone houses with scalloped roofs and a standing bell-tower stump, wrapped in vines.
A Cantemiric Velothi ruin on the eastern mesa, one of the Velothi towns of this country, half buried under vine and silt south of Ayiin.
The ruin has no living inhabitants. Ayiin's hunters cross it by day and turn back before dark.
Broken walls and open cellars under vine, half-full of silt from the rains; scavengers visit from Thorn.
The platform is safe; below it the spires hold dreugh, and a diver's breath runs out in the deep.

Salvage from the spires: bronze, vakka stones, jewellery and brass; Lilmoth merchants buy the finds, and the steward sets aside the council's share of each haul in kind before the crew sells the rest.
Divers pray to the Hist and the drowned before descent; none carry Hist amulets, for the tree cannot hear them here.

Built in the generations after 4E 48, when divers working Lilmoth's ruined waterfront found the spires of the land that sank in the Dawn Era; Lilmoth's merchant council sent a crew of delta kin to the platform to bring the salvage up for it.
A diver who failed to come up; a diver who wants a find kept off the steward's scale; a bell hauled up with something clinging to it.
A timber platform on pilings with winches, copper bells hanging on chains, drying diving gear, bunks in a hut and a lantern mast.
A working platform at sea, east of Lilmoth, whose diving bells reach the drowned spires. No other settlement stands in Benthic Yobesh.
Argonian bell-divers, a steward of the Archein line and a few hired Khajiit and Imperial specialists.
Eight crew live on the platform: bell-tenders, divers, a winch-master and a steward who weighs every find and takes the council's share of each haul.
Inside, guarded and watchful; the lake margins hold gar and crocodilians; the boardwalks' feuds are real. The marsh around has rebel earthworks, Lilmothiit dens and Rose-bred outlaws on the roads.
Tolls and transit at the three-river confluence, lake commerce by canoe, fish and reeds and whatever comes out of the Rose by water or by raft.
Hist drowned in the lake, with the island core controlling hatching and naming; Sithis shrines on the boardwalks; a Lilmothiit-era sense of the ground as owned by the dead.

Built by the Lilmothiit; Kothringi and Yespest lived nearby. Red Bramman's bandit kingdom stood here around 1E 1033. The Imperial rebuild followed 1E 2837; the 2E rumoured it ruined; the city raised an army against the Third Empire and was broken by the battlemage Welloc's vampiric cloud.

Lilmothiit foundations under the island core, the drowned Hist's dive, the quarrel with the Rose, Welloc's vampiric cloud and what the rebel army left behind and a smuggler contact for Bramman's river.

A walled island core of stone, most of the city over the lake on stilt and boardwalk districts raised well above the water, shore quarters at the feeder mouths, canoes everywhere, mist off the water at dawn.
A major city in a lake in south-central Black Marsh where three rivers converge. The Rose lies off in the marsh and is not the city's, though outsiders assume it is.
Argonian-majority, with prison staff families, ex-prisoners, deserters, refugees and coerced migrants. Distrust of battlemages and of the Rose runs through all of them.

Functioning but diminished, with ruined and rebuilt quarters of several ages and old siege earthworks in the marsh from Welloc's campaign. The island core holds the toll and the hatching. Its Hist lies drowned in the lake, reached only by boat and dive.
Blackguard bands above, Naga and undead below and a sanctum path left open to test challengers.
Highway tolls and robbery, stripping the old Imperial settlements around it, smuggling through Blackrose's channels.
Sithis and a Naga raj-kaal's necromantic rites; the old Hist tradition is absent behind these walls.

Raised by Pelladil Direnni with stone atronachs for Potentate Versidue-Shaie, abandoned in the Second Empire's fall, held by the inmates' descendants, reclaimed by the Third Empire and broken again late in the Third Era. When the Empire left at the secession, the inmates' heirs took it a third time.
A quest to break in, to bargain with the raj-kaal, to find what Jagar Tharn's last associates left or to learn why the Rose is not the city's.
A grey stone fortress of Lilmothiit rubble, part-flooded, with bastions the marsh has crept into and Blackguard banners and fires on the upper wall.
The Imperial prison, 'the Rose', a day's march from Blackrose city. It is a ruin reoccupied by the Blackguards' heirs.
Blackguards' heirs, escapees' descendants, exiles and outlaws, Naga allies and a few dozen hangers-on. They raid the roads and trade quietly with the lake villages.
Held by Blackguard families many generations deep and a Naga raj-kaal who resent the word prison. The upper walls are their stronghold. The lower levels are held by the undead.
Wild predators roam the empty stilts. Scavengers from Toklea's rival towns raid the footings for stone and metal.
Toklea's people strip Bucalos for salvage, hauling its stone and metal across to build and mend their own town.
The Chime-Keepers' custom of hanging bead strings on the doorposts survives at Bucalos as rotting cord. Its minder moved to Toklea with the people, so the shrine here is left to the damp.
A Kothringi town before 2E 560, resettled by Argonians and left empty in the generations since.
Footings that hide a Kothringi cache; a ghostly chime-singer.
Stone footings, a half-fallen hall, rusted chimes and green moss.
Bucalos is a set of stone footings, a half-fallen hall and rusted chimes under green moss. Toklea's people quarry its stone.
Bucalos holds no residents, only Toklea fishermen who tie up at its landing in bad weather and a family of eel-trappers who camp on the southern platforms when the water drops.
Stone footings and a collapsed hall; Toklea's people quarry its stone.
Sarpa archers shoot from the ledges inside the mouth, and spearmen hold the narrow passage behind. A rockfall trap guards the nest gallery.
It serves as a larder and nest, with a little hoarded loot from raided travellers.
The Sarpa keep to the Hist of High-Flower, their own tree; eggs are carried there for the hatching.
A natural cave hunters have known for generations; the Sarpa took it when their warband settled the mesa edge, and every visitor since has had to fight to go in.
A clutch of Stone-Sleeper eggs carried off from Oxayo and kept in the nest gallery, and a Sarpa elder in the back chamber who will talk instead of fight if a visitor comes in with no weapon drawn.
A wide crack in the mesa wall with bone heaps and feathers at the mouth, nests on its ledges.
Sahlpesh Cave is a wide cave in the mesa's western wall beside the Sarpa camp, the warband's larder and nest. Sahlpesh is what the Stone-Sleepers of Oxayo call it.
Sarpa Argonians, a winged breed hostile to outsiders and their young.
Used by the Sarpa warband from the nearby camp as a cold store and a roost; it holds their kills and their eggs.
The crew fight anyone who finds them, and the flooded inner chamber is a long swim with slaughterfish in it.
The cave is a store for moon sugar in transit, which is illegal in the province and for salvage the crew pulls from wrecks in the bay.
A Khajiit charm of moon-shaped shell hangs in the cave mouth above the kelp, for the crew's safe sailing under Jone and Jode.
Pirates have used the coves of Topal Bay since Red Bramman's day. This cave is the one on Aphon that the Warden watch at the Belvedere cannot see, which is why the present crew chose it.
The crew's moon sugar waiting for a Gideon buyer, an Argonian pilot who wants out of the crew or the Warden captain at the Belvedere wanting the cave cleared.
A low black cave mouth hung with kelp, a rock ledge with a rope ladder and an inner pool lit green from below by the light through a sea-cut tunnel.
A sea-cut cave on Aphon Isle's eastern shore, on the side away from the Belvedere. Its outer chamber is dry; its inner chamber is flooded and reached by swimming.
Khajiit sailors out of Senchal under a captain who has worked the bay for years, with one Argonian pilot from Olvani who knows the reef.
A Khajiit crew of six land moon sugar from Senchal here and keep it until Gideon's buyers send a boat. They have a sloop moored out of sight in the cave mouth.
Highwaymen on the Percar road, burn-scar gas east of the village.
Chasepoint lives by carting on the Percar road, salvage from wrecks, inns for travellers and the tolls that it collects.

Chasepoint's Sithis shrine is a plain stone slab beside the carters' yard where drivers pour a drop of oil before a night run. Its hatchlings go inland by cart once a year to the Banujha tree, and the shrine keeper remembers every egg that went.
A road stage of the Third Era timber trade, Soulrest's eastern neighbour.
A cart gone missing, a salvage dispute, a smuggler's drop for Bramman's river.
Timber and stone stilt houses on a spit, carts under sheds, a salvage yard of ship timber.
Chasepoint is a spit of timber and stone stilt houses with carts under sheds and a salvage yard of ship timber. Soulrest's merchant council rules it and takes its toll.
Argonian carters, wreck-salvagers and a few Imperial-descended families who run the inn and the yard.
Chasepoint answers to Soulrest's merchant council, which takes a toll on the carts and goods that pass the village.
Crocodilians lie in the delta channel beside the raft. Outlaws watch the road on either approach to the landing.
The raft earns fares from travellers on the Lilmoth road and carries rice in freight across the delta channel.
The ferrymen have hung a carved gar-tooth on the landing post as a gift to Sithis, and every ferryman raps it once before casting off.
Rebuilt in the generations after 4E 48, when Lilmoth was rebuilt and the Blackrose road was reopened.
Smugglers hiding goods in rice sacks; a message to be carried.
A plank landing runs out to a winch raft, and a lamp post at the end guides the crossing after dark.
A ferry landing on the delta channel on the road to Lilmoth.
The landing is worked by Argonian ferrymen, who live with their families in huts beside the raft on the delta bank.

The ferry-folk are kin to Lilmoth's boatmen and keep the crossing with the merchant council's goodwill: the council's barges are let past free, and in return its water-guards keep the landing at either bank.
Dreugh, drowning where a diver's breath runs out and cold; sounds that draw divers over the edge.
It has no trade; it is the edge of what salvage can reach and the reason the nearby spires are not yet stripped.
Argonians hold the trench to be a place where the drowned dwell, and the old Hist sings them down.
Probably the drowned edge of the land the Hist's domain lost to the sea; Argonian legend says Murkmire was swallowed by the Southern Sea.
A diver who followed the echo down and came up silent; a sealed spire at its bottom; a dreugh lair on the rim.
A wall of black water on the sea floor, cold and dark, with sound returning from below.
A deep trench in the sea floor in the middle of Benthic Yobesh; its name is the Bell Station divers'.
The trench has no inhabitants. Divers speak of voices; Argonian divers say it is the old Hist singing.
Divers avoid it; the bell-tenders at Bell Station refuse to lower below the rim.
Slaughterfish and young crocodilians live in the dykes, and thieves use the road that crosses the estate to Lilmoth. The family's hunters and dogs keep the house itself safe.
Rice for Lilmoth's market and the lighters, with a little sugar-cane pressed for rum. The steward sells cooked rice and rice-wine from the veranda to travellers on the road.

Hatchlings are carried to Lilmoth's young Hist tree for naming, though the people of Lilmoth watch that tree with open fear. On the veranda a post holds rice-wine poured out for the Breton dead, whose bones lie in the old cellar.

Breton planters laid out the paddies on the Hereguard model in the Third Era and were gone long before the secession, leaving the house to rot. In the generations after 4E 48 a family from rebuilt Lilmoth patched the roof, cleared the dykes and planted again.
The family has walled up the old cellar, where the planters' strongbox lies and the unstaked Breton dead are not at rest. A rival family claims the east dykes and has cut the sluice twice.
A long plank house on posts with a tiled roof, paddies like green mirrors, a boat landing and a bell on a post.
A rice estate north-west of Lilmoth, built in an old planter's house and held by one Argonian family and their tenants.
Eight Argonians of two kin-lines: the landholder, her brothers and their mates and hatchlings. Tenant kin from Lilmoth come for the planting.
Eight people live in the great house and the huts beside it; paddies run toward the road.
Hired guards and dogs watch the barn, and the reed channels hide mudcrabs and slaughterfish. Thieves at night are the usual trouble, since the north road is busy.
The estate grows rice and reed and hires out its boats to the Lilmoth harbour.

The family and its tenants carry their eggs to Lilmoth's tree for hatching and naming. A small post of woven reed at the channel landing holds offerings for the water-spirits, left before every cutting.

The Archein planters who built the house left it empty in the Third Era. In the first generation after 4E 48 the family moved in, salvaging beams and fittings from the drowned Imperial quarter of Lilmoth to make it sound.
A salvage chest from the drowned quarter lies hidden in the cellar, and the family will not say whose it was. A cousin who left for the Warden fort has come back wanting a share of the boats.
Low thatched halls on stilts, a large rice-barn and reed-lined channels.
A rice and reed estate on the road north of Lilmoth, in an Archein planter's house that an Argonian family now holds.
An Argonian landholder lives with his kin and the tenant families who cut the reeds and work the paddies.
Six people live on the estate; the family hires out its boats to the harbour.
Sentries on the veranda and dogs guard the barn, and the shore dykes shelter crocodilians. Idle hands from Fort Reedmoth and smugglers using the landing at night are the likelier trouble.
The rice goes by lighter to Archon and Lilmoth. The estate hires out its oarsmen to Fort Reedmoth's keepers.
The tenants carry their eggs to Lilmoth's tree for hatching and naming. The lighter crews touch a post at the landing before each crossing, a habit older than the family.

The Archein planters left the house derelict in the Third Era, and Fort Reedmoth beside it passed from the Legion at the secession to ex-Archein families who keep it in the Archwardens' name. In the generations after 4E 48 a family from the Lilmoth coast moved into the house and replanted the paddies.
The steward hides a kinsman who ran from Fort Reedmoth's keepers and wants him gone before they ask. A lighter of rice has not reached Archon, and its crew say nothing.
A square two-storey house of timber and brick with a veranda, a rice-barn, a landing and tall palms.
A rice estate on the south shore of the northern island, close to Fort Reedmoth.
An Argonian landholder, his mate and hatchlings, a steward and a few tenant kin.
Six people live in the house and the quarters beside the landing.
Slaughterfish hunt the shallows along the shore, and the low shore is open to anything that lands from a boat.
The family grows roots and gourds and keeps fowl, and sends the roots and eggs to Karketa.
The family carries its eggs and its dead to Lilmoth's tree, a long boat journey north and sees the Hist rarely. By the door a post hung with shells stands for sailors drowned on the southern shoals.

Ixa-Ruu was cleared in the generations after 4E 48, when families spread back to the southern tip of the island. Southwatch Keep stands close by and its keepers have watched the shore since before the farm.
A hawker offers odd things from wrecks on the southern shoals. A lost fowl has wandered into a hollow among the wreck timbers.
A thatched stilt house, a garden of gourds on a rise and chicken coops.
A family of three keeps Ixa-Ruu, a thatched stilt house with a gourd garden on a rise and chicken coops. Patrols from Southwatch Keep are welcomed at the door.
A family of three keeps Ixa-Ruu, which stands alone at the island's southern tip.
The family sells roots and eggs at Karketa and mends its own thatch. Patrols from the keep are welcomed at the door; others are watched from the garden rise.
Crocodiles and giant snakes from the marsh edge come for the guar at night, so the paddock is stockaded.
The farm sells guar meat and hide and reed-roots at Lilmoth.
Seeku's family carries its eggs to Lilmoth's young tree and its dead to burial, an easy walk east. Beside the paddock gate a reed post holds the horns of guar killed by predators.

Seeku was cleared in the generations after 4E 48, on the firm ground west of Lilmoth that the town's rebuilders left to smallholders. The guar stock came from the first family's marsh-guar, bred up over the years.
A guar has not come back from the marsh edge. A stranger asks to rent the barn and will not say why.
A low house, a guar paddock with a stockade and fences of reed.
A family of four keeps Seeku: a low house, a stockaded guar paddock and a vegetable plot, a short walk from Lilmoth's tree.
A family of four keeps Seeku, tending the guar and a vegetable plot.
The family keeps the guar paddock stockade in repair and drives animals to Lilmoth's market. They know their neighbours on the road and keep watch for anyone who loiters near the pens.
Slaughterfish swim in the pond. Wasps nest in the fruit trees.
The family lives on fruit from its trees, fish from the pond and honey from a few hives.
The family carries its eggs and its dead to Lilmoth's tree. At the pool's edge a driftwood post with a fish-bone string marks the water-spirit they thank before netting.

Wattle-Pool was cleared in the generations after 4E 48, on the island's firm centre where a spring-fed pool made fishing and fruit possible. The wattle ring round the pool is the work of the first couple, who kept slaughterfish out of the shallows.
The honey from the hive by the old stump tastes of sap and sends those who eat it to sleep. A stranger has been sleeping in the shed.
A small stilt house, fruit trees and a pond ringed with wattle.
A couple and a child keep Wattle-Pool, a small stilt house among fruit trees beside a pond ringed with wattle. They sell honey and fruit at the nearest village.
A couple and their child keep Wattle-Pool, a small family on the isle's firm centre.
The couple tend the fruit trees and hives and net the pool in turn. They sell honey and fruit at the nearest village, and a stranger who sleeps in their shed is sent off by morning.
Road bandits and passing soldiers both trouble the farm on the island road.
The farm sends rice and eggs to the cook-house of Fort Reedmoth.

The family sends its hatchlings to Lilmoth's tree and buries its dead at Sal-Axan's moot ground when the road is clear. A post by the door is hung with scraps of soldiers' cloth, left for travellers who died on the road.
Tal-Neesh was cleared in the generations after 4E 48, on the island road between Sal-Axan and Fort Reedmoth. It grew by supplying the fort's cook-house, and the family has outlasted three keepers.
A soldier wants rice on credit and will not say who sent him. A bandit has stuck a knife in the barn post as a warning to pay.
A low plain house stands beside a rice-paddy, with a woodpile against its wall.
A family of three keeps Tal-Neesh, a low plain house with a rice-paddy and a woodpile. It sells rice and eggs to the keepers of Fort Reedmoth.
A family of three keeps Tal-Neesh and sells its crops to the keepers of Fort Reedmoth.
The family sells rice and eggs to the fort's cooks and bars its door at night against the road. Soldiers pass and trade on credit; the family remembers every sack owed.
Mudcrabs on the pans and smugglers passing on the road.
Sea-salt boiled in clay pans, sedge for roofing and hardy marsh vegetables. The family sells to Seafalls.
They go to Seafalls for the death-dances and keep a painted shell at the door.
A Seafalls family cleared it for growing the food they cannot fish.
The youngest child has found a smuggler's cache in the pans and is afraid to tell anyone.
Flat grey salt-pans, stacked sedge, a single reed house on a mound, drying racks and a boiling shed with a stack.
A farm on the salt flats inland of Seafalls, where the household raises salt-tolerant rice and fowl for the harbour.
Three Argonians of Seafalls live here, a mother and her two grown children.
A working holding that sells its salt and sedge to Seafalls.
Crocodiles in the paddy, marsh predators for the herd and smuggler thieves.
Guar hide, milk and rice, sold at Seafalls. A few of the herd go to Archon on the pilots' boats.
They keep a clay guar at the door and leave the sea's old stories to the village.
Founded by a Seafalls family who fell out with the pilot-elder and wanted their own ground.
A guar has been taken and tracks lead toward the Vicrium mine. The family carries an old grudge against the pilot-elder.
A green meadow with guar, a rice paddy, a reed house on a low mound, a clay fence and salt wind.
A guar farm on the meadow between Seafalls and the Khiar road.
Four Argonians of Seafalls keep the meadow: two adults and two hatchlings.
A small guar herd and a rice paddy, with a path to Seafalls.
Marsh predators come up the channel bank to the paddies and the boat landing, so the family keeps watch at night.
The farm grows rice in its paddies, cuts reeds along the channel bank and takes fish for its own table and the market.
A household shrine to Sithis; hatchlings go to the Lilmoth tree.
The land was cleared from marsh in the generations after 4E 48. The family has farmed the channel bank since.
One paddy is failing for no clear reason. The family's boat has gone missing from the landing.
A stilted house stands above the paddies on the channel bank, with a rice shed beside it for the harvest.

A family rice farm on the channel bank on the road to Tei-Kur, named Reedfall for the reed beds that lean over its landing. The family sells its rice to Blackrose and the travellers on the Lilmoth road.
The household is a single Argonian farming family, with hatchlings and elders living under one stilted roof.
One Argonian family runs the whole farm, working the paddies and selling the harvest at Tei-Kur and Delta Ferry.
Crocodiles lie in the irrigation ditch. A thief sometimes comes up the valley road at night. Stormhold's patrols ride past the farm.
Saltrice and eels carried to Stormhold on the causeway; the family pays the causeway toll at the post like any carter.
Ancestor stones by the door and a Hist shoot in a clay pot, the family's one concession to both.
A smallholding on raised ground since the Dunmer colonial period; the family has worked it through the generations since.
A missing son who went to the Silyanorn tunnels for crystal; a stranger who asks to rent the barn for a week.
A long stone barn and a two-storey mud-plaster house on a mound ringed by paddy dikes and a stone causeway.

Vandrel Farm is one of the Dunmer-descended smallholdings that ring Stormhold: Stormhold has the oldest Dunmer minority in the province, descended from the colonial slave-trade years and its families farm the raised causeway ground south of the city. The name is Dunmeri, like the family's.
Dunmer-descended farmer, his Argonian wife and children; seasonal Argonian field labour.
One household and two hired hands work a few flooded fields and a stone barn on a mound.
Wildlife in the ditches and fields is the only danger at this quiet farm.
The farm sends saltrice and eels to Stormhold along the northern road.
Ancestor stones from the Dunmer side of the family stand by the house, beside a Hist shoot from the Argonian side.
A smallholding on raised ground west of Jal-Veesa, beside the northern road.
A traveller asks to rent the Urvyns' barn for a few nights, and the Argonian wife has seen him by the Gandranen creek at dusk.
A stone barn and a stone house stand on a mound that lifts the farm above the flooded fields.

Urvyn Farm is a Dunmer-descended family's smallholding west of Jal-Veesa, the furthest of the Stormhold causeway farms; it stands where the northern road lifts out of the reed beds. The family has a Dunmeri name, from the city's old minority.
A Dunmer-descended farmer and his Argonian wife of the Urvyn family keep the farm.
One household works a few flooded fields beside the northern road, with a stone barn on a mound.
The garrison holds the walls and the road, and Sarpa raids come to its western approach.
The garrison of Fort Chalkmoth lives on tolls from the mesa road and on a share of the chalk that its carters take on to Thorn.
No Hist; the garrison goes to Noota Nara's tree for hatching and burial.
The Empire built it to guard the chalk and limestone working beside it. The Legion left at the secession (4E 5-10), and an ex-Archein family has kept the keys in the Archwardens' name since.
A garrison captain whose chalk cart and its driver vanished on the western road, and a cellar wall that rings hollow where the Legion's masons bricked up something older.
Pale grey stone walls dusted white with chalk, a gatehouse and a square watch tower on a mesa shoulder.
An Imperial fort named in the Legion's '-moth' style, in 4E 201 a toll and watch post across the mesa.
Argonian garrison families of old Archein lines, with a Dunmer quartermaster.
A dozen at most man it; they take a toll on the chalk carts that leave the mesa and keep watch on the Sarpa to the west.
A fortified post is safe inside; outside lies open water and boat-robbers; the chain and the garrison's tempers are the usual hazards.
A toll on lake boats. The garrison buys food from Yalugo and fish from Luntoc.
The fort has no Hist, so the garrison goes home to a village tree to hatch and bury; a small stone chapel of the Nine, empty but swept, is kept out of habit.

Built by the Empire as a lake post on the interior boat road. The Legion left at the secession (4E 5–10). Archein families took the keys and kept the toll in the Archwardens' name, as at the other forts.
A boat paid the toll at dusk and was never seen to leave the lake; a cellar under the keep has been bricked shut since the Legion left; Truowa's council would pay to see the garrison replaced.
A squat stone keep and curtain wall on an islet, mossed and re-roofed in reed, a toll chain across the channel and a signal lantern on the tower.
Fort Gysilla is a small stone fort on an islet at the lake's southern end, one of the Empire's old posts now garrisoned by Archein families in the Archwardens' name.
About ten: Archein families who still keep Imperial-style ranks and drill, and a few grandchildren of freed labourers who row the toll boats.
A garrison of about ten keeps the toll and watch for the Archwardens, who barely supervise it. It is cool with Truowa's council and in a standing quarrel with Yalugo over the price of grain.
The garrison turns on anyone who runs the chain, smugglers land at night on the east shingle and mud-crocodiles lie in the marsh round the island road.
Tolls on the road and the strait; fish and rice bought from Sal-Axan. The quartermaster sells the surplus to travellers.
No Hist grows at the fort; the garrison goes to Lilmoth to hatch its young, name them and bury its dead.
Built by the Legion with a '-moth' name. The Legion left at the secession, 4E 5-10 and the Archwardens have kept the fort since.
A smuggler's tip about a night landing on the east shingle. A quarrel over the toll with the Three Waters families, who say the chain is theirs by older right.
A low square fort of stone and timber with a tower, a toll chain across the channel and a moss-grown wall.
A stone fort held as a toll station and watch on the east end of the northern island, facing Archon's coast across the strait.
Argonian garrison families, some Archein-line officers, no Imperials. The Three Waters raft-families come through often and know every man at the gate.
Ten men of Archein descent keep the gate, take tolls on the road and the strait and check cargo for the Warden customs. They hold the keys in the Archwardens' name.
The fort is guarded and safe inside; wildlife and hackwings are the hazard on the Blackwood Road outside its walls.
Tolls on the Blackwood Road, a levy on goods bound for Gideon and Leyawiin and fines on smugglers.
No Hist: Imperial foundation. The garrison hatch and bury at village trees.
Built by the Third Empire to command the Blackwood Road; not Imperial since the secession, when the Legion left and an ex-Archein family took the keys in the Archwardens' name.
A captain who has been paid not to look at a cart; a barracks storeroom short of arrows and armour, and a sergeant who says the captain is selling them to the Sul-Xan.
A square stone keep with corner towers and a yard, the Imperial eagle over the gate, a moat that is now a reed pond.

Fort Rustmoth belongs to the Legion's '-moth' series of forts. The Third Empire's Fort Swampmoth stood on the same road between Slough Point and Gideon, and Rustmoth fits that placement and may be the same fort under a later name.
Argonian soldiers under an old Archein-lineage captain; a few Nibenese families in the kitchens.
Held, but not by the Empire: an Archwarden garrison charges the road toll and the customs on goods bound for Gideon and Leyawiin, with the old Imperial drill.
Bay pirates test the fort's landing at night, and slaughterfish crowd the rocks below its sea wall.
The garrison collects tolls and keeps a ferry for its own needs.
The soldiers honour Sithis and keep a small shrine to the Nine.
The Legion built it to guard the harbour approach to Soulrest. Its Imperial garrison left at the secession, and Archein families have held it in the Archwardens' name since.
A smuggler in the lock-up, a missing log or a captain bribed.
Grey stone walls on the shore, a signal tower and a sea-gate.
A small stone fort at the mouth of Topal Bay near Soulrest, one of the '-moth' forts.
Argonian soldiers of Archein descent garrison the fort, with a Khajiit pilot.
Eight soldiers log shipping and collect tolls; they co-operate with Soulrest's merchant council.
Safe on the road; the fort has been attacked by Naga raiders and bay pirates. The captain closes the road to a traveller who gives a wrong word.
Tolls, a fort farm of saltrice and a barracks market that sells salt and iron to travellers.
Sithis in private, the Nine in old habit; there is a small Imperial shrine to Zenithar the quartermaster still kept.

The Legion built it as a road fort. The Imperial garrison left at the secession, and the Archein families who had served in it stayed and held the gate in the Archwardens' name, so the same toll is taken at the same bar under a new banner.
A trader who swears he paid the toll last time, a smuggler held in the stockade whom Gideon wants handed over and a captain whose family once owned the land under Gideon's south gardens.
Grey stone walls and a tower at a road bend, moss on the parapet, a toll chain across the road, reeds all around and a flag of the successor state.
A small stone fort on the Gideon-Soulrest road, one of the '-moth' forts of the old Legion naming. In 4E 201 it is the Archwardens' toll post and river-watch at the southern approach to Gideon.
Argonian soldiers of Archein-descended families, under a captain who still gives orders in Cyrodiilic. The fort has no Hist; the soldiers go home to a village tree to hatch and bury.

Eight soldiers man it, take a toll from traders at the bar across the road and watch the coast for bay pirates. They are courteous to Gideon's merchants and wary of the Mine-Burners' carts from the basin.
A smugglers' watch holds the cellars, mud-crocodiles lie in the ditch round the rise and the stair-tower is broken above the first landing.
It makes nothing. The stores of the dead garrison, a few rusted Imperial arms and a smugglers' cache are what draw people.
Imperial forts carry no Hist; a bare stone shrine to the Nine on the ground floor has long gone to moss.
Built by the Legion as a road fort in the '-moth' manner. The Legion left at the secession, 4E 5-10 and no one has held the keep since.
A smugglers' cache waiting to be moved. A locked cellar door below the old garrison's strongroom. A faded Imperial banner still hangs in the upper hall.
A square stone keep with a broken stair-tower, green with moss and vine, on a low rise in the reeds with a paving fragment at the gate.
A stone keep outside the Archwardens' garrison network, on firm ground on the road inland from Archon.
No garrison. Aroxhu families rest in the upper floor on their road, smugglers use the cellars as a cache and an old ex-privateer keeps a room as his home.
The fort is unheld. Part of the roof is gone, and the upper floor is dry enough to sleep on. Fort Reedmoth keeps a garrison; this keep has none.
The garrison keeps the road. Bribery and smuggled goods make the gate a place to be careful with money more than with a blade.
Tolls on carts, boats and travellers entering Thorn from the jungle and the south; a share goes to the Archwardens and the rest stays in the fort.
The fort has no Hist, so its people go home to the village tree to hatch and bury; a small Imperial shrine in the yard is kept up out of habit.

The Empire built it to protect Thorn and its saltrice trade, and it kept an Imperial garrison until the Legion left at the secession (4E 5-10). An ex-Archein family took the keys then and has held it in the Archwardens' name since.

A captain who wants an outsider to carry a word to Thorn without passing the gate, a guard who lets a certain cart through untouched every few days and a locked store room full of moon sugar the garrison took from smugglers and has not burned.

Square grey stone walls and a gatehouse on a low rise above the shore, with the Imperial banner gone and Argonian reed-cord pennants in its place; a toll bar across the road and a jetty for the watch boat.

A fort beside Thorn on the western approach, named in the Legion's '-moth' style. In 4E 201 it is a toll station, river watch and the south end of the frontier screen facing Morrowind. It stands a short way west of the town.

Argonian garrison families of old Archein lines, led by a captain who answers to the Archwardens and dines with Thorn's Vicecanons. A Dunmer quartermaster keeps the store, and Dunmer drivers wait at the gate with their carts.

A dozen at most man it: a watch captain, gate guards who take the toll and a few who keep the store room and the watch boat. The captain still drills them in the Legion's way, a habit the garrison kept from Imperial days.
The post is guarded; outside the gate there is road-side wildlife and the odd thief.
Tolls on the road and the river, a levy on Dunmer and Argonian goods crossing to Morrowind and a small market of traders who camp outside the walls.
No Hist: Imperial forts carry none. The garrison go home to a village tree to hatch and bury.

Built by the Third Empire as a border fort beside Stormhold. The Legion marched out at the secession (4E 5-10), and an ex-Archein family took the keys and has held the fort in the Archwardens' name since.
A Dunmer trader's raft held at the gate for a cargo of slaves' shackles nobody will explain; a tower watchman who sees fires in the Morrowind hills and is not believed.
A squat grey Imperial stone fort with a gate, a yard and a watch-tower; moss climbs the walls and the old Imperial relief is still over the gate. A wooden jetty and toll-bar sit on the road outside.
Fort Willowmoth is one of the Legion's '-moth' forts, named in the same style as Swampmoth, Moonmoth and Frostmoth. It stands a short walk east of Stormhold.
Argonian soldiers under a captain of an ex-Archein family; the captain answers to the Archwardens for the tolls and the screen, and keeps on terms with Stormhold's Vicecanons.

A garrison of a few Archwarden soldiers takes the road and river tolls and watches the crossing to Morrowind. The ranks and drill are half Cyrodiilic, kept by the old Archein family that holds the keys.
The Fenlord's undead slave-guardians walk the tomb halls. The library's own wards guard its shelves.
Once a library and tomb; now a treasure for scholars and thieves.
Hermaeus Mora and the Fenlord's death-cult; the Veesa-Teeleel avoid it.
Built by a sorceress of Hermaeus Mora to attract books; the halls drew in The Lusty Argonian Maid and Ruminations on the Elder Scrolls. Zahra entered about 2E 582 to find the Crown of Ascension.
A book that should not exist in the library; the Fenlord's vault.
A half-sunk pale-stone ruin on a reed island among black water; shelf-lined halls in the dry part.
Gandranen is a Barsaebic Ayleid ruin in Shadowfen: a library of magical halls that draws books from any time, and a Fenlord's tomb crawling with undead slave-guardians.
The ruin has no residents. An occasional scholar comes to the library, while the Fenlord's undead keep the tomb.
Volumes still turn up on its shelves; the Fenlord's undead guards still walk the tomb.
Lake crocodiles, slaughterfish in the shallows and travellers from Yulca who arrive muddled by illusions.
Dried fish, eel-paste and rice go to Yulca and Aroxhu. Gaweja buys reed rafts and small illusion charms from the Agaceph.
Gaweja sends its eggs to the Hist at Aroxhu. A fishers' post of woven reeds stands on the point with a knotted cord for every boat lost.
The clay-mound people's furthest settlement toward Yulca. It began as a fishing post and became the place where Oxhu and Agaceph rafters trade.
An Agaceph rafter has gone missing and the fishers found his raft empty in the reeds. Their nets bring up worked stones, and a stranger digs the shallows by night.
Stilted mounds along the lake edge, drying racks of eel, rice terraces with water-lilies, reed boats pulled up and a small stone cairn on the point.
A village on the lake edge on the western side of the mound country, where the Oxhu-Teeleel meet the Agaceph.
About eleven Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel, fishers and rice-growers, with a few Agaceph visitors on the landing.
A quiet village. Its elders keep good terms with Yulca, which is rare. Agaceph rafters tie up at its landing to trade.
Undead walk the flooded halls of the sunken vaults, and crocodiles and giant snakes lurk in the water. Rockfall traps are set in the lower halls.
Once the Conclave's vault; now a source of tablet fragments and relics for scavengers and Stormhold scholars.
The Conclave worshipped learning and bore Molag Bal's name in its title; the Veesa-Teeleel call the ground sick.
The vaults sank when an associate of the Conclave cast a powerful spell. In the Simulacrum the Eternal Champion was sent in to recover the tablet.
The tablet itself; a Stormhold scholar who needs someone to swim the drowned lowest hall.
A collapsed stone vault entrance in a slope of reeds; half-sunk columns, flooded halls and rune-marked walls.

The Vaults of Gemin are a ruined structure in Stormhold's city-state that once belonged to the Conclave of Baal. They kept the ancient tablet for deciphering the Elder Scrolls and divining Murkwood's place, and sank into the ground when a spell failed.
The vaults have no residents. Treasure-seekers from Stormhold go down into the flooded ruin on their own account.
A sunk, half-flooded ruin; the Conclave of Baal is long gone from Stormhold, and nobody can locate Murkwood without the tablet.
The town is guarded and safe by day. The closed Ayleid sections, the Ruction Ring's cut-throats and the swamp at the gates (hackwings and crocodiles) are where visitors get hurt.

Hunting produce, herbs, red-clay pottery from the Onkobra delta and the Leyawiin trade keep the market busy. The cooks serve outsiders swamp food they can stomach. River boats bring Middle Argonian goods down to the quay, and salt and iron go out to the Naka-Desh river stations.

Dibella is worshipped openly in the old Dorcia Martius manor, a devotion the Nibenese took from the Kothringi substrate; Sithis is honoured in private by the Argonians. The Hist garden holds a planted cutting whose ownership is disputed.

Barsaebic Ayleids founded it as Twyllbek; the Kothringi left a Dibella devotion in the soil; Imperial settlers built the mansion, the temple and Castle Giovesse beside it. The An-Xileel's weapon killed Gideon's Lukiul in 4E 48 and the undead host of Umbriel overran the town, yet Gideon's destruction was light and it stayed an active settlement.

A Hist cutting in the Ayleid gardens that two families both claim, a cellar door in the closed Ayleid quarter that has been forced, a Kothringi silver mask sold twice in one week and the old quarrel with Soulrest over who ships the bay's trade.

Imperial brick and timber along Blackwood Way, wet red clay underfoot, crooked alleys running off the causeway and Ayleid white-stone stumps in the plaza and the southern gardens. Steam rises from the bathhouses and fog lies in the streets at dawn.

Gideon is the first settlement on the Blackwood Road from Leyawiin: a governor's mansion, a courthouse, a Temple of Dibella, an arena and mud bathhouses in a maze of cramped streets. Most buildings stand along Blackwood Way because it is the only dry ground through the town.

Most people are Lukiul Argonians who speak Cyrodiilic, trade with outsiders and stand apart from Argonian philosophy, beside Nibenese-descended families two centuries settled. Archein families survive as landholders and council servants. About 90 people live in the walls; Khajiit and Bosmer traders pass through.

In 4E 201 the council still sits in the Governor's Mansion and the courthouse still hears cases and keeps its records, an Imperial habit the town never dropped. Gideon denies the successor state's claim and deals with the Archwardens only at Fort Silvermoth's toll gate. Carts on the Blackwood Road to Leyawiin leave from the east gate.
Ghosts and restless dead haunt the ruin itself; the huts are safe enough, but the track north to the castle is not walked after dark.

Guiding, scavenged stone and iron from the castle walls, eels and herbs sold at Gideon's gate. The ruin once housed a lord and a prison. Little of value is left in it beyond urns and a rotted strongbox.
They leave Dibella offerings at a roadside shrine for the dead of the castle, and keep Sithis's name for the nights when something moves on the rise.
Calvus Vanin was the first lord; Empress Tavia was held here from 1E 2899. The castle fell to ruin. By the modern era it is described as haunted. The name now belongs to the hamlet.
Empress Tavia's old cell behind a rusted door, a ghost that wants its name carved on a grave-stake by the north gate and digging crews who go into the castle and do not all come out.
Grey, root-split castle walls on a low mound, a dozen huts below on stilts, a plank causeway to Gideon's gate and lamps burning all night.
Castle Giovesse was the Imperial ducal seat above Gideon and the prison of Empress Tavia; the ruin stands on a rise, and a hamlet of a few families has grown at its foot.
Poor Lukiul Argonian families and a few Nibenese diggers, led by an old woman who keeps the ruin's door-keys from the days when it was closed.
About nine people live in lean-to huts on stilts below the castle. They sell guided walks to the ruin, tend small yam beds and pay Gideon a gate-toll for the right to shelter under its guard.
Safe in town; the roads are wild and Paatru camps lie west of the river.
Salt, iron and herbs for river fish and clay; a caravan yard; river boats for the Onkobra line.
A Dibella wayside shrine and a Naka-Desh chime post where riddle-games are played.

Gul-Tej grew where the river east of Gideon forks, as the market where the Naka-Desh brought fish and clay from the interior and took away Gideon's salt and iron. The fork made it a meeting place long before the Empire came.
A riddle contest with a prize, a trade dispute over salt, a caravan that has not come.
A plank market on a river fork, reed-thatched stalls, red mud, boats tied in rows and chimes on the eaves.
A town of stilt houses and a plank market on a river fork north-east of Gideon, the last settled stop before the Naka-Desh river stations. It is Gideon's eastern gate to the interior.
Lukiul traders, Naka-Desh fishers who trade osheeja gar for salt and iron and a few Nibenese herb dealers.
About twenty people live here, and a market council of traders settles disputes. No Warden toll gate stands on the fork; the market council answers to Gideon's council.
The village is peaceful but the wilderness behind it is full of predators.
Sap, smoked fish, hides and feathers; they buy salt and cloth from Thorn.
They keep the Hist's word by custom: eggs are laid in a root hollow near the village and the dead returned to the roots.

The Root-Folk have kept stations at the edge of the jungle since before the Empire. Archein families once took a share of its sap for the right to tap near their fields; since the secession the Archein families no longer ask for it.
A clutch of eggs in the root hollow that has not hatched, which the headwoman wants Tsonac's tree-minder to see and a smuggler's raft hidden in the reeds whose crew bought sap with false coin.
Reed-roofed stilt houses joined by rope bridges, drying racks, dugouts on the mud and thick jungle behind.
A small Argonian stilt hamlet on the bay's southern shore, one of the Root-Folk's outposts at the eastern edge of the jungle.
Saxhleel Argonians, a headwoman and her kin; they have no quarrel with the sky-blue Stone-Sleepers and a mutual dislike of Thorn's field-owners.
Eight or so live there, hunting, tapping sap and tending a clutch of eggs; they sell to the Thorn market.

The city's alleys are as dangerous as they are fine. Its guard has a bad name. The danger is social: a levy that answers to no stranger, assembly politics and a sour-spring cycle the assembly will not discuss. Past the city every approach is deep swamp.

Helstrom does not trade outward; it receives and redistributes, because the rivers all drain to it. Rootworm and raft traffic, the Panther River fork and pilgrimage to the Root Talk bring it goods. Its market traders sell Murkwood feathers, sap, eggs and river fish.

The Hist, above all. Helstrom's city tree and its tree-minders matter more than any office, and the Root Talk, the occasion at which the Hist's alignment becomes audible to all the tribes, is held here in the holy month Hist-Tsoko. Sithis is honoured quietly; the Nine have no temple.

Helstrom was already active in the late First Era, during the Blackwater War. After the defeat at the Battle of Argonia in 1E 2811 the native armies retreated here. The Empire refused to follow and never besieged the city. In 1E 2836 the Argonians simply stopped fighting. In the Third Era it became an incorporated city-state, and villages were built around it. Umbriel's path in 4E 48 passed it by.

A stranger stranded on the approaches is pulled out by an Agaceph raftsman; the assembly will not speak of its sour spring in open session; the Root Talk draws every naheesh in the interior; boat-robbers pick through the drowned Third Era villages on the city's edge.

Stilt and root-hollow houses of reed, mud and living wood, with no stone and no outward wall, because the marsh is the wall. Black Heart-Mud pools between the roots, the air is thick and warm and rafts and plank walks thread the districts.

Helstrom is one of Black Marsh's great cities, in the reputedly inhospitable middle of the province and many call it the immortal capital of the Argonians. It meets the Root Talk and is run by its own people, not by any distant government.

Overwhelmingly Argonian, drawn from the interior's exclusive breeds: Agaceph on tail-poled rafts, with Paatru and Naga visitors and a very small outsider presence of perhaps a few dozen, each there on a naheesh's word. The guard is a tribal levy answerable to the assembly, not to strangers.

In 4E 201 Helstrom is intact and the least Imperialised city in the province. The state's formal seat is lodged here and largely ignored. The assembly of naheesh and tree-minders decides by consensus. A half-swallowed ring of Third Era villages lies on its approaches.
The hamlet is peaceful. Its guards rarely draw a blade. Its Agaceph illusionists test strangers with glamours and false paths before they let them in.
The Agaceph of Hirecan trade books, illusion work, river fish and rare reeds, carried by raft to Icalca and Yulca.
They follow the Hist like other Argonians, but they also keep the books their forebears took from the dead Maran mission at Umpholo and read them aloud at hatchings.
A hamlet founded as the Agaceph spread along the mesa's rivers.

An Agaceph reader wants her forebear's bronze mission lamp from the drowned lower floor of a chapel downriver, reached only by swimming and a traveller stands frozen by a spell in a doorway, held there since he tried to steal a raft.
Stilt houses on slender posts, raft racks along the water, bright painted shutters and a reed-roofed house where the mission books are kept dry.
A hamlet of the Agaceph, the Middle Argonian breed that is not a camp people.
Agaceph with rainbow scales, readers and illusionists, wary of strangers and quick to freeze an intruder with a spell.
Eight Agaceph live there; they ride their thin rafts to Icalca and Yulca.
Hackwings hunt in the reeds on both sides of the causeway. A crocodile lies under the ferry stage. Strangers are watched, though not harmed.
Ferrying, reed-thatch, smoked eel and a trade in herbs for Gideon's dealers; caravan drivers pay for the dry sleeping platform on the road.
A small Sithis shrine on a raft that moves with the village; Dibella charms hang from the ferry post.

The Argonian Account names Hixinoag on the northern road in the Imperial era. The village outlasted the Empire, and when Gideon's Lukiul quarters burned under Umbriel in 4E 48 it took in families from the plantation country south of it.
A house-raft found cut from its stake with a passenger still aboard and its rope slashed, a caravan driver who will not let anyone near one crate or a feud between two clans over the same channel.
Tiered stilt huts, reed rafts roped end to end, black water, crows on the roof-poles and a long causeway of laid planks running out to the road.

A village of stilt houses and house-rafts moored to stakes on the northern caravan road above Gideon. The families can pole a raft to a new mooring when a channel silts up, and the ring of rafts has been moored where it is for years.
Lukiul and Naka-Desh families, headed by a river-headwoman who judges disputes over rafts and channel rights.

About ten people keep a ferry and a rest-house for caravans. They bargain with the Archein landholders for reed rights and with Gideon for salt, and send the Archwardens nothing, since no toll gate stands on their channels.
Mudcrabs on the shingle, and smugglers who sometimes land at night and take what they find.
The household twists nets, rope and cord from coast-grass and sells them to Seafalls. They dig clams on the shingle and dry fish on racks.
They hang a knotted cord on the fence for every wreck on this coast, in the way of the Spray-Folk.
A net-maker of Seafalls built the house here because she wanted the quiet of the shore, and her niece came to live with her.
The old net-maker once wove a net for a smuggler and knows his boat. She tells her friends where he beaches it.
A single stilt house above the shingle, nets spread on the fence, a tarred boat pulled up the beach.
A single house on the shingle between the farms and the sea, a day's walk from Seafalls.
Two Argonians live at Tidewatch, an old net-maker and her niece, who take turns keeping watch on the beach.
The household sells nets and rope to Seafalls and to coast boats, and sells the walker a meal and a floor to sleep on.
Illusions that freeze, calm or turn strangers on each other; lake crocodiles in the shallows; and the bandits Icalca keeps out.
Maran books, scrolls and illusion-work are sold or swapped. Fish and lake-grain keep the hamlet fed.
They hold a weak respect for the Hist. They read the Maran books for amusement.
The Agaceph looted the dead Maran mission at Umpholo for its books, and the books were shared out among their hamlets. Icalca keeps a shelf of them.

A Gaweja fisher has taken a raft-pole the eldest valued, and the eldest wants it back. The eldest also speaks of a ruin in the reeds that no raft has found, and will pay in Illusion tomes to learn where it lies.
Raft-houses lashed together on a blue-green lake, reed screens painted in bright scale-colours, long thin rafts hauled onto mats.
An Agaceph hamlet on a lake in the west of Okuwun-Rahei. The Agaceph are a people of Middle Argonia and live nowhere else.
About eight Agaceph with rainbow scales and needle faces, riding razor-thin rafts; the eldest reads three languages.
