A hamlet of raft-houses and stilts, bounded by reed screens. The Agaceph keep to their lake and sell tomes and illusion-work to those who ask politely.
The water-filled cellar is the main risk, with snakes in the wall-gaps and a squatters' lookout on the north wall. Holes in the floor by the old armoury drop into the cellar.
The Legion built it with a toll bar and a signal brazier on the road between Karketa and Lilmoth. Salvagers now strip the iron fittings and the brick for the village huts.

No Hist grows here, and the chapel niche in the east wall is empty of its icon of the Nine, though candle stubs show a squatter still lights it. The squatters call the yard unlucky and do not sleep inside.
Built by the Legion as a road post. The Legion left at the secession, 4E 5-10 and the Archwardens did not re-garrison it.
A locked cage in the armoury still holds an Imperial officer's sword. A squatter wants a lost kinsman found, last seen heading for the fort.
A low square fort of stone and brick, the wall broken at one corner, green with vines.
Fort Sallowmoth is a low square fort of stone and brick, its wall broken at one corner and green with vines. Squatters hold the roofless yard.
Fort Sallowmoth has no residents, but squatters keep a watch from the roofless yard and smugglers pass through. Karketa's villagers know the faces and say little to strangers.
Roofless; the walls stand, the cellar holds standing water and squatters use the yard.
The sea-cave has a deep pool where breath runs out for the unwary, and snakes nest in the tower rubble. Smugglers who guard the cache attack strangers without warning.
The Company kept a shed for bonded goods and a lamp to signal Lilmoth. Scavengers now carry off the lamp brackets and brick, and smugglers keep their cache below.
There is no Hist and no shrine, only a rusted iron ring in the shed wall where the customs men hung a charm to Julianos. Fishers touch it as they shelter.
Built by the Company to collect duty on coasting vessels. The Company left with the Legion at the secession, 4E 5-10 and the Archwardens kept their customs at the ports instead.
A smugglers' cache in the sea-cave beneath. A bonded strongbox bolted to the shed floor that no key on the shore fits.
A low brick shed, a toppled signal tower, a rusted iron lamp bracket.
Brackwater Waystation is a low brick shed with a toppled signal tower beside it and a sea-cave beneath. Smugglers use the cave.
Brackwater Waystation has no residents, but smugglers use the sea-cave and fishers from Nundi stop in the shed during squalls. Both groups know the sea-cave and do not discuss it.
The tower has fallen; the shed's walls stand, with a sea-cave beneath.
Outlaws sleep in the cellars, marsh predators come in from the washes and the lower cellars stand flooded.
The Legion once took tolls at Mudmoth, its road station. Now scavengers pull salvage from its tumbled stone.
No shrine or worship survives at Mudmoth; the Imperial crest is all that is left of the ruin's old observance.
Built by the Empire as a road post on the washes road; left when the Legion marched out at the secession (4E 5-10), and never garrisoned since.
The station's paymaster sank his iron strongbox in the flooded cellar when the Legion left, and it has never been raised. Smugglers meet in the yard on moonless nights.
A broken stone tower and wall on a mud rise, creepers over its Imperial crest.
A tumbled Imperial waystation on the Soulrest-Blackrose road, named in the Legion's '-moth' fashion like the forts the Archwardens keep elsewhere.
Only passing outlaws use Mudmoth, sleeping in the cellars for a night or two and moving on.
The waystation stands empty. Outlaws and scavengers shelter in it with no garrison to move them on.
Bandits with a leader and a lookout hold the shell, and gaps in the burnt floors open onto the cellar below. The garrison's patrols avoid the ruin, so the approach along the island road is unwatched.
It once held a small customs post and a stock of signal fuel for Reedmoth. Now the bandits sell what they find in the char to dealers on the island road.
The burnt shrine of the Nine is only blackened stone on a plinth, and the bandits spit on it for luck. Reedmoth's garrison calls the ruin cursed and will not patrol its walls.
Built as Reedmoth's outlier and burnt out when the Legion was driven from the island at the secession, 4E 5-10. The Archwardens kept Reedmoth and left this fort empty.
A bandit leader with a price on his head, wanted by the Reedmoth garrison. A strongroom behind an iron door, which the fire did not reach.
A burnt shell, its timbers charred black and only the stone footings standing.
Fort Lowmoth is a burnt shell of charred timbers and stone footings, built as an outlier of Fort Reedmoth. Road bandits hold it.
Fort Lowmoth has no residents, but the bandits who use it as a lair post watchers on the island road. Villagers from Sal-Axan and the Tal-Neesh farm pay them in rice and do not argue.
Black with old fire and half fallen in, it is used by road bandits as a lair.
Smugglers use the tower and post their own guard on it. Sea-birds nest in the broken top and attack climbers.
It was a south-shore watch post and signal tower for the Imperial coast, left at the secession; it now draws scavengers after worked stone and brass, and the odd smuggler.

A chipped Imperial Divines' niche in the tower base holds a rain-filled bowl. The smugglers' signal-keeper comes of an Imperial-descended family and still fills it for Kynareth before each run, and Xal-Tarek's men do not touch it.
Mistwatch was built as a coast watch on the cape's south shore, and was left empty when the Legion withdrew at the secession.
A smugglers' signal lamp shows from the tower at night. The old watch's brass signal mirror is still bolted to the top, and Mistfall Light's keepers want it.
A broken stone tower stands on a rise above the shore, open to the weather at the top.

Mistwatch is a broken stone tower on a rise, with a chipped Divines' niche at its base. It signalled ships bound for Soulrest when Soulrest was the Imperial capital of the province; smugglers use it now.
Mistwatch has no residents. Xal-Tarek's patrols pass by, and sea-wreckers sometimes light a fire in the tower stump.
The tower stands empty. Smugglers use it as a lookout and a place to hide goods.
Wildlife is the main danger in the thicket around the ruined tower.
Once a border watch of the Empire, the tower is now stripped of anything useful.
A small shrine niche of the Divines is cut into the tower base, empty now. The Hutan-Tzel do not touch it.
Built by the Third Empire to watch the border hills in the far west, and left to fall when the Legion marched out at the secession.
A Legion courier's bones lie in the rubble at the tower's foot, still wearing an officer's silver ring.
A broken tower and a wall stand in a thicket on the far-west hills.

Aldanus Watchtower is a Third Empire watchtower on the border hills above the Blackwood Road. The Empire watched the road to Leyawiin until the secession, and no one re-held a tower so far from the trunk routes.
Aldanus Watchtower has no residents. Hutan-Veel scouts climb it for the view and sleep rough in its yard when they range south.
A stump of a tower and a length of wall stand in a thicket on the border hills.
Bandits hold it, with archers on the tower top who watch the road. The granary floor is rotten and the cellar hides traps set by smugglers.
A waystation for couriers and carts, with a granary to feed them. Now only the bandits who rob the road below and the scavengers after the iron nails of its door make a living from it.
The waystation kept a small shrine to the Nine in the tower's lowest room, and a statue of Zenithar stood by the granary. Both are broken, though a Gideon traveller sometimes leaves a coin.

Nine Reeds Waystation was built in Imperial times on the road north of Gideon, a stone tower with a granary and a signal-fire platform for travellers and couriers. Its Imperial keepers left at the secession and the tower has had no keepers since.
A Legion pay-chest that carters swear is bricked into the granary floor, a carter held for ransom in the tower or the bandit leader who holds the tower top.
A square stone tower with a fallen roof, a granary block at its foot and a hearth platform on the top where the signal fire stood. Nine tall reeds grow in a ring where the well was.
A ruined Imperial waystation in the Nha Enasa, on the road north of Gideon: a stone tower with a granary and a signal fire.
The tower is uninhabited. A band of road-bandits holds it by turns with a gang of smugglers. Gideon's guard looks in only when a caravan goes missing.
The tower is empty and open to the weather. Bandits who rob caravans on the Gideon road use it as a bolt-hole, and smugglers store goods in its dry cellar.
Outlaws camp in the yard and predators come in through the flooded gate.
It was a fort on the north coast of the cape, guarding the Topal Bay road; its stone and timber now draw Naxan builders and scavengers after Legion iron.
A weathered Imperial standard-shrine at the gate has lost its image. Naxan fishermen leave a shell on the sill for the soldiers who died here.
Wrackmoth is a Legion '-moth' fort on the north coast, left when the Legion marched out at the secession and never re-held.
The fort's iron-doored strongroom under the gatehouse has never been opened. Outlaws have hidden a stash in the yard.
Stone walls are grown over with creepers. The gate stands open to the flooded yard.
Wrackmoth is a flooded fort of stone walls grown over with creepers. It guarded the Topal Bay road for the Legion; the Archwardens keep their watch on Aphon instead and left it empty.
Wrackmoth has no residents. Naxan fishermen shelter in its gate on wet nights, and scavengers camp in its yard.
The fort is empty and its yard and lower rooms stand flooded.
Smugglers armed with crossbows watch the pier, and the tower's lean makes its stair dangerous. Crocodiles wait in the dark water under the pier.
A watch on the delta approaches, paid for out of Gideon's harbour dues. Now it works as a mooring and drop-point for smugglers, and the iron of its door and grille is prised away for scrap.
The watch kept a small Akatosh candle-niche in the tower stair for the soldiers on night watch. The niche is cold now. The garrison's Imperial altar is long gone.
Gideon South Watch was built under the Empire on the mangrove edge south of Gideon, to see boats coming up through the delta. Its garrison left at the secession with the rest of the Imperial forces.
A hidden cellar under the tower where moon sugar comes ashore, a Gideon buyer who meets the boats here or Gideon's watch wanting the pier cleared.
A round stone watch-tower that leans on a mud bank, with a broken lantern room on top and green weed around its base. A rotted pier runs out into the channel.
A ruined Imperial watch tower in the Kotherra Mangroves, on the south side of Gideon, built to watch the delta approaches.
The tower is uninhabited. Smugglers meet their buyers at its foot, and Gideon's watch rows down now and then to move them on.
The tower is unheld and half sunk in mud. Smugglers who bring goods up through the delta channels moor beneath it, and a few bandits use its top room to watch for guard patrols.
Wind and a loose parapet make the climb risky. The smugglers will not welcome visitors, and mudcrabs crowd the rocks around its base.
A signal post for the bay's shipping, kept by Imperial dues. Today its main value is as a lookout for smugglers and a source of dressed stone for fishers' huts.
Sailors who shelter on the isle leave a knot of rope on the tower door for Kynareth and for safe sailing.

Aphon Signal Tower stands on the high ground of Aphon Isle, paired with the Belvedere so that a fire on one could be seen from the other across the bay. It was built under the Empire. Its lamp has not been kept since the secession.
A smugglers' lookout who signals boats with a lantern from the top, a Khajiit crew waiting below for the signal or the Belvedere's watch wanting the tower cleared.
A tall tower of grey stone on a bare rock crest, with the lamp-room blackened by old fires and a stair that winds up outside the wall. Gulls nest in its broken parapet.
A ruined Imperial signal tower on the high ground of Aphon Isle, paired with Aphon Belvedere to watch the bay.
The tower is uninhabited. A small band of sea-smugglers keeps watch from its top, and Aphon's fishers pass it without a word.
The tower is unheld, a landmark for fishing boats rounding the isle. Smugglers who work the bay use its top as a lookout and keep a cache in the base.
Wildlife and the odd thief lurk in the reeds around the ruin. Hackwings swarm over the mud in the heat.
Once a waystation for the Legion's couriers; now stripped of any metal.
No shrine survives: Imperial shrines had no Hist, and the waystation kept only a plinth with a worn eagle.
Built by the Third Empire as a staging post on the road toward Morrowind; empty since the Legion marched out at the secession.
A hoard hidden in the plinth by a Legion courier; a scavenger who wants a witness.
A low stone wall and arch in a field of reeds; a plinth with a worn Imperial eagle.

Calvian Waystation is a Third Empire staging post on the northern road toward Morrowind. The Empire ran its roads with posts like it until the Legion left at the secession; the name is the Cyrodiilic one its builders gave it.
The roofless waystation has no residents. Scavengers sleep in its corners as they pass along the northern road.
Roofless, with a standing gate arch and wall; scavengers sleep in its corners.
Safe by day. Slaughterfish and mud-crabs fill the channel, so swimming it instead of paying the ferry is the risk.
Ferry fares in coin or goods, fish and a small trade in spare poles, rope and lamp oil. The ferry-master tells the elder what crossed.
They tie a feather to the ferry rope at each crossing to ask the water for passage; hatching families walk to Uluo.

The hamlet grew around a raft crossing used by Cyrodiilic and Company traders; the Company's road is gone since the secession but the crossing is older than it. The ferry families keep the crossing in their songs.
Travellers who cannot pay want an escort across the slaughterfish water. The ferryman knows who crossed unseen last night. A raft-master bets that nobody can swim the channel.
Six raft-houses on pole stilts either side of the channel, a long guide-rope between two stump posts, lanterns on poles and boats pulled onto mud.
A hamlet at the point where the road from Archon toward the north crosses a wide channel. The raft ferry here is the reason it exists.
Three Waters Argonians; the ferry-master is chosen by the elder at Uluo. Travellers from Archon, Aroxhu and the north pass daily.
Eight or so raft-families run the ferry in turns, tell travellers which bank the slaughterfish keep to and keep a lamp lit for night crossings.
Safe in the town. Pickpockets, and a few Naga road-robbers working alone on the river road.
Clay, pottery and dye are sold in bulk; Inoja takes a toll on the market ground and runs the river ferry. Aroxhu's elders say which families may sell to outsiders.
Small clay shrines to the dead line the market. The Hist of Aroxhu is the town's tree, and its sap-gatherers walk there from Inoja to bring sap back.
Grew from a ferry crossing at a river fork into the confederacy's market. The Aroxhu elders do not want strangers inside their mounds, and Inoja is a day's walk away.
A Thorn buyer has paid for a barge of pots that never arrived. The ferryman saw something on the river that night but will only tell a friend.
Terraced mounds along the river, a broad market-ground with reed awnings and stacks of pots in red and brown, a rope ferry and stilted inns over the water.
A town of about twenty on the river fork where roads from Aroxhu, Arorha and the southern villages meet. It is where outsiders deal with the confederacy.
About twenty-one Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel: traders, boatmen, ferrymen and inn-keepers, with a handful of visiting Dunmer and Khajiit.
A busy market. Dunmer clay-buyers from Thorn, Okuwun boatmen and now and then a Khajiit trader bargain here. The elders rule disputes between buyers and sellers.
The town is quiet. Its own wardens patrol. Off the road, crocodiles in the weir channels and looters and Naga brigands on the track toward the ruins.

Reed mats, rope, boats and dried fish sold to Stormhold; weir fees from the fish traps on the creeks. Its warriors also guard the ruins of Gemin, Nenria and Loriasel against looters, paid in kind by Stormhold's trading halls.
A Hist tree in a pool at the heart of the town, tended by a tree-minder; hatchlings come here. The Veesa-Teeleel hold the Barsaebic ruins to be sick ground and teach children not to touch them.

A Hist pool and sedge beds on high ground in an area ringed by Barsaebic ruins was settled early by Argonians; the Dunmer slave-raids of the Dres period came through this border country and are remembered here.

A looter caught with Ayleid goods, and the elders' refusal to hand him to Stormhold; a weir warden who sees lights at Nenria at night; the tree-minder asking the player to carry a phial of the pool's sap to the Root-Folk at Vel-Sapha Stand.
Pale reed-thatched stilt houses on a ring of mud banks around a pool, boat-lanes between them cut through the sedge, mats drying on racks, fish racks smoking on the road side.
Jal-Veesa is the one town of the Veesa-Teeleel, the northern Argonians of the valleys between Stormhold and the Barsaebic ruins. It sits on the road west of Stormhold.
Veesa-Teeleel Argonians, courteous to Dunmer without trusting them. Elders and a tree-minder at the pool; a few Stormhold buyers lodge on market days.

A town of stilt houses and reed jetties on a Hist pool. The elders settle disputes themselves and refuse the Vicecanons' courts, but send men to the frontier screen for pay and trade every day with Stormhold.
Safe for the tribes' friends; strangers from the coast are questioned and sometimes held. Outlying posts are hostile.
Fishing, salvaged mine metal, trade with Kharaxos and the toll every Soulrest Argonian pays to come inland to hatch, name or bury.
Sithis and the nearest Hist to Soulrest, which the townsfolk guard; burning is a rite, and the burned mine-mouths are shrines.

The tribes of the basin burned the Imperial mines and timber concessions in 3E 427 and never made peace with the coast. The basin's oldest Hist stands at Jarecai. The town grew round it and is where their elders meet.
A Soulrest egg-tender whose clutch must reach the Jarecai Hist before it hatches, a young warrior's trial at the burned mine or the elders' price for passage through the basin.
Tiered timber halls on stilts, a palisade of burned stakes, black-scorched mine timbers used as posts, boats at every landing and smoke over the water.
A fortified town on stilts over the Banujha waters, the seat of the basin tribes. It is the political centre of the people who cut Soulrest off from its hinterland.
Mine-Burner Argonians, council elders and war-leaders; no Imperial-descended family lives here, and ex-Imperial administrators from Soulrest are unwelcome.

About 28 people live in tiered halls behind a palisade of stakes. The elders judge disputes, take a toll from Soulrest Argonians who come inland to the hatching grounds and use the grounds as a lever on the port.
Steep pit walls to fall from, crocodiles at the river mouth and Sarpa raiders from the west who come for tools.
Red clay is dug in blocks, fired in the village kiln and floated down the river to Inoja and Aroxhu. Joxhi clay fires a deep brick red and sells for double.
The village sends its eggs to the Hist at Aroxhu. Diggers press a clay figure into the pit wall for any who died in a fall, and the grave-singer names them at the kiln fire.
A hatchling of the first Inoja families found the red seam, and the diggers have worked it for generations. The village stands on its own spoil.
The diggers have broken through into a buried stone hall of old Ayleid make and will not go back down; the elder wants someone to look, and the Sarpa have heard of it.
Stilted mounds beside a river bend, raw red pits edged with reed fencing, drying clay blocks, an orange-stained river and a domed kiln.
A village beside a river bend in the northern mounds, known for its red clay pits.
About ten Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel, mostly diggers and carriers. The elder is a former potter who still thumps every cartload to hear if it is sound.
A working village, wary of the Sarpa camp to the west and of Thorn's buyers who offer too much.
A Naga band hunts the delta shallows; crocodiles in the braid; the ferry is the weak point.
Saltrice, a ferry toll across the braid and small trade with Helstrom's outposts for sap and eggs.
Hist and Sithis at a little roadside tree; the Dunmer grandmother still tends a household Ancestor shrine.

No stake tells of its founding. A farm in the Stormhold manner this far inland is read as one set up by families who left the northern river in the generations after 4E 48 and brought stone footings with them.
The ferry-rope has been cut twice; a cairn on the nearest firm bank has been opened; a salt trader's body washed up at the paddies.
Low stone footings with reed-and-mud walls, a causeway of laid stone out to the ferry post, flat rice paddies fenced with reed and the lake's wide grey sheet beyond.
Julo is a hamlet of about six people at the delta where Helstrom's waters spread into the lake. It follows the Stormhold manner of raised stone footings and causeways.
About six residents: Argonian farmers and one grandmother of Dunmer descent, from a Stormhold border family, who settles every quarrel over the rice.
In 4E 201 it holds a small saltrice patch and a ferry. It sends a gift of rice to Helstrom at each Root Talk and keeps good terms with the Root-Folk stations upstream.
Gar in the channel, bandit boats at night and drowning under the stilts.
Ka-Asei sets fish traps in the channel, builds boat hulls for the lake and delta and pays and collects a toll on passing boats.

Ka-Asei has no tree of its own, so its minder sends each clutch by lake barge to the Blackrose Hist and ties a knot in a cord under the longhouse eaves for every hatchling named there. Mourners tie a reed to a stilt for every death. The posts at the channel mouth are covered with reeds.
It grew from a fishing platform to a village as the Delta Ferry trade rose in the Fourth Era.
A stolen boat, a hidden cargo under the platforms or a fisher's feud with Amalaja.
Houses on tall stilts joined by rope bridges, boats moored below, nets drying on the walkways.
A water-village on stilts in the channel southeast of the island core, on the route to Amalaja and the delta.
Ka-Asei's households are Argonian fishers who also build boats, on stilts over the channel southeast of the island core.
It pays the island core a channel toll and takes its patrol boat's visits.
Flu-dead undead in the lower halls, loose stone and falling masonry.
Once a mason town; now a quarry of dressed stone for Tsonac and a source of Velothi goods.
Mephala is the god the Cantemiric Velothi followed by the Chimeri story; some shrine marks may stand.
Settled by Dunmer dissidents in the First or Second Era and emptied by the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560-603; the Hist have not claimed the ground.
A Tsonac mason who left his grandfather's chisel in the cellars when the dead rose, and the herbalist, who asks for a sick Stone-Sleeper child to be carried to her from Oxayo.
Squared Dunmer stone, curved roof ribs under vine, a central well and a stair into the mesa.
A ruin of the Cantemiric Velothi, the Dunmer settlers of the eastern coast, standing on the mesa top south of Tsonac as part of the Velothi settlement of the country.
The halls have no living inhabitants. A Dunmer herbalist from Thorn has lived for years in an outer tomb at the ruin's edge, gathering the fungus that grows in the dark.
Roofless stone houses on the mesa edge, the dead in their halls; Tsonac's quarrymen take dressed stone from its outer wall.
Sea-drakes are seen beyond the reef, and cutpurses work the Lilmoth road.
Fresh and salted fish, sea salt, boat repair and ferry service to the northern island.
They take their hatchlings to Lilmoth's third Hist and keep a prayer-post carved for the drowned.
An old coast village on a shore the Lilmothiit left long before the Flu; it was spared when Umbriel fell on Lilmoth in 4E 48 and sent people to help the town's rebuilding.
A boat lost beyond the reef with a villager's father aboard; a salt pan taken by a Lilmoth family for an unpaid debt; a stranger who asks the headwoman for a boat at night.
Stilt houses on grey pilings facing the sea, drying racks, salt pans and a long jetty with a tower lamp.
A coastal village on the road between Lilmoth and Southwatch Keep, in the Lilmoth coast's orbit.
Argonians of the Lilmoth coast; the headwoman's family has kept the boats for generations.
Twelve households net, salt fish and keep boats and sell their catch to Lilmoth's council market.
Safe in town; war-bands are heavily armed and the east road is wild.
Kharaxos trades salvaged mine metal and fish in a river market on the basin's eastern shore.
The people honour Sithis and the Hist. Posts of burned timber mark their graves.

Kharaxos bears a name older than the Mine-Burners, from the Kothringi who held the basin's east shore before the Knahaten Flu. The tribes who settled there after the Flu kept the name, as Argonian resettlers did across the old Kothringi country.
A metal dispute, a war-band muster or a Chime-Keeper wedding.
Dark timber halls on stilts, a black-scorched palisade, tin chimes from Oeneas on the market posts.
A fortified town of stilt halls on the basin's eastern shore, the tribes' gateway to the Chime-Keepers' towns toward Blackrose.
Mine-Burner Argonians and some Chime-Keeper traders from Oeneas.
About 22 people live here. It is a trade stop for metal and fish and a muster point for the basin's war-bands.
Marsh predators and a Blackguard watch post that has been seen at night.
What it was: a chime-maker's town on the Ka-Asei channel. Now its stone footings and metal draw scavengers.
The Chime-Keepers' tin and glass chimes still hang in the dead town's central tree, rung only by wind. The minder's shrine beneath them is dry. It has not been visited since the town emptied.
A Kothringi town before 2E 560; resettled by Argonians; left empty when the Ka-Asei channel silted and its families moved away.
Chimes that ring with no wind; a chime-maker's stash under the footings.
Stone footings under collapsed stilt houses, tin chimes rusting in the reeds.
Khariton is a dozen rotted stilt houses on stone footings, with tin chimes rusting in the reeds. It stood on the Ka-Asei channel.
Khariton is uninhabited. Delta Ferry hunters shelter under its few sound roofs on long hunts, and scavengers strip the last pegs from its stilt halls.
A dozen stilt houses on stone footings stand rotted, chimes still hung from some eaves.
Undead of the flu-dead, pit traps and scavenger crews who guard their finds; it is dark and cold below.
It was a settlement of masons and farmers; now it is a quarry of cut stone and a source of old Velothi goods for Thorn's markets.
Cantemiric Velothi followed Mephala, according to the Chimeri story; some shrine marks may remain. The Hist hold the ground to be sick.
The Velothi settled the coast between the First Era and the Second. The Knahaten Flu of 2E 560-603 killed every non-Argonian in the province, the Velothi among them.
A Thorn scavenger crew that went down the stair to the lower halls and has not come back up, and a Dunmer grandmother in Thorn who wants a carved ancestor mask from the household shrine below.
Dunmer-style stone houses with curved roof ribs, half buried in vine, a cracked central plaza and a stair down to the lower halls.
A ruin of the Cantemiric Velothi, the Dunmer dissident settlers of the eastern seaboard around Thorn, Archon and Arnesia.

The ruin has no living inhabitants. A scavenger crew out of Thorn camps among the walls when it is working the halls, and the Dunmer families of Thorn come to leave food and incense for ancestors whose names they have lost.
Roofless, overgrown and picked over by Thorn's scavengers; the lower halls are cut into the slope and still hold what the scavengers have not reached.
Crocodiles at the inlet, smuggler landings on the cape and the ghosts of Mazurath on the headland.
Dried and salted fish, shellfish and boat-timber, traded for clay goods and for Seafalls pearls.
Khiar sends its eggs inland to the Hist at Aroxhu. Fishers leave a clay fish on the cape stones for a good catch.
Founded as a fishing station to feed the mound country, then grew into a village. The Mazurath ruin on the next headland is older than the village and has stood empty since the Flu.
The boat-wright is building a ship for a stranger who paid in old bronze pieces from the headland ruin. The ruin glows after dark.
Reed houses on stilts on a low rise above a sandy cape, nets and fish-racks on every pole and a breakwater of piled clay.
A cape village south of Seafalls, the confederacy's southern coastal outlier.
About nine Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel: fishers, net-makers and an old boat-wright.
A steady fishing village. Its boats go out at dawn and sell to Seafalls, and its people dislike the Skeith smugglers' habit of landing at the cape.
Ancestor ghosts within, crabs and hackwings on the beach and a sinkhole in the courtyard floor that drops to the sea cave beneath.
Once a watch-hold that signalled the Velothi's boats. Now a landmark for smugglers and a source of ash-glass shards that lie on the beach below.
Velothi ancestor shrine niches line the inner hall. The ghosts of the hold's household remain at their posts.
Cantemiric Velothi built along the eastern seaboard between Archon and Thorn and died in the Knahaten Flu (2E 560-603). Its seaward point would suit a watch-hold over the sea lanes.
A signal brazier at the top of the tower holds a spell-lit fire that has never gone out. A smuggler's cache lies in the sea cave beneath the hall, left by a crew that did not come back.
Dark Velothi stonework in low rounded courses with a broken watch-tower at the seaward end, sand heaped in the courtyard, sea-grass growing through the floor, surf loud against the headland.
A ruined Velothi coastal hold on the headland at the bight's seaward edge, one of the Cantemiric Velothi holds of this coast.
The ruin has no residents. It is known to the Skeith smugglers as a landmark and to the Arorha clay-men as a place not to dig.
Roofless but standing. A smuggler's lantern sometimes burns on the headland, though the smugglers do not go inside.

The town itself is safe: its elders keep a watch and predators seldom cross its ring of water. Beyond the channel lie Ultherus swamp with its dragon's-tongue, Tumnatu hunters and deep-water predators.

It makes tuned chimes, metal-woven rope and shallow-draft sail-and-paddle boats and trades them up the channels to Helstrom, Truowa and Blackrose for tin, copper, sap and dragon's-tongue gathered in the swamp.

Sithis and the Hist. The chime-smiths also keep a small chime-hung shrine to Z'en, the god of toil that the Kothringi worshipped, as a habit they took over with the houses. The town's tree-minder tends a village tree where eggs are laid.

A Kothringi town until the Knahaten Flu (2E 560–603) emptied it. Argonians, immune to the flu, moved into the empty houses and kept the old name because it belonged to the place. Over the centuries they took up Kothringi habits that the Hist did not forbid. Nativists elsewhere in Black Marsh called them half-foreign.
A Kothringi cairn of beads lies under the oldest footings; one chime rings on a still night; the guild elders quarrel over who may tune the Hist-shrine chime; a boatwright needs rare Ultherus herbs.

Stilt houses on stone footings, a Kothringi habit; chimes of tin and copper hung from every eave; a market square on the ring of ground; boats moored three deep in the surrounding channel. The air hums with metal.

Korydon is a market town of about two dozen residents on a ring of dry ground surrounded by water, the chief of the Kothringi-named towns of the Ultherus country. The name is a Kothringi one, kept by the Argonians who moved in; no source describes the place itself.

About 22 residents, nearly all Argonian with a few mixed families: chime-smiths, rope-weavers, boat-wrights, a tin trader and the elders. A few families keep a stone cairn for the old Kothringi dead whose houses they took.

In 4E 201 Korydon is the most orderly town in the interior, run by a council of guild elders, cold toward the Archwardens and warm toward Gideon. Its chimes ring from every eave and the elders strike the great chime at dawn and dusk.
Mine-Burner watchers say the dead play the hall at night, and two of the tall columns lean over the floor with their footings cracked. Mine-Burner watchers shoot at anyone carrying off chimes.
A hall of music and festival. Today its columns' bronze chime-fittings are prised off for scrap, and a few chimes of fine Kothringi tuning are carried away as curiosities.
Music was the Kothringi's prayer to Dibella and Kynareth, and the columns were tuned so that the wind would sing for both. Mine-Burner tribesmen do not enter the hall, out of respect.

Kyrenos was a music-hall of the Kothringi, a long building whose columns held rows of chimes tuned in a scale. The hall fell silent when the Flu of 2E 560 killed its players, and the Mine-Burner tribes later passed it by when they burned the mines.
A tuned set of chimes that sounds only at dusk, a Mine-Burner who guards the hall or a Chime-Keeper claim to the stones.
A long hall of tall stone columns open to the sky, each with an iron arm at the top where the chimes once hung. A few chimes still turn in the wind and the floor is covered in drifted leaves.
The Kothringi, the Blackwood's silver-skinned humans, played and feasted here until the Knahaten Flu. It is a long music-hall whose columns once held rows of chimes.
The hall is uninhabited. The Mine-Burner watchers sometimes shelter in the porch. The occasional bard from Gideon makes the walk to hear the columns sing.
The hall is unheld. It stands on dry ground on the north edge of the Banujha Basin, and Mine-Burner watchers from the nearby posts know it as a place where the wind still sounds the chimes.
Restless dead rise from the oldest cairns, and Sul-Xan diggers work the south side by day.
Once a craft town of glass beads and moonstone. Treasure-diggers now work it, as do the Sul-Xan raiders who come for the cairns.
The Kothringi honoured Z'en, Dibella, Mara and Kynareth and their cairns still hold bead strings. Naka-Desh chimes hang in a single thorn tree beside the largest cairn.
Meliton was a Kothringi town in the western hills that the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560 left empty, part of a homeland that once held many such towns. The dead were laid in the cairns outside it.
A cairn with a humming doll the Naka-Desh will not discuss, and a Sul-Xan trench a Hutan-Aru elder wants filled.
Rings of stone footings on a hill, cairns heaped with glass beads and a chime-hung thorn tree at the centre. Hutan-Aru's smoke shows to the north.

Meliton is a Kothringi town in the western hills, named like Korydon and Toklea. Canon makes this Blackwood country the Kothringi homeland, which the Knahaten Flu emptied by 2E 603; the ruin above Hutan-Aru is one of those towns.
The ruin has no residents. The Naka-Desh come on foot from the west, and Hutan-Aru hunters leave them alone.
Cairns, footings and two standing walls on a hill-shoulder above Hutan-Aru, where Naka-Desh come now and then to hang chimes for the dead.
The planking is rotten and the slip ends over deep water where slaughterfish feed. Crocodiles lie below the quay in the shade of the boat-house.
A boatyard on the river trade between Gideon and the interior. Now it is a source of ship-timber and iron fittings, and a place where the old Kothringi boat design can still be seen.
The Kothringi hung a Kynareth wind-chime from the quay's end to ask for fair wind, and the Naka-Desh still cut a small notch on the mooring stone for a safe journey. Nothing grander is kept.

Pelaxis was the Kothringi river quay and boat-house on the channel east of Gideon, where shallow-draft sail-and-paddle boats were built and repaired. When the Flu emptied it in 2E 560, the last boat was left half-planked on the slip.
A boat-builder's tools, a sunken boat with something aboard or smugglers using the quay.
A stone quay with mooring posts sunk in the bank, a long boat-house with its roof half gone and a launching slip with a half-built hull still on it. Weed hangs from the quay edge.
Kothringi boatwrights worked here until the Knahaten Flu emptied the Blackwood of their people. It is a river quay and a boat-house for shallow-draft Kothringi sail-and-paddle boats.
The quay is uninhabited. Naka-Desh fishers sleep under the boat-house roof in bad weather. Boatwrights from Gideon visit now and then to look at the Kothringi hull design.
The quay is unheld. A few Naka-Desh river-folk beach their boats against the old mooring stones, and diggers from Gideon come to see the abandoned slip.
Giant snakes nest in the back room behind the broken roof-beam, and the Paatru will challenge strangers who use the hearth. A pressure plate in the strongroom passage still drops a spiked grate.

It was a merchant family's hall, once rich in goods carried up from the coast. Today it holds scavenged stone and an iron door to a back room the Paatru say is the family's strongroom, which no digger has yet forced.
The family honoured Kynareth for the winds that carried their ships, and the horn on the lintel is set above a wind-chime hook. The Paatru, who are not of that faith, leave a bone charm at the door.

Dorianth was the longhouse of a seafaring Kothringi family, the sort who sailed the coast and traded up the Nha Enasa channels. The leviathan-horn on its lintel was the family's mark, and none of the family survived the Flu of 2E 560.
The horn itself, a family tomb or a haunting that follows the hall's old boat-song.
A long hall of pale stone with a carved leviathan horn over its doorway, a hearth at the end and a fallen roof-beam across the middle. Reeds grow through the floor flags.
A Kothringi family lived here; their silver-skinned people all died in the Knahaten Flu. It is a hall with a leviathan-horn carved on its lintel, the longhouse of a seafaring family.
The hall is uninhabited. Paatru hunters from the camps to the east use the hall's hearth during the rains. A Gideon scholar comes now and then to copy the lintel.
It is unheld. Visitors come to see its carved lintel. Paatru and Naka-Desh both know the hall and sleep in it when the rain is heavy.
The dead of the terrace stir at night and the pool is deep with mudcrabs. Naka-Desh watchers will shoot at a looter who disturbs the graves.
The terrace was the Kothringi's burial ground, so it never traded. Now it draws grave-robbers after the burial goods. The Naka-Desh keep it as a place of memory.

Each grave is marked with a stone and a chime-post, and the Kothringi hung tin and copper chimes there to speak to the dead. The Naka-Desh, friends of the Kothringi in life, keep the ring of posts in repair.

Mnemosa is a burial terrace of the Kothringi on the high ground of Nha Enasa, east of Gideon. The terrace was filled at the height of the Flu in 2E 560, so the stones carry far more names than the settlement ever had.
A burial offering a descendant wants returned, a dig that disturbed the dead or a Naka-Desh riddle carved on the stones.
Stepped terraces of grave-stones set in a ring of weathered chime-posts, with the posts hung with green-crusted tin and copper. Reeds have taken the lowest step and a shallow pool sits in the middle.
Here the Kothringi, silver-skinned humans wiped out by the Knahaten Flu, buried their dead. It is a terrace of burial stones with a ring of chime-posts.
The terrace is uninhabited. Naka-Desh come in pairs at the turn of the year to tend the chime-posts. Now and then a grave-robber from Gideon is found in the reeds.

It is unheld. The Naka-Desh treat it as a place to be visited, not lived in and paddle up from the channels to renew their chimes. Diggers who rob the terraces are driven off if the river-folk catch them.
Restless dead at the four cairns, and Sul-Xan raiders camped in a trench on the stream side.
It was a craft town with beadwork and a pottery lane. Treasure-diggers and Cyrodilic relic-buyers from Nahk-Zeel Station now visit it.
The Kothringi's four powers are marked by four small cairns at the town's centre, each with a different colour of glass. Naka-Desh chimes hang from one tin frame.
Aithros was a Kothringi town in the far western hills, emptied by the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560 and never resettled. It lies a day south-west of Hutan-Veel, close to the Cyrodiil border.
A pottery heap with unbroken Kothringi bowls that a Nahk-Zeel buyer pays well for, and a raider who left his tools in the trench.
Stone footings in a loose ring around four coloured cairns, with a tin chime-frame and a pottery heap by the stream. The border road is a day to the north.
Aithros is a Kothringi town near the Cyrodiil border, one of the homeland's towns the Flu left empty. Its four cairns for Z'en, Dibella, Mara and Kynareth follow the Kothringi faith canon gives.
The ruin has no residents. Naka-Desh come in small parties and Hixinoag villagers cut wood on the slope below without crossing it.
Footings, cairns and a few walls above a stream; small Naka-Desh parties come from the border road to hang chimes.
Mangrove crocodiles and mudcrabs lie in the channel at the landing, and the pools round the altar are deep enough to drown in. Gideon's diggers say ghost lights at dusk lead the careless into them.
It was a place of offerings, not of trade. Now the leaf-carved stone is prised out and carried to Gideon, and small gold and silver votives still turn up in the root-mud round the altar.

The altar slab is Dibella's, and the leaf-and-wave carving on it is the Kothringi sign of her. Gideon's Nibenese bring flowers and wine to it, and the Naka-Desh hang tin chimes in the mangroves above.

Calyphe was a Dibella shrine of the Kothringi at the western end of the mangrove country, a few miles from the Gideon road. When the Knahaten Flu emptied the Blackwood in 2E 560 its keepers died untended, and the mangroves have grown through the floor since.
A buried offering-vault, a chime-keeper who guards the roots or a Gideon digger hunting a Dibella relic.
Leaf-carved grey stone sunk to the lintels in black mud, with mangrove roots arched over the altar and the broken pillars. Chimes tick in the branches over it.
The Kothringi, the silver-skinned humans of the Blackwood, raised this shrine before the Knahaten Flu killed them. It is a Dibella shrine of leaf-carved stone half sunk in mangrove roots.
The shrine is uninhabited. A Nibenese shrine-seeker from Gideon may leave an offering at the altar slab. The diggers keep a camp on the dry hummock beside it.
The shrine is unheld. Diggers from Gideon reach it by flat-bottomed boat through the mangrove channels, and Naka-Desh boatmen tie a chime to the roots at the landing on their way past.
Restless dead of the knights walk the barracks at night, and wild boars and wolves den in the roofless nave. The tomb steps are slick and the cellar floor is rotten.
The knights' hall was kept by the garrison's pay and the grain the farms around Gideon sent it. Today it yields dressed stone for Gideon's builders and the odd corroded blade or buckle.
The knights took Kynareth and Mara as their patrons, as many Kothringi did and the hall's end wall carries a worn wave-and-wind carving. A Gideon soldier will leave a coin on it for luck.

Eurydike was a hall of Kothringi knights who served in Gideon's garrison in the Second Era. They died in the Knahaten Flu with the rest of their people, and the hall has stood empty since; its barracks block fell in long ago.
A knight's silver helm missing from the last tomb still sealed, a re-opened grave or a quarrel over a silver-skinned mummy that two diggers both found.
A long low hall of grey-white stone with its roof gone, a row of broken columns down the middle and a tumbled barracks wing at the back. A rusted shield-hook still hangs from one wall.
A ruin of the Kothringi, the silver-skinned humans of the Blackwood who died of the Knahaten Flu. It is a hall of Kothringi knights who served in Gideon's garrison in the Second Era.
The hall is uninhabited. Off-duty guards from Gideon sometimes camp in its doorway and tell the hall's story to newcomers. Treasure-hunters come for the knights' tombs.
Nothing holds it. It lies within a day's walk of Gideon, so Gideon's watch and the diggers both know it and carts on the Gideon road steer by its broken gable.
Shoals lie off the point. Sea-drakes work the water below the rock.
The keepers rely on oil and fish that passing boats leave at the rock.
A Sithis token of knotted net hangs on the tower stair, and the keepers touch it on their way up to the lamp.
The light was first built by the Empire and was rebuilt by the Archwardens after the old tower fell.
Wreckers show a false light on the shore with a brass lamp stolen from the tower's store, and a keeper who went to find it has not come back.
A stone tower on a rock with a stilt keeper's house, rimed with sea salt.
A lighthouse on the south coast at the edge of the Sea of Mists.
A keeper's family of four lives at the light, parents and two children who help with the lamp.
A keeper family lives in the stilt house at the base and tends the lamp each night.

The town centre is mostly safe: guarded by the council's men, with slaughterfish in the canals and cutpurses in Pusbottom. The drowned Imperial quarter and the Hist's roots are dangerous, with sea-drakes in the deep water beyond.
Lighterage, bay trade, salvage from the drowned quarter and saltrice from the beds of the delta villages. Pusbottom, repopulated as a slum, supplies the criminal trade of the coast.

The third Hist is walled but open, tended by two minders at once and no faction may hold exclusive access. A sunken shrine to Xhon-Mehl the Fisher, the Ancestral Organ Lord of Lilmoth, is known to divers.

Founded by the Lilmothiit, ruled by Priest-Kings and taken by the Empire; its Imperial Quarter was looted when the An-Xileel drove the Empire out at the secession. Its second Hist grew mad and summoned Umbriel in 4E 48, and the Slaughter at Lilmoth destroyed the city. The site was resettled in the generations after, because the harbour has no rival nearby.

The drowned quarter, whose name locals will not say to strangers and the villas that salvagers dive for. The young Hist with its two minders, and the story its people tell of the mad tree before it. Pusbottom's thieves and the docks-only law some officials still enforce. The sunken shrine of Xhon-Mehl can be reached by diving as far as breath allows.

Ninety percent of the fabric is Argonian stilts and platforms that climb into the air, wired together by walkways, over a drowned layer of Imperial villas. Old Imperial walls survive in places; mould, vines, big bamboo, sleeping palms and harmless drifting shines mark the drowned quarter.

A merchant port on the southern point of the Althii islands, built over shallow water so large ships anchor out and lighter their goods in. It is the biggest town on the south coast and the market for the delta villages and estates of the Althii islands.

About four in five are Argonians, with a working foreign dock population of Bretons, Khajiit and Imperial-descended traders. Elders, including retired Shadowscales, settle disputes. Tree-minders rotate through the Hist's post so that no one holds it alone.

Rebuilt but not restored: smaller, lower and wholly Argonian in its fabric. The merchant council sets the dock tolls and pays the guards. Its people are hostile to the successor state, whose party killed the old town and the officials who once kept unlicensed foreigners on the docks enforce that law in some places and let it lapse in others.
Sinkholes under the turf, snakes in the burrow roofs and the shades of the plague dead at the third dome. A stranger is likelier to be lost than attacked.
The den housed about a family and the small trades it kept: dye roots, fox-fur work and bead-dyeing. It now draws antiquaries and burrow-robbers from Natai.
Fox-kite tokens hang in a ring of three burrows facing south, spirit tokens for the fox-folk dead. Some are fresh, left by people who do not say who they are.

Kit Mounds was one of the fox-folk dens near the inland edge of the washes. Its families went inland toward Blackrose over generations in the Lilmothiit's long withdrawal, and the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560 finished the last of them.
A Blackrose antiquary wants the carved fox-kite pole from the south dome brought to her whole, and a Natai herb-woman says a fox-folk mask lies in the third dome with the last of its dead.
Three low turf domes with doorways no taller than a seated Argonian, leaf-lined and flooded to the knee. A line of rotting fox-kite poles runs between them, pointing toward Mudmoth.
Kit Mounds is a Lilmothiit ruin, a cluster of turf domes standing near the south of the washes.
There are no Lilmothiit left to live here. The nearest living people are Lujei hunters and Natai fishermen, who avoid the mounds and a Blackrose scholar who camps here when the rain eases.
The domes are overgrown with sedge and standing water fills the lower burrows. Scholars from Blackrose have dug here twice and left pegs in the turf.
Thorn tangles that hold a person like a net, venomous snakes in the burrow roofs and plague-dead who rise on the crown at dusk. The brambles are the worst of it.
The den kept bramble-fruit presses and fox-pelt work, and it now draws delta antiquaries and fruit-pickers from Delta Ferry when the brambles fruit.
A cluster of spirit stones faces the lake, each with a small notch for a fox-tail charm. Delta Ferry boatmen add a thread for luck on the crossing.

Brushmound was a Lilmothiit den between Khariton and the delta ferry, left empty in the fox-folk's long withdrawal inland; the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560 took the few who stayed. Bramble overran the mound afterward.
A Delta Ferry boatman needs the thorn cut back from a buried ferry cache, and a Blackrose scholar wants one of the notched spirit stones carried out to her.
A thorn-wrapped mound of turf with three burrow mouths and a bramble canopy so thick that the roofs look like a single hill. A ferry track skirts it on the east.
A Lilmothiit ruin: a bramble-covered den north-east of Ka-Asei.
No living Lilmothiit remain; Delta Ferry boatmen and Khariton scavengers cross the mound and a patient scholar from Blackrose has dug a test pit.
Bramble hides the mound's three doorways and the burrows are shallow with standing water. Delta Ferry traders sometimes camp on its dry crown.
Mudcrabs and hackwings hold the beach below. Restless dead walk the midden at night, a wraith keeps the child's tomb and old traps guard the grave-passages.
While it lasted the den's fox-folk traded shells and salted fish with the Argonian villages. Now treasure-hunters come for its grave-goods and beachcombers for the shell.
The den's graves are lined with shell and bone, which suggests care for ancestors by the shore. The Lilmothiit's own beliefs are not remembered, so the rest is guesswork.

The Lilmothiit drew inland from the coast over generations, and the Knahaten Flu (2E 560-603) emptied the last dens, this one among them. Argonians have fished the shore ever since and left the den alone.
A fox-tail charm lies in a child's tomb, and a carved bone flute among the shells. The fishermen who hear the kits at night want the tomb quieted.
Low turf-and-leaf domes, cracked and weed-grown, with a midden of shells.
Ashiit Den is a cluster of low turf-and-leaf domes, cracked and weed-grown, above a midden of shells. Vine covers it and Argonians keep away.
Ashiit has no inhabitants, though fishermen swear they hear kits' voices on still nights. Beachcombers and a few treasure-hunters visit and do not stay.
Ashiit Den stands on the south-western shore of the southern island, half fallen in and swallowed by vine. Argonians who pass along the coast avoid it as a place of the old sickness.
Old bone-chime tripwires hang in the tunnels, and the smugglers' door is guarded by armed crews. At night the wind-driven sand sounds like footsteps.

Kitsa was a small burrow of kits and elders who gleaned the southern shore for eggs, shells and wreck-wood. Now smugglers hide moon sugar and stolen goods in its tunnels and a few treasure-hunters dig for bones.
Tiny shell charms hang in the tunnel niches, and the walls show kit-stories scratched in ash. Their meaning is lost, though they read as a hearth-faith of ancestors and small guardian beasts.
A small den of kits and elders, built over and silted up across the centuries and left empty when the Knahaten Flu ended in 2E 603.
A kit's story scratched on the walls; a smugglers' door added to the tunnel, with moon-sugar crates behind it.
Kitsa Burrow's domes sit half buried in dune sand, with tunnels running under the dunes.
Kitsa Burrow is a set of domes half buried in dune sand, with a door that smugglers have cut into its tunnel.
Kitsa Burrow is uninhabited. Smugglers have cut a door into the tunnel, and they alone use it; the crews are mostly Khajiit off the Southern Sea sloops.
Kitsa Burrow lies at the southern tip of the island, its domes half buried in dune sand and its tunnels half full of it. Passing Argonians keep to the water side of the dunes.
The crown is hollow and the island farmers say the undead guard the chieftain's tomb. Giant snakes and skeevers nest in the lower galleries.

It was the meeting-ground where the island's dens traded and settled disputes, and the chieftain's household lived on the crown. Treasure-hunters now come for the burial hoard and are rarely seen again.
The ring of posts and the central mound suggest a gathering-place for the dead, with a chieftain's burial under the crown. How the fox-folk honoured it is not remembered.
Once the meeting-ground of the island's fox-folk, and the last of their dens to empty when the Knahaten Flu (2E 560-603) took the remnant.
A chieftain's burial hoard lies under the mound, with a fox-bone talisman beside it. The farmers would pay to see the lights end.
A large turf mound crowned with a fallen leaf-roof and ringed by fallen posts.
Reknaa-iit is a large turf mound crowned with a fallen leaf-roof and ringed by fallen posts. It was the meeting-ground of the island's fox-folk until the Knahaten Flu.
The mound is empty of residents and no village stands near it. Island farmers like Wattle-Pool's couple see lights there some nights and stay indoors.
Reknaa-iit stands at the centre of the southern island, the largest den-mound on the isle and half fallen in. Argonians crossing the island steer well clear of its ring of fallen posts.
Crocodiles and skeevers hold the tunnels, and Argonians nearby say the dead stir beyond them. Old pit-traps lie in the mound passages.
Rushiit was a den of foragers living on the northern island's wetland game and reed. Treasure-hunters come now, but crocodilians turn most of them back at the door.
The Lilmothiit's beliefs are not remembered, though the surviving charms show care for the dead and for fox-spirits. The tunnels are too fouled by predators to show more.
A den emptied when the Knahaten Flu (2E 560-603) took its last people; its tunnels were taken by crocodiles and skeevers.
The lost treasure-hunters' packs lie somewhere in the tunnels; a crocodile with a golden ring in its nest.
Mounds of turf and leaf, the entrance gnawed wide by predators.
Rushiit Den is a set of turf-and-leaf mounds whose entrance predators have gnawed wide. Crocodiles and skeevers hold the tunnels.
Rushiit is deserted. The predators have driven off even beachcombers, and a party of treasure-hunters from Archon went in some years back and did not return.
Rushiit Den lies in the heart of the northern island, its mounds gnawed open and now a lair for marsh predators. Argonians in the area say the place is wrong and keep their children from it.
Undead in the tomb-rooms and smugglers in the lower hall, with cracked domes overhead. The shore path from Fort Reedmoth is the only easy approach.
Tailfall's fishers are remembered in the tales told along this shore. Smugglers and treasure-hunters use the den now, and story-singers come to see the carvings.
A ring of tails carved into the doorposts shows an ancestor cult built around the fox-tail, and a kit-fable on a lintel tells a founding story. The dead are laid facing the shore.
It was a den of fishers, emptied by the Knahaten Flu (2E 560-603), and tales of its kits survive in Argonian stories.
A kit-fable carved on a lintel; a hideout used by smugglers, and a garrison that looks away.
Domes overlooking the shore, a ring of tails carved in the doorposts.
Tailfall Mound is a set of domes overlooking the shore, with a ring of tails carved in its doorposts. Smugglers hide in the lower rooms.
Tailfall is deserted but for smugglers, who hide in the lower rooms and watch the strait. Reedmoth's soldiers pretend not to know.

Tailfall Mound looks out over the north-eastern shore of the northern island, close to Fort Reedmoth, an old Imperial '-moth' fort now held by the Archwardens. Argonians who pass avoid its domes, and the garrison does not patrol it.
The lower tunnels lie wholly under water with no air pocket, snakes nest in the fallen roof and plague-dead wait in the lower burrow. A swimmer who goes too far into the tunnels drowns.
The den kept a small reed-dye trade and a few hides. It now draws reed-cutters from Mir-Xal and treasure-hunters after fox-kite relics.
Faded fox-kite cloth hangs in the dry roots of a leaning tree at the den's edge, and the Mir-Xal hunter ties a thread to it for a safe return.

Tailhollow was a fox-folk den at the western edge of the washes. Its families moved inland toward Blackrose over generations, as the Lilmothiit withdrew from the coasts and the Knahaten Flu in the 2E 560s killed those still here. A hollow where the roof fell in gave it its name.
A Mir-Xal reed-cutter has found a sealed clay jar in the hollow that he will not open, and the Mir-Xal hunter asks that his blind be left alone.
A roofless turf hollow with its tunnel mouths half under water and a ring of black stumps around it. Fox-kite poles lie fallen across the mud.
Tailhollow is a Lilmothiit ruin, a flooded fox-folk den lying in the west washes.
Tailhollow has no residents. Mir-Xal reed-cutters work the edges and an old Mir-Xal hunter keeps a blind in the hollow.
The den is waterlogged. The roof has fallen in and the burrows are open to the sky. Mir-Xal watermen use it as a landmark on the western channel.
The turf roof has fallen in at the back and the dome's low passages are dark and narrow. Mudcrabs and a giant mudcrab den in the hearth chamber, and crocodiles lie in the pools round the mound.
Once a camp of the fox-folk, it now offers scraps of fox-kite fabric and bone-charms to those who dig.
Charms of orange paper to the fox spirits still hang inside the dome.

The Lilmothiit once held the southern coast and founded Lilmoth and Blackrose. Over generations they withdrew inland toward Blackrose, and the Knahaten Flu finished those who were left; this den was abandoned in that long withdrawal.
A fox-folk charm, a hidden kit-cache or a scholar seeking Lilmothiit lore.
A low grass-covered dome with a door, a hearth ring and faded orange paper.
A dome den of the Lilmothiit, turf and leaf-woven, left to the weather.
The den has no residents. The Lilmothiit were nomadic and left little behind.
The den is uninhabited and half left to the weather; scholars and diggers come only rarely.
The camp is close to Thorn's patrols. Slaughterfish swarm the water below the landing, where offcuts and scraps are thrown in and take anyone who swims there.
Logs and sawn planks floated to Thorn; the loggers buy food and rope from Guxal.
The Argonian sawyers press a smear of sap from each felled trunk onto the camp's oldest stump, asking the Hist pardon for the cut; the Dunmer among them laugh at it and do the same.
It grew out of the Archein concession timber camps that fed Thorn's building; the field-owners kept it when the Archeins fell.
A gang boss whose best raft broke loose and lodged at the Ovezza quay among the ruin's dead, and a stand of old hardwood the Argonian sawyers will not cut because grave-stakes stand among its roots.
A bunkhouse and plank-drying sheds on pilings above a raw earth bank, log rafts moored along the water, stumps and sawdust round a saw-pit.

A timber camp on the inlet's southern shore, west of Thorn, named by its crews for the raw bank the water has cut beside the landing. It is the nearest timber to Thorn that the field-holders own outright.
Five or six: a gang boss hired by a field-holding family, a cook and sawyers from Thorn's riverside villages, Argonian and Dunmer, who go home to their own villages between fellings.
A handful of crews cut and raft timber for Thorn's builders and for the garrison at Fort Thornmoth.
Crocodiles and giant snakes prowl the stand, and the Mine-Burners come with bows when the camp's fee is late.
The loggers sell red mangrove timber and bark to Soulrest's merchants.
Sithis, with a Bosmer shipwright's Y'ffre charm over the door.
The tribes burned Soulrest's timber concessions in 3E 427. This camp is a small one the Mine-Burners allow, because it cuts only the red mangrove at the basin's edge and pays them for it.
A late fee, a lost log-raft or a body found in the timber could put the camp in trouble.
Log huts, a skid-road, piled red logs and a landing on the channel.
A logging camp of a few huts and a log-landing, cutting for Soulrest's merchant council.
Argonians from Soulrest cut the timber, under a Khajiit foreman who came up from the port.
Five loggers and a foreman work a stand of red mangrove; the Mine-Burners put up with them for a fee.
Predators prowl the forest around the clearing. Falling timber kills loggers who work carelessly.
Redgum Camp fells red gum and hauls the logs along the track to Soulrest, which buys all it cuts.
The loggers nail a gar jaw to the felling-post as a Sithis-token, and each man touches it before the first cut of the day.
Redgum Camp carries on the timber trade of the Third Era concession, cutting the same red gum stands.
One of the loggers has gone missing in the forest. A Banujha band has cut mine-burner signs into the best red gums and warns the camp off them.
A clearing in the forest holds a bunk house, a log yard stacked with red gum and the start of a haul track.
Redgum Camp is a timber camp in the forest of the Percar hills, west of Chasepoint on the cape.
Five Argonian loggers live and work at Redgum Camp, sharing a single bunk house.
The camp cuts for Soulrest, whose merchant council takes the logs and in return feeds and guards the crew.
Lamias, undead knights and wards fed by the keystones guard the citadel and the caverns beneath it, making the hill deadly to anyone who enters.
Once the Ayleid cult centre and keystone workshop; now a source of Ayleid relics, keystone shards and tombs for scavengers.
The Ten Ancestors; a Hist-shoot tended by the Veesa-Teeleel stands outside; Argonians remember the keystones as a theft of their dead.

Built after 1E 198 over subjugated Argonians. The Liege Lord bound his knights; the Enchanter turned the binding on him and had the knights kill him. In 2E 582 Dominion soldiers, lamia and ancient Ayleid warriors held it.
A keystone that still holds a soul; the Hist-shoot outside and its keeper; a looter band that went into the caverns and has not come out.
A hilltop amphitheatre with a ring of ruined seats, an inner bailey and tomb wings below; pale stone and dead trees.
Loriasel is a ruined Ayleid citadel and amphitheatre built by the Barsaebics for the Ten Ancestors on a hill over the Venomous Fens.
None live here; lamias and undead; a guarded visitor's track from Jal-Veesa.
The ghost-knights were freed in 2E 582; the Enchanter's works and the keystones remain. The Veesa-Teeleel guard the ruin from looters.
Gar and crocodilians in the channel; bandits on the track; the washes beyond are wild.
Lujei lives on fish, eels and cut reeds from the channel shallows and on the ferry fare and the hire of its pole-boats.

Lujei's tree-minder knows every egg the ferry families lay and carries the dead out by boat to the drowned Blackrose tree, a short pole across the lake. The elders pay a share of the crossing tolls to the island core as the price of that burial right.
A fishing village that grew into the island's west landing after the late-3E rebellion, when the city could no longer keep a bridge there.
A missing ferryman, a toll quarrel with the island core, a night crossing with a passenger's sealed chest.
Stilt houses on a muddy shore, a fish-drying rack frame, a lantern post at the landing, a tarred pole-boat yard.
A lakeshore village on the west bank, with Lujei Ferry just to its west, facing Blackrose across the channel.
Lujei's families are Argonian fishers on the west bank of the channel, among them a few descended from the old Imperial prison's inmates.
Its elders pay the island core for protection and keep the ferry crew, who report to them.
Gar and crocodiles in the channel; night crossings are by lantern only.
The crew charges a fare per head and per cart across the Blackrose channel, with an extra charge for each beast of livestock.
A knot of eel-skin, a Sithis-token, is tied to the landing post and the polemen touch it before a night crossing.
Run since the road was cut in the Third Era; the Imperial bridge fell in the late-3E rebellion and was not rebuilt.
A passenger who must not be seen, or a raft cable that has been cut.
A plank landing, a cable and winch, a lantern pole, a thatched shelter on stilts.
A ferry landing on the channel: a cable raft, a landing hut and a waiting shelter.
The landing is kept by Argonian ferry families who live beside the raft, in huts on the Lujei shore of the channel.
A crew of two families keep the raft for Lujei's elders and the island core.
Slaughterfish near the landing; the shoal causeway runs under knee-deep water and a giant mudcrab lairs in its reeds.
Eels, fish, piloting fees and the lantern toll from boats crossing between Julo and Yalugo.
Sithis and the lake itself; a stone cairn on the high point is where the island's dead are laid.
No stake tells of its founding. The island's stone footings are read as the work of incomers in the generations after 4E 48; before them the island was a bare reed bank.
A lantern on the island has been answered from open water; the old pilot knows a hidden passage across the lake; the eel pots keep coming up crushed by something large in the reeds.
Low reed-and-stone houses on a hump of silt, eel pots drying on poles, a lantern post at the south tip and flat water on every side.
Luntoc is a small island hamlet in the lake, built in the stone-footed Stormhold manner; it serves as a pilot station for the shoals.
About five residents: one Argonian fishing family and a boy who pilots strangers across the shoals.
Five people keep eel traps, a lantern for night boats and a causeway of stones across a shoal that surfaces at low water.
Quiet by day. Slaughterfish in the shallows below the kilns, and now and then a raid by a hungry Tumnatu party or a Naga band off the north road.
Red-clay pottery and dye, fish and eels. Pots go by canoe to Truowa and Aroxhu; salt and tin come back.
Hist and Sithis; the mound's small tree is tended by a tree-minder who also keeps the eggs of the three neighbouring camps.
No stake tells of its founding. The mound-building habit and the Tumnatu camp to the west imply a village set up as a lake landing for Aroxhu's pottery trade in the generations after 4E 48.

The kiln-fired clay will not set since lake water got into the kiln-pit; Aroxhu's potters want the secret of Marzai's red glaze; the ferryman has seen a lantern on the lake at night where no boat should be.
Low reed houses on a raised red-clay mound, drying racks of pots and dyed cloth, a kiln-smoke haze and canoes drawn up on the lake shore.
Marzai is a village of about ten on a raised mound of red clay where the lake meets the eastern shore, a western outlier of the Clay-Mound People of Aroxhu.
About ten residents of the Oxhu-Teeleel people: potters, fishers, a ferryman and an elder-woman who sings the story of the mound and its families.
It sends two elders to the Aroxhu council and keeps cool peace with its Tumnatu neighbours across the water, trading eggs and smoked fish for clay-fired pots.
There is rockfall inside and an old tunnel behind the north wall. The outside is mostly safe, as the road to Oxayo is watched from Fort Chalkmoth.
The pit yields building stone, cut in blocks and floated down the river to Tsonac.
A cairn of cut chips stands at the gallery mouth; every new quarryman adds one on his first day. The crew ask the sleeping Hist of Tsonac, through Oxayo's elder, for sound rock.

Xanuc Diggings has cut building stone from the mesa wall since Imperial times, when the Legion's masons took stone for Fort Chalkmoth; the Stone-Sleepers of Oxayo took it over when the Legion left at the secession.
The north gallery has broken through into a rough older tunnel full of webs, and the foreman's youngest hand went in after a dropped lamp and has not come out.
A raw cut in the mesa wall above Oxayo with grey spoil heaps down the slope and a timbered entrance. The ox-cart track winds down beside it.
Xanuc Diggings is a quarry mine in the wall of Chixathe Mesa between Oxayo and Fort Chalkmoth, and the best building stone on the mesa.
Four quarrymen, a foreman and a cart-driver, all Stone-Sleepers, who live in Oxayo and walk up each morning.
A crew works one gallery and a cutting face, with an ox-cart track down the mesa side to Oxayo.
A rockfall risk inside; mostly safe outside because the road is watched.
The pit yields chalk and limestone, burned to lime for mortar and saltrice-pan lining.
Lime-white handprints mark the pit's inner wall, one for each worker burned at the kilns. The crew ask Noota Nara's Hist to keep the rain off the kiln.
Chalkmoth Pit is the chalk and limestone working that Fort Chalkmoth was sited to guard, cut since Imperial times for lime. It lies on the mesa shoulder between the fort and Noota Nara.
A carter who drove a load of lime west and came back without cart, ox or lime, telling of Sarpa and an old chalk face that has fallen open onto a bricked Imperial storeroom.
A white-scarred pit in the mesa with a lime kiln and smoke above it, and a cart track running to Noota Nara.
Chalkmoth Pit is a chalk pit on the mesa shoulder between Fort Chalkmoth and Noota Nara, named for the fort above it.
A kiln-master, four diggers and a carter, all from Noota Nara, who pay the fort's toll on every cart that leaves.
A crew works one chalk face and a burning kiln, and the white dust shows from the fort's wall.
Rockfall inside and a long drop at the cutting edge. The outside is mostly safe because the Ayiin road is watched.
The pit yields dressed building stone sold to Thorn's builders.
A cairn at the gallery mouth is kept by the Ayiin crew, who ask Tsonac's sleeping Hist to keep the flank sound. The Thorn masons step round it without a word.
Thorn's builders first quarried the east flank in Imperial times; the Stone-Sleepers of Ayiin took the cut over when they settled the river below, and work it still.
A cart of dressed blocks for Thorn lies smashed at the foot of the track with its driver gone, and the crew hear tapping behind the gallery's north wall at night.
A sheer cut in the mesa's east flank above Ayiin, with square blocks stacked beside a timbered entrance and a steep cart track.
Kalaxo Cut is a sheer quarry face and gallery on the mesa's east flank above Ayiin, the nearest good stone to Thorn.
Four quarrymen, a foreman and a cart-driver from Ayiin and now and then a Thorn mason who walks up to choose his blocks.
A crew works one gallery and a cutting face, hauling blocks down to the Ayiin road in ox-carts.
The older shaft is half-fallen, its side galleries blocked by rock; brine pools with rotting water lie below, and mudcrabs nest in the spoil heap.
Rock-salt for curing: blocks go to Thorn, ground salt to Arorha for fish. The salt is cheap but its trade is steady.
The workers carry small hatching-stones from their home villages and leave a pinch of salt at the mine mouth for those buried underground.
Imperial-era bonded labour first cut the salt-bed for the East Empire Company's saltrice and fish trade; the shafts were kept running by Thorn's field-owners after the Company left.

The old shaft was walled off after a collapse that killed bonded labourers; one of their descendants wants the bodies brought out and staked, and the overseer refuses. Something has broken through the walled-off gallery wall from the other side.
A cut face of grey-white rock streaked with rust, a timber headframe, wooden carts and stacked salt blocks under reed roofs. The air smells of brine and wet stone.
A small rock-salt mine in the rise between Thorn and the bight, worked by hired hands for Thorn's field-owners. The name is the Warden Marches' plain Imperial-style naming for a cold brine pit.
About five Argonians, descendants of freed labourers, plus an overseer from an old Archein family who keeps the mine's keys and the one cart-horse.
A handful of workers cut brine-hard salt blocks in two shafts and load them on carts. A warden from Fort Thornmoth comes each month for the toll on the carts.
Rockfall traps in the timber-propped galleries. Giant spiders nest in the old walled-off galleries deeper in.
Raw crystal sold to Stormhold's crystal-cutters; a share of every load goes to the Vicecanons for the right to dig.
A small ancestor shrine stands at the mouth of the adit, where the delvers pause before going down.
The crystals under Stormhold were dug by Warden Varus's prisoners in the 3E; the market remained and private diggers moved in.
A vein that sings at night; a pit-boss who wants someone to go through the wall the old delvers built across a gallery.
A timber-propped adit in a hillside, a tipping-yard of spoil and a few huts.

Tenmal Pits is a crystal pit above Tenmal village. Canon puts the Stormhold Crystals in the tunnels under the city, dug in the late 3E; a seam running into the hills east of it would be worked by the nearest village once the prison diggings stopped.
Argonian and Dunmer delvers; a pit-boss who knows how to read a vein.
An adit and a tipping-yard where delvers bring up raw crystal for a Stormhold buyer.
The lower shafts stand full of black water, rotten props have dropped stone across two galleries and predators and outlaws shelter in the workings.
Old Goldseam was a gold mine worked under the Soulrest concession until the tribes burned it in 3E 427.
A crooked Hist-token on a pole at the mine mouth is the last shrine, put up by tribal raiders who burned the works in 3E 427. Rain has bleached it to bare wood.
Dug by the Empire's Soulrest concession; destroyed in 3E 427.
A buried payroll, a rich vein left unmined and a rescue of trapped diggers.
Rusted rails run from the mine mouth past collapsed timber props to a broken sluice.
Old Goldseam is a run of rusted rails, collapsed timber props and a broken sluice, with flooded shafts and a ruined winch house. Outlaws from the Percar hills shelter in the mine mouth.
Old Goldseam has no residents. A few outlaws from the Percar hills shelter in the mine mouth, and scavengers pass between Stonecut Quarry and Zeh-Orun.
The mine is a ruin of flooded shafts and a winch house fallen into disrepair, with outlaws sheltering at its mouth.
Gas gathers in the fallen galleries, loose-rock traps hang where the props have rotted and scavengers at the portal are armed.
It once cut timber and gold-bearing ore together for the Imperial concession. Now Chasepoint salvagers haul its iron and charred beams away.
A half-burned plank where the miners scratched Sithis marks hangs near the portal, still in place. Chasepoint carters make the sign as they pass.
Blackdrift was dug under the Soulrest concession for timber and ore, and was burned in 3E 427.
A gallery behind the fallen stone is sealed. The gold the overseers stored there when the tribes came in 3E 427 may lie inside.
Black-scorched timbers lean over a collapsed portal, and the old overseer's shed stands crooked beside it.
Blackdrift is a mine of black-scorched timbers and a collapsed portal, with a scavenger camp at the portal. It cut timber and gold-bearing ore together.
Blackdrift has no residents. Salvagers from Chasepoint work its timber, and an outlaw crew sometimes uses the old overseer's shed as a lookout.
Sealed or collapsed, with a camp of scavengers at the portal.
The flooded galleries drown the unwary. The smugglers who store goods in the mine are not friendly to strangers.
It was the ninth numbered shaft of the Imperial concession on the south of the cape; now it draws salvagers for iron ties and rail, and Xal-Tarek's garrison discourages the bolder ones.
A cracked Imperial votive niche is cut into the shaft head and holds a single drowned lamp. Miners say that the ninth shaft took a toll of lives, and Xal-Tarek's men avoid the name.
Ninth Shaft was part of the Imperial concession on the south of the cape, and was burned in 3E 427 with the others.
A smugglers' store is hidden in the lower galleries. Whoever finds it will have to deal with its owners.
A timber headframe stands over a wide shaft mouth, black with old fire and rotted at the base.
Ninth Shaft has a timber headframe over a wide mouth, flooded below, with smugglers storing goods above.
Ninth Shaft has no residents. Xal-Tarek's patrols check the portal on their rounds, and a few scavengers work its spoil by night.
The lower galleries are flooded. Smugglers use the dry upper levels to store their goods.
Gas collects in the pit, vents in the burned floor burst into flame when stepped on and fire-scarred undead wander the floor of the cut.
It was an open cut worked for ore by the Imperial concession and burned in the uprisings of 3E 427; it now draws scavengers who dig the slag for scrap and Naxan boys who find glass in the ash.
A scorched Hist-token is nailed to a charred post where the cut begins, and loggers touch it as they cross.
Dug under the concession; fired in 3E 427; the Great Burn's network lies beneath.
A forgotten vent shaft in the cut leads down into the Great Burn's network of burned passages.
The cut is a black pit with gas shimmering over it, ringed by ash-grey slopes where the timber has burned away.
Ashfall Cut is a black pit with gas shimmering over it. Redtimber loggers cut through it on the way to Naxan.
Ashfall Cut is empty of residents. Redtimber loggers cut through it on the way to Naxan, and scavengers camp in the lee of the cut.
Gas vents hiss through the ash on the floor of the cut, and nothing grows on its burned slopes.
Safe in town; the surrounding marsh roads carry bandits and the wild washes have predators.
Tolls on the Soulrest road, carting timber and stone and a river quay for Blackrose-bound goods.
