Small Sithis shrines stand along its main street. Its dead are carried out to the Banujha tree and are not buried in the washes.
A waystation of the Third Era timber trade; it kept its trade when the mines burned in 3E 427 and grew as a toll town.
A toll dispute, a smuggler caught with Bramman's river cargo, a message for the Banujha tribes.
Timber and reed buildings on raised ground, a toll gate on the road, a warehouse quay, red clay tracks.
A pentagon town on the road between Soulrest and the Blackrose lakes, on the only broad dry rise in the washes.
Argonians, a few Khajiit teamsters and two Imperial-descended families who keep the toll house for Soulrest.
It answers to Soulrest's merchant council, though its reeve hears the mine-burning tribes' complaints too.
Dragon's-tongue patches are deadly to the careless; channels hide predators; Tumnatu parties pass by.
Dragon's-tongue and other swamp herbs, fish and a small guide fee for boats going south.
Sithis and a small chime kept for travellers; the hamlet's eggs are laid at Korydon.
The name is Kothringi in style. Argonians resettled the place after the Flu began in 2E 560. Its chime-post is the oldest working one in the Ultherus country.
The chime-tender has gone silent and the boats run blind in the fog; a boat came up from Blackrose with a dead man aboard; a spriggan guards the hummock where the rarest dragon's-tongue grows.
Stilt houses on a hummock, a tall chime-post of tin and copper above the roofs, herb racks and boats tied to every post.
Myroleon is a hamlet of about six Chime-Keepers at the southern end of the Ultherus swamp country, on the first channels toward Blackrose.
About six Argonian herb-gatherers; one of them strikes the post's chime for boats in fog.
In 4E 201 it keeps the chime-post for boats, gathers dragon's-tongue and sells it up to Korydon.
Paatru and Naga raiders cross the ridge; wild lizards in the pens.
Penned marsh-lizards, hides and tin chimes traded with the Paatru and taken as gifts to Helstrom at the Root Talk.
The families here honour Sithis and the Hist, and keep a small cairn on the ridge shoulder for the old dead of the Kothringi place.
A Kothringi-named place resettled by Argonians after the Knahaten Flu (2E 560–603); the ridge made it a lookout.
The Paatru camp wants a chime tuned; a Naga band is watching the pass; the old watchman saw a light on the peak where no fire should be.
Low stone-footed huts on a ridge shoulder, lizard pens, windchimes everywhere, wide views over the marsh.
Nacydes is a hamlet of about five on a ridge shoulder at the west of the Aunike country, among the few Chime-Keeper places that sit on drier ground.
About five Argonians, lizard-keepers and a chime-maker; they deal with the Paatru across the ridge only through hard bargaining.
Five people hold the hamlet, keep lizard-steeds and trade chimes for hides. They post a watch on the nearest peak.
Sea-drakes and surf off the shore; the wreck's cargo draws scavengers.
Natai lives on shellfish, sea fish, salt from its pans and cargo salvaged from the wreck beyond its shore.
The Natai tree-minder keeps a driftwood shrine of Sithis on the beach above the salt pans; the dead are carried to the Blackrose Hist by boat once a year.
Settled by Blackrose fisherfolk who followed the southern channels to the coast; it has salvaged the wreck to its east for a generation.
A wreck to dive, a salt-pan dispute, a smuggler landing that avoids Soulrest.
Low stilt houses along the beach, salt pans, drying racks, weathered salvage timber.
A coastal village on the south shore of the washes, at the tip where the land meets the Sea of Mists.
Natai's villagers are Argonian shellfish-gatherers who also strip the wreck off their shore for anything that washes loose.
Under the island core's nominal protection, though it is a long way off; it governs itself.
Pirates of the bay raid the coast boats. River predators prowl the channels near the village.
Naxan lives on fish, on hauling timber from the forest to the log landing and on coastal boats along the bay.

Naxan's Sithis shrine is a ring of pale stones on the headland, where fishermen and loggers both pause on the way to the Topal Bay road. The families share a single egg-chest that goes to the Banujha tree once a year by Soulrest's coast road.
Naxan began as a shore village of the Third Era timber trade on the cape's north coast. The timber trade is still its main work.
A boat has been hijacked off Naxan's coast. The loggers need a crew to raft a load of timber down to the landing before the rains.
Timber stilt houses stand on the shore, with a log landing at the water and drying racks for the catch.
Naxan has timber stilt houses, a log landing and drying racks at the western end of the Topal Bay road. A reeve governs it for Soulrest, and the ruined fort of Wrackmoth lies on the same coast.
Naxan's people are Argonian fishers and loggers, many of whom do both in a year.
A reeve governs Naxan on behalf of Soulrest's merchant council and settles disputes between its fishers and loggers.
Wild at night; predators on the bank; Tumnatu hunters in the reeds.
Staging fees, herbs, fish and mending. Most of the income comes from passing traffic.
The family worships Sithis, and its eggs are laid at the Hist tree in Korydon, the nearest town upriver.
No stake tells of its founding. The place is read as a Kothringi site resettled by Argonians, and it has stayed small.
A wrecked boat lies in the reeds with its goods unsold; a Kothringi cairn is hidden behind the houses; the lantern is lit from the water side at night and the family has not seen who does it.
A few stilt houses beside a green waterway, hung with chimes; a lantern post; mossy moorings.
Nemeon is a small hamlet on a side waterway between Lake Ulaish and Korydon. Its form follows the Kothringi-named towns.
About six Argonians: a boat-wife, her sons and a hired herb-picker.
It stages boats going between the lake and Korydon and keeps a waystation bench and a lantern.

The flooded undercroft is the danger: giant snakes lie in the drowned cellar and Ayleid dead stand at the broken arch. The mound top is open ground, and the way in from the Urvyn Farm side is the dry one.
Once an outlying hall of the Ayleid settlement; now a source of loot for scavengers.
Ayleid shrine fragments; the Veesa-Teeleel's ward-stakes ring the mound.
Barsaebic Ayleids settled this country after 1E 198 and were beaten by the Hist, by legend. Of this hall, the wardens know only that their grandmothers ringed it with stakes.
A Welkynd stone that lights by itself in the undercroft; ward-stakes pulled up one by one, and a Jal-Veesa youth seen near the mound at dusk.
White stone arches and fallen columns half-covered with vine on a reed-ringed mound; black water in the undercroft.

Nenria is a small Barsaebic Ayleid hall in the marsh south of Jal-Veesa. The Barsaebics settled this country after 1E 198 and left halls round Silyanorn and Loriasel; this one stands among them, and its name is of Ayleid shape.
The ruin has no residents; a hermit scavenger sometimes lives there.
Half-flooded and avoided. The Veesa-Teeleel call it sick ground and keep their own away.
The village is safe by day; the mesa edge above it is wilder.
Clay pots, spears with fire-hardened tips, fish and trade with the fort.
A Hist tree grows in the village. A dragon-spear is displayed beside it as a relic.

Long ago, in the legend the villagers tell, a dragon burned the village's walls to the ground. The villagers heated their spear-tips in the dragonfire, took the enchantment and pierced it; In the telling, Dreekius carried the head to Stros M'Kai, to hang in the Draggin Tail Inn in Port Hunding.
A spear-smith's apprentice says she can make the dragonfire spear-tips again if someone brings her fire salts, and the elders speak of the dragon's head, lost across the sea and wish it home.
A walled village of mounds and reed roofs, with a single burned-black post kept where the old gate stood.
Noota Nara is a village in Black Marsh and the original home of the Argonian Dreekius. It sits on the river below Fort Chalkmoth.
A dozen or so households of Argonians who follow the Clay-Mound customs of the east, led by a council of elders; hunters, potters and spearsmiths.
The village survives. It rebuilt its walls in timber and clay and still tells the story, with the head's loss as an old grievance.
Slaughterfish and mudcrabs lurk in the paddies around the village, and the paddy banks hold a few crocodiles.
Rice, fish and a ferry across the strait to the southern island.
Hatching families take their eggs to Lilmoth or Uluo; a carved post stands on the rice dyke for the dead of the paddies.
Founded by Lilmoth-coast families who drained rice ground; its boundary with Three Waters land is fixed by custom and kin ties.
A boundary quarrel with Uluo's families; a ferryman missing; a drained field that turned up old bones without grave-stakes.
Stilt houses beside paddies cut in low ground, sluice gates and a ferry pier.
A coastal village on the south shore of the northern island, between Uluo and the east coast road.
Argonians of the Lilmoth coast with some Three Waters in-laws.
Ten households farm rice, net fish and trade with both Uluo and Lilmoth.
The hamlet is safe, but the reeds of the basin around it are wild.
Tin and copper chimes, metal-woven rope and shallow-draft boats.
Z'en and Dibella beside Sithis; a chime for each of the dead.
The Kothringi named the place, and the Argonians who resettled it after the Knahaten Flu kept the name, as they did across the old Kothringi towns.
A chime-maker's commission, a boat race or a stolen tuning-fork.
Stone footings under stilt houses, tin and copper chimes on every eave and a long landing.
A hamlet of stilt houses with stone footings, kept by Argonians who resettled Kothringi-named places after 2E 560.
Chime-Keeper Argonians live here as craftsmen and traders, resettlers of a hamlet that bears a Kothringi name.
About eight people make chimes, boats and rope. The hamlet is orderly. Its people treat the Archwardens' officials coldly and Gideon's traders warmly.
Safe in the village; a sea-drake is seen now and then off the channel posts, and slaughterfish crowd the shallows.
Toll for the landing, lodging, boat repair, fish and a small trade in lantern oil and rope.
A post in the channel carved for the drowned; hatching families walk the long way to Lilmoth's tree, the third Hist.
Grew as a half-way stop on the Archon, Lilmoth, Soulrest and Tear line, where small boats rest and hand cargo across.
A boat found drifting with its crew gone; a boatman whose family owes both Archon and Lilmoth kin; goods that were not meant to be on the ferry.
Stilt houses and platforms linked by gangways, a hostel with a long deck, boats tied three deep and a lantern on a mast.
A village built over the water of the strait, at the narrowest crossing between the Nushara shore and the islands.
Argonians of the Lilmoth coast, with Archon and Lilmoth boatmen resting overnight.
Ten or so households keep the landing, a lantern and a hostel; most of the custom comes from Lilmoth, so its boat-owners pay Lilmoth's council a toll to land there.
Bay pirates come ashore at night when no fighters are home, and slaughterfish crowd the deep channel off the end of the jetty. Anyone who swims out after a lost net is bitten.
Fish, salt-fish and dried eel go up to Gideon and the ferry to Aphon carries the Warden watch's supplies. Gideon's council takes a small toll from boats at the landing.

Every boat is blessed before its first trip, with a prayer to Dibella for the Nibenese side of the family and a word to Sithis for the Argonian side. A shrine to the drowned stands at the water's edge, with a grave-stake for each one lost.

Olvani grew up at the estuary landing where Gideon's Imperial-era trade met Topal Bay's boats. When the Imperial ships left at the secession the landing's trade ended. The families who stayed lived by fishing and by the ferry to Aphon Isle.
A ferry that never came back from Aphon, a crate of moon sugar left under the jetty for a buyer who did not come or a quarrel over a net that ends at Gideon's courthouse.
Stilt houses on a long mudflat, drying racks, upturned punts, grey light off the bay and a smell of brine and smoke.
A village at the mouth of Gideon's estuary on Topal Bay's eastern shore. It is Gideon's fishing port and the landing for boats to Aphon Isle and the Topal Bay coast.
Lukiul families with Cyrodiilic names and a Khajiit sailor or two who came on a bay-boat and stayed.
About twelve people haul nets on the mudflats and ferry travellers to Aphon Isle. They report smugglers to Gideon when there is a reward and say nothing when there is not.
Armed lookouts who attack strangers quickly; the coves are strung with snares and tripwires, and the bluff caves hold mudcrabs and a trapped store room.

They move moon sugar, salt, ash-glass, Dunmer wine and untaxed saltrice and take a cut from every cargo. They are outlaws in full, unlike the chartered pirates of Marque Landing and the two crews are rivals.
Mostly none; some Dunmer keep a Tribunal-era charm, some Argonians a village-tree token. Everyone shows the sea respect.

Customs stand only at the recognised ports, so smugglers use any unwatched beach near one. Skeith lies between Thorn, Seafalls and Archon, which makes it the obvious cache for goods that dodge both customs houses.
The leader will hire a stranger to carry a cargo past Marshgate Watch. A rival pirate crew has burned one of his boats, and war between the two camps is close.
Lean-tos of driftwood, tarred canvas and reed roofs, boats hauled up on grey shingle, barrels hidden under nets, a smoking drying-rack.
Hollow Tide Camp is a smugglers' camp in the lee of Skeith Isle's low south-western bluffs, hidden from the sea lanes between Thorn and Archon.

Mixed crews: Argonian boatmen of the Okuwun coast, a few Dunmer from Tear, runaway Archein families and Khajiit moon-sugar dealers. The leader is a former Archon harbour hand who knows every customs man on the quay by name.
About fourteen men and women live in lean-to huts above the shingle, with two hidden coves and a cache in the caves under the bluff. They bring their boats in on moonless nights.
Bow and crossbow lookouts and a camp that fights as a crew. The keep above is a stronghold, and the water below the jetty is thick with slaughterfish.
Prize cargoes, ransom, protection from coast boats and the occasional commission to chase a rival. They sell to Archon quietly.
A rough sea-faith: each ship has a carved figurehead its crew swears by, and the dead are put out on a raft.

The Archon coast was riddled with pirates, and in the Blackwater War General Falco sent letters of marque to them. The tradition survived as a half-chartered fleet in 4E 201, the state's stand-in for a navy.
The captain wants the Hollow Tide leader's best boat burned at its mooring. A stranger who does it is taken aboard as crew and sails with a privateer's protection.
A line of hulks and stilt-houses on grey water, ropes and nets slung between, a stone jetty at the keep's foot, smoke and lanterns.
Marque Landing is a stilt-and-hulk pirate camp in the shallows on Skeith Isle's western shore, serving Rainbreaker Keep above it.

About twenty pirates, mostly Argonian boat-crews with a few Dunmer and Khajiit seamen. The pirate-captain, a one-eyed Argonian, sails on a commission that the Archwardens neither honour nor repudiate.
Four ships' crews share the camp. They hold the keep above as a strong room and raid shipping, but leave Archon's own boats alone.
Crocodiles lie around the weir and hackwings swarm over the drying racks in the heat, though the camp itself is safe for the wardens' families.
Eels, gar and reed bundles sold up river to Stormhold; weir fees from passing boats.
A small Hist-shoot shrine fed with the first eel of each catch.
The weirs are older than Stormhold's modern city-state and have been kept by the Sedge-Wardens since before the Dunmer came.
Someone is pulling up the weir stakes at night and leaving the crocodiles a way in; a boat of Dunmer traders asks to cross without paying.
Pale stilt huts on a mud bank, a woven fish-weir across the creek, mats and fish drying on racks.

Sedgeweir is one of the Veesa-Teeleel fish-weirs that feed Stormhold: the reed-wardens of Jal-Veesa keep the creeks round the city, and the creek south-east of the city is where they set one of their weirs. The name is the wardens' plain word for it.
Veesa-Teeleel families on rotation from Jal-Veesa; a weir-warden who knows every trap.
A few stilt huts and a drying-rack yard on the bank, with a boat landing and a weir across the creek.
The Naga camp to the north hunts here; predators come to the sap-skins and the station keeps spears at each door.
Sap tapped from the Hist-tended trees on the bank goes down to Helstrom's market; the station barters it for dried fish and cloth.
There is no Hist at the station; the keepers carry hatchlings and the dead to the nearest village tree. A small totem-post at the landing, carved with a sap-drop, is touched on leaving.
A hunters' camp for Helstrom's market that grew into a station kept all year. The interior tribes never left in 4E 48, and the Root-Folk have used this bank for as long as their songs go back.
A sap-skin has been slashed and swapped for a skin of plain water; the young egg-tender wants a clutch carried to Helstrom without the Naga seeing.
Four stilt huts and a drying frame of sap-skins on a firm bank, an eel-trap line across the shallows and a canoe landing wreathed in hanging moss.
Five Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom keep it, tapping sap from the trees along the bank and answering to a tree-minder in Helstrom.
About five Saxhleel sap-gatherers, a young egg-tender and a boy sent to learn the trees.
Five Saxhleel keep the station all year, tapping sap from the trees along the bank. They take the news to a tree-minder in Helstrom by boat and carry it in speech.
Naga and Tumnatu parties pass here; slaughterfish crowd the deep water where the river arms meet.
Hatchery eggs, fish and sap exchanged with boats going between Helstrom and the lake.
The station has no Hist of its own, so hatching and burial are done at the nearest village tree. A totem-post carved with a heron stands at the landing, and boatmen bow to it passing.
The junction's old nest-pits are read as sites that the Root-Folk kept from before the Empire; the station is the watch they keep on them.
A clutch is missing from the nest-pits; boats pass that did not come up the river; the old sap-speaker will name who took it for a price.
Tall stilt platforms over a wide river junction, nest-pits of clay lined with moss, a watch post with a lantern and a horn.
Five Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom hold its stilt platforms over the junction and tend eggs in clay nest-pits.
About five egg-tenders and watchers; one is an old sap-speaker.
Five Saxhleel hold the station where the river arms spread into the delta. They tend eggs, watch the water for strangers and send word to Helstrom's tree-minders at each new moon.
Large predators and the odd hunter-turned-bandit threaten the rise at the western end of the jungle.
The hunters of Xuvagol sell pelts, feathers and smoked meat and buy salt and arrowheads in return.
A small root shrine at the camp's edge for the Hist's speech.
Root-Folk hunters have used the rise for generations as a place from which to watch the jungle edge.

A trapper who saw torches moving at night among the Kaochalit ruin, which has no living inhabitants and an old giant snake as thick as a man that has taken three of the camp's snares and a hunter's arm.
Stilt houses under the trees, with pelts stretched on frames and a lookout in a tall trunk.
Xuvagol is a Root-Folk hunting station on a forested rise at the jungle's western end, the last stilt houses before the mesa road. The name is the hunters' own.
Saxhleel hunters and their kin, led by an old trapper who knows every path to Tsonac and has buried two sons under the rise.
Six Root-Folk live on the forested rise a day beyond Tselan; they hunt the jungle edge and trade pelts at Tselan.
Slaughterfish in the open water; smugglers use the islet at night and the keepers pretend not to see them.
Fish, eggs and a small fee for tying up, from boats on the Marzai-Truowa run.
The islet has no Hist; hatchlings are rowed to the nearest village tree. A totem-post at the landing is hung with Marzai shells, and the keepers touch it before a crossing.
A lake station kept by the Root-Folk to guard their share of the lake's eastern trade.
A cask left on the platform is marked with Truowa's quay-mark and nobody has come for it; the egg-tender has found new eggs in a nest abandoned for years.
A reed-built platform on silt with a lamp tower, an eel line and a stack of dried fish racks.
Four Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom hold a reed-built platform with a lamp tower and racks of dried fish.
About four Saxhleel live on the reed platform in the lake's eastern reaches: watchers, and an egg-tender.
Four Saxhleel hold the islet, watching the water between Marzai and Truowa and tending eggs. They pass news of the eastern shore to a tree-minder when a boat comes by.
The country around the post is wild, with predators in the sedge. A Naga camp lies a short way south. Its raiders watch the road.
Ferry fares, a night's bed, smoked meat for the road to Helstrom.
There is no formal worship; the family keeps a row of grave-stakes for its dead on a rise behind the house.
A ferry point where the road toward Helstrom crosses the eastern branch of the river, kept since the colonial period.
The ferryman sells directions and warns against the camp to the south; a body washed up at the landing.
A timber landing, a rope-hauled flat barge and a long low house of stone and reed.

Ranvos Landing is the ferry where the road from Stormhold toward Helstrom meets the river's eastern branch, kept by a Dunmer-descended family of the Stormhold country. The Dunmeri house name follows the city's old minority.
A Dunmer-descended ferryman and his Argonian crew, the one family that keeps the landing with the Vicecanons' leave.
One family keeps a flat ferry and a roadhouse and sells directions south.
Ultherus herbs can kill the careless; predators in the open water south; Tumnatu parties.
Lodging for boatmen, dragon's-tongue and swamp herbs, fish and mending.
There is no Hist at the station; the keepers go to Korydon's tree for hatching and burial. A totem-post at the jetty is carved with a boat-prow, and the crews touch it for fair passage.
A waystation of the Root-Folk in forest country south of Korydon. The Helstrom assembly hears of the Blackrose waters from its keepers.
A herb-gatherer wants dragon's-tongue taken to Korydon before it spoils; a boat from Blackrose never put in.
Stilt huts around a boat-yard with a bell at the landing and herb racks on every rail.
Five Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom keep stilt huts round a boat-yard, with a bell at the landing.
About five Saxhleel live at the waystation south of Korydon, boatmen who lodge the crews and herb-gatherers who rack their harvest.
Five Saxhleel keep the waystation, feeding boat crews bound south and watching the great water. They report to the tree-minder of Korydon at each full moon.
Crocodiles, giant snakes and the Root-Folk's own traps on every path.
Hunting, eggs and sap-gathering; they sell hides and skins to Aroxhu.
The eggs are warmed to a rhythm that they say the Hist sets from afar; they hold no tree here.
Helstrom's Root-Folk keep stations through the inner swamp, and Tazhul tends eggs on a warm mud-bank and hunts the marsh around it.
Two eggs have failed to hatch and the egg-minder believes someone has cursed them. A hunter has found a Sarpa feather in a trap.
Root-hollow lodges and stilt-houses on a mud-bank, egg-racks, drying hides, marsh herons.
Tazhul is a Root-Folk station on the edge of Okuwun-Rahei, a small outpost of Helstrom's people.
About four Saxhleel, hunters and an egg-minder, wary of strangers.
A small station with a rack of eggs and a hunters' lodge; the Root-Folk keep apart from the mounds and the Agaceph.
The road past the post is watched, and travellers are stopped at the chain. After dark giant snakes come down from the jungle to hunt round the well.
Small tolls and a share of whatever the travellers carry; it sells water and dried fish.
A hollow in the gatepost holds small gifts of food for the Hist, left by Stone-Sleeper carters who mistrust a post with no tree.
The Legion kept a chain of waystations on the track to guard Thorn's western road; at the secession the Archwardens' garrison at Fort Thornmoth kept this one as a toll post and let the rest fall in.
A Tsonac stone-carver's cart found abandoned a mile up the track with its ox killed by a giant snake, and a Stone-Sleeper carter who refuses the toll and blocks the chain with his load.
A stilted watch house with a lantern pole, a stone-lined well and a heavy chain across the track between two posts.
A roadside toll post called Thornway Watch by the garrison, set where the Tsonac track meets the bay's southern shore. Every load of Stone-Sleeper stone bound for Thorn passes its chain.
Argonian guards from the fort's garrison families, and a Dunmer runner who carries word to the fort and sells dye on the side.
Four of Fort Thornmoth's garrison take turns at the post, lifting the chain for carts once the toll is paid and sending runners to the fort when trouble comes up the track.
Mesa predators and the odd bandit from the Balormaak road make this a risky post.
Hides and feathers go to Ayiin and Joxhi, and the outpost gets cloth and salt in return. A guiding fee for travellers to Balormaak is a smaller income.
A small shrine to the Hist at the settlement edge, tended by the elder; eggs go north to the tribe's tree at Helstrom.
Yuvexa is an old watch point on the southern lip of the mesa, used by Root-Folk hunters from Helstrom for generations to watch the Balormaak ruin and the Ayiin road.

The elder's grandson went to Vorannuhl on a dare and came back silent, with a bronze ring that no family in Yuvexa has seen before; a pair of giant snakes has started taking goats from the post's pen.
Stilt houses under a few trees on the mesa's south edge, drying racks and a lookout in a trunk that faces the Velothi ruins.
Yuvexa is a Root-Folk post on the mesa's south lip, its lookout trunk facing the ruins of Vorannuhl.
Two Root-Folk families from Helstrom's hunting clans, one elder and a few youths, one of whom guides travellers to the ruins for coin.
Five or so people live here, hunting and gathering and trading to Ayiin. A lookout post faces Vorannuhl.
Smuggler bands from the coast and Sarpa raiders from the west.
The tolls are spent on spear-shafts, food and mats for the post. The elders of Renhu and Khiar are paid in fish and clay.
None official. The spears carry hatching-stones from their home villages.
Built after Arorha's boatmen lost goods to coast robbers, and manned by volunteers from Renhu and Khiar.
The watch has taken a smuggler alive, a Skeith man with Archon coin in his pack. The leader wants someone neutral to take him to Aroxhu before his crew comes for him.
A clay mound with a palisade of cut reeds, a round thatched watch-hut, a bar across the road and a rack of spears.
A watchpost of the Oxhu-Teeleel on a clay mound above the Renhu-Seafalls road.
Five Argonians who rotate in from Renhu and Khiar, led by a woman of Khiar who knows the road.
Five spears keep the watch, with a bar across the road. They pass Seafalls folk and Aroxhu carts free and take a toll of outsiders.
Giant snakes, swamp-crocodiles in the ditch and smugglers landing by night who fight when asked to pay.
Tolls, a few septims per cart. The post buys fish and bread from Arorha and sells nothing.
None officially. The wardens go home to their village trees to hatch and bury.

Built by the Imperial Commission as a toll and way-station for the Thorn-Archon road. It stood empty from the secession until the Archwardens' detachment took it back as a customs point on the east road.
A warden has been letting Skeith smugglers' boats through for pay. The sergeant wants the man caught before the blame falls on the sergeant.
A square stone-and-timber blockhouse on a mud-brick plinth, a toll bar across the road, a signal pole and a few huts of reed round it.
A small garrison post where the Thorn road crosses the neck of land at the bight's northern end. The name follows the Marches' habit of naming posts for what they watch.
Six Argonian wardens of old Archein lines, in patched half-Imperial livery, led by a sergeant who owns the post's one cutlass.
Six wardens rotate through from Fort Thornmoth. They take the customs toll on clay and salt and watch the shore for boats that avoid Thorn.
Mesa predators and a bandit now and then on the Tenmal road make this a risky post.
Hides and reeds go to Tenmal and the pit crews; the post gets lamp oil and iron in return.
A small shrine to the Hist at the post's edge; eggs are carried north to the Helstrom tree, and the elder holds the naming.
Nuxhal is a Root-Folk hunters' post on the western part of the mesa, used for generations as a gathering station for hunts beyond Tenmal Pits.

A pair of giant snakes has denned in the gully below the post and killed a youth on his first hunt, and the pit crews at Tenmal owe Nuxhal a debt of iron for last year's hides and keep putting it off.
Stilt houses under a stand of trees, drying racks and a lookout built in a trunk facing Tenmal Pits' smoke.
Nuxhal is a Root-Folk post at the mesa's north-west edge, the hunters' own name for it. Its stilt houses stand under a stand of trees, with a lookout built into a trunk.
Two Root-Folk families, an elder who names the post's hatchlings and a few youths from Helstrom who came for the hunting.
Five or so people hunt and gather, trading with Tenmal and Tenmal Pits, the nearest settlements.
Murkwood's medusas lie to the west. The keepers never go beyond the third bend after dusk. Fellrunners also bite.
Fellrunner feathers and pelts traded to Helstrom's market; a single armband of the pale down lets a hunter cross Murkwood unseen.
No Hist grows here; the keepers go to a village tree for hatching and burial. A feather-hung totem-post stands at the bend, and the first feather of each hunt is given to it.
A hunters' stand that uses Murkwood's fellrunner trade, settled once the hunters kept their feathers here between runs.
A hunter went into Murkwood wearing a feather band and has not come back; a feather-trader will pay for a missing band recovered.
A hummock hung with drying skins and feather bundles, three stilt huts and a narrow canoe lane under overhanging roots.
Four Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom keep three stilt huts on a hummock hung with drying skins and feather bundles.
About four Saxhleel hunters and a feather-trader live on the hummock east of Helstrom, sharing three stilt huts.
Four Saxhleel keep the hummock, hunting along the bend and trading fellrunner feathers to passing boats. They answer to a tree-minder in Helstrom and send a share of every sale.
Mesa predators and a dark cave nearby make this a risky post. The wardens forbid their children to enter the cave.
Reed, feathers and hides go to Ranvos Landing and Tenmal Pits and the post gets lamp oil and salt back.
A small shrine to the Hist stands at the post's edge; eggs go north to the Jal-Veesa Hist pool, and the elder knows every egg the post has sent.
Reeka-Veesa is a Sedge-Warden post on the mesa's west side, used for generations to watch the road between Tenmal and Ranvos Landing and to gather reed and feather.

A child of the post has slipped off to Sahlpesh Cave, which the wardens forbid, to see the Sarpa nests and the reed-cutters have found a Sarpa arrow in a sedge bed only a stone's throw from the houses.
Stilt houses under a few trees, drying racks of reed and feather and a lookout in a trunk that faces Sahlpesh Cave.

Reeka-Veesa is the Sedge-Wardens' southernmost post, its name taken from Jal-Veesa, their town. Its stilt houses stand under a few trees on the mesa's west side, with drying racks of reed and feather.
Sedge-Warden families from Jal-Veesa, one elder and a few youths who will go back north to marry.
Five or so people live here, hunting and gathering. They answer to Jal-Veesa's wardens.
Slaughterfish round the islet's eel-traps; Tumnatu canoes pass without leave.
Eels and lake fish traded to Marzai, Julo and passing boats.

The islet has no Hist, so the keepers row to a village tree on the shore for hatching and burial. A totem-post carved with an eel stands at the landing, and the first eel from each new trap is given to it.
A lake station of the Root-Folk, founded to keep the lake's northern fishing open to the Helstrom country.
A canoe was found drifting with its paddles shipped. The lantern was lit although no boat had come.
An islet of silt with two reed huts, eel pots on poles and a lantern at the water's edge.
Four Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom live in two reed huts, with eel pots on poles round the islet.
About four Saxhleel live on the islet in the lake's northern shallows: eel-trappers, and one who keeps watch over the water.
Four Saxhleel live on the islet, trapping eels and watching the lake's north shallows. Their news goes to a tree-minder in Helstrom with any boat bound there.
Highway wildlife and the odd thief are the only threats at this small guarded toll-house at the head of the causeway.
A toll on goods leaving the city, a lamp-oil trade and a few stalls.
A grave-stake for the post's dead and a Dunmer ancestor-stone from the colonial period.
A post where the northern road leaves the mounds north-west of Fort Willowmoth, taking tolls on reed and fish cargoes since the colonial period.
A cart with a nailed-shut crate that the reeve has been paid to wave through; a night guard who has seen lights on the northern road.
A low stone toll-house with a lamp post and a wooden bar across a causeway.

Causeway-Head Post stands where the northern road leaves Stormhold's mounds, north-west of Fort Willowmoth. Stormhold's toll-keepers take tolls on its causeways and river, and keep a bar at the head of the busiest one; it is named for where it stands.
A Vicecanon's reeve with two Argonian guards; the reeve knows every carter by face and who still owes the toll.
A small stone hut and a bar across the road, with a shed for the reeve and room for a cart.
Watchers with bows cover the channel, and a chain stretched below the surface stops a boat that will not pay. Crocodiles use the same channel.
Watching, fishing and a small toll on boats heading to Soulrest.
The post's eggs are carried to the Hist at Jarecai to hatch, and its dead go back there to be staked. A fang charm hangs over the landing.

Banu-Veeth Post is a Mine-Burner watch post at the south of the Banujha Basin, covering the water toward Soulrest. The tribes who burned the Imperial mines in 3E 427 set the first watch here against Soulrest's diggers.
A toll dispute, a coastal stranger to question or a message for Jarecai.
A stilt watch-post on the water with a lookout platform and a long boat-landing, with a toll chain across the channel. A heap of salt sacks sits under a lean-to.
Banu-Veeth Post is a stilt watch-post with a lookout platform, a long boat-landing and a toll chain across the channel. Six Mine-Burner watchers live on it.
Six Mine-Burner Argonians: three watchers, a ferryman, a cook and a boy who runs messages to the basin. They are hostile to anyone from the coast.
A few Mine-Burner tribesmen hold the post year-round, watching for boats from Soulrest and the coast. They stop every boat and take a toll of salt or iron.
Crocodiles lie below the weir where the offal goes in, and the log walk is slick. The camp is safe; the creek downstream toward Mirasel is not.
Eels and gar from the traps are sold to Jal-Veesa's market and on to Stormhold.
A Hist-shoot post stands at the landing. The wardens give it the first catch.
The weirs date back to before the Dunmer and are kept by the Veesa-Teeleel wardens of Jal-Veesa.
The weir traps are being robbed at night. The wardens want the thief found.
Pale stilt huts on a mud bank and a woven weir across the creek.

Reed-Sill Weir is a Veesa-Teeleel weir on the creek north-east of Gandranen. The Sedge-Wardens hold the creeks of Barsaebica and sell their catch at Jal-Veesa; an outpost on a creek in their country is one of their weirs.
Veesa-Teeleel families take turns at the weir, sent in rotation from Jal-Veesa, whose market the traps feed.
Six or so wardens live here in stilt huts around a log weir with a landing, running the eel and fish traps that supply Jal-Veesa's market.
The post is far from help; wildlife and the odd thief are the dangers on this stretch of road.
The post takes a small toll and sells lamp oil and dried fish from a stall to passing carters.
A grave-stake stands for the post's dead. It is the post's sole mark of worship.
A post on the long road from Stormhold to the western frontier, west of Loriasel on the Slough Point road.
A reeve who wants word sent to Stormhold; a guard who saw lights at Loriasel.
A low stone hut and a wooden gate stand across a causeway on the road west of Loriasel.

Ashgate Post is a Vicecanon's road post west of Loriasel on the Slough Point road. The Vicecanons keep the road toward the western frontier and its toll; the gate stands where the track to the ruins leaves it.
A Vicecanon's reeve and two guards hold the post, a long way from any other garrison.
A small stone hut and a gate across the road mark the post. The reeve and guards watch the track toward the ruins.
Meddling with a totem draws dangerous beasts; Paatru raiders from the west camp.
Tolls and trade with river traders from the Gideon country who come openly.
A rune-carved totem marks the ground by the landing. The Hutan-Tzel say that meddling with one draws dangerous beasts, and the keepers wipe it clean and speak to it at dawn.
The Hutan-Tzel keep fortified outposts along the Panther River, as the tribe is known to do.
A totem has been moved and the beasts have come; the rune-carver can read the stolen one.
A fenced bank with a palisade of reed, rune-carved totems and a ferry.
Six Hutan-Tzel keep a fenced bank with a reed palisade, rune-carved totems and a ferry.
About six Hutan-Tzel hold the fenced bank on the Panther River: watchers for the ferry and tolls, and a rune-carver who tends the totems.
Six Hutan-Tzel keep the bank, watching the river and taking a small toll from boats. They answer to the naheesh at their own tree and not to Helstrom. They send a share of every toll to that naheesh.
Bow-watchers cover the channel and the watchers blow the signal horn to call reinforcements. Ruin-diggers who ignore the warning are shot.
The Mine-Burners watch the channel, fish it and take a small toll on boats between Jarecai and Kharaxos.
Jarecai's Hist is the watchers' tree, a short paddle up the channel, where they hatch their eggs and stake their dead. They leave small offerings at the ruins' edge when passing.
Jal-Resh Post is a Mine-Burner watch post on the water between Jarecai and Kharaxos. The tribes built it to keep diggers off the burned mine ground between the two towns.
A watch-leader who needs a message carried to Jarecai by word of mouth, a wrecked boat in the channel or a stranger held for digging.
A stilt post at a channel bend, a lookout tower with a signal horn and a landing with two war-canoes drawn up. The ruined cities show faintly through the haze on either side.
Jal-Resh Post is a stilt post at a channel bend with a lookout tower, a signal horn and two war-canoes drawn up at the landing. Six Mine-Burners keep the watch here.
Six Mine-Burner Argonians: three bow-watchers, a boatman, a cook and a young one learning to read tracks. They know every digger who has come this way.
A few Mine-Burner tribesmen hold the post and watch the channel for diggers heading for the ruins. They turn back anyone who cannot give a reason.
Crocodiles lie at the landing, and strangers who mock the river-folk may be turned away by arrow. Mine-Burner watchers are close at hand.
Osheeja gar fishing, smoked fish and barter for salt and iron.
The river-folk keep a chime-post at the landing for the Kothringi and the dead of the river. The river-folk go to their tree for hatching and burial, a boat-journey of several days.

Ukeel Station is a net-mending landing on the Banujha where the Naka-Desh river-folk meet the basin's Mine-Burners. The same few families have held it for generations and rebuild its stilts when they rot.
A riddle for passage, a net-snag with a surprise or a gar-hunter asking help.
A stilt platform of reed thatch above the Banujha, a fish-rack, a net-drying frame and a boat landing with a chime-post at the end. Fish scales glitter on the planks.
Ukeel Station is a reed-thatched stilt platform above the Banujha with a fish-rack, a net-drying frame and a boat landing. Five Naka-Desh keep it.
Five Naka-Desh: a net-boss, two fishers, a smoker of fish and a child who learns the river's ways. They love a riddle and give a good one in return for a gift of salt.

The station is held through the year by a handful of Naka-Desh fishers, who net osheeja gar from the Banujha and trade the catch at the water's edge. They watch strangers from the platform and ask for riddles.
The watchers are hostile to Imperial-descended visitors and turn them away from the platform.
The watchers spend their days watching the approaches to Soulrest and fishing from the platform and the boat.
The watchers keep a Banujha tree-token shrine on the platform. A token hangs at the lookout.
The tribes placed the Xal-Tarek watch post after the 3E 427 uprising to keep an eye on Soulrest's approaches.
A message must be carried to the council. One of the watchers has been wounded and needs help.
A tall stilt platform rises from the water with a lookout at the top and a boat tied below.
A watch post of the mine-burning tribes, on stilts at the water's edge.
Six Banujha tribesmen live on the Xal-Tarek platform, sharing watches in turns.
Watchers man the platform day and night, taking turns at the lookout and the boat.
The Hutan-Tzel say beasts come for anyone who touches a totem, so strangers keep their hands off the carvings.

Hutan-Aru's people hunt and guide travellers across the river branch, and sell hides and smoked fish to Umpholo and the Naka-Desh who come to Meliton. They bargain hard over bridge-tolls, which every passing caravan must pay.
The Hutan-Tzel carve their totems with runes that only they can read.
The Hutan-Tzel hold a chain of river outposts in the far west and have held them for generations; Hutan-Aru is one link.
A traveller can bargain here for passage. One of the totems has been defaced.
A palisade of dark posts encloses a rune-carved totem and a few huts, with a landing on the river branch.

Hutan-Aru is a Hutan-Tzel palisade on a river branch in the far west. The spine sets the Hutan-Tzel as river-folk of Blackwood who hold the crossings, and this palisade on the branch is one of their posts; the name is in their style.
Hutan-Tzel guards live at the outpost under a local naheesh, an elder of the tribe.
A palisade of dark posts surrounds a few huts, with a totem carved in runes standing inside.
Wildlife roams the swamp around the stand. The Root-Folk are hostile to uninvited guests.
The stand lives on tapped sap and tended eggs, the Root-Folk's work on the edge of Barsaebica.
A young Hist tree stands at the centre of the camp. The Root-Folk worship at it.
The sapling rose in the generations after 4E 48, and Root-Folk came from the interior to tend it.
The sapling at the heart of the stand is dying. The Root-Folk offer an invitation to the Root Talk.
Root-hollows and stilt huts sit under a thick canopy on the Barsaebica edge.

Vel-Sapha Stand is a Root-Folk stand round a young Hist at the western edge of Barsaebica. The Root-Folk of Helstrom carry sap and eggs to new trees, and a Hist that rose far from the others would draw a few of them to tend it; the name is in their tongue.
Root-Folk of the Saxhleel tend the stand, sap-gatherers who came from the interior swamp.
Stilt huts stand in a ring around a young Hist sapling, with sap-tapping and egg-tending going on beneath the canopy.
The watchers are armed and treat strangers as suspects. Crocodiles and marsh snakes lie on both sides of the border water.
The watchers keep the Nha Enasa border and take a small toll on caravans.
The watchers were hatched under Jarecai's Hist and go back to it to lay and to bury, a two-day paddle across the basin. Burn-marks on the gate honour the burned mine-mouths.

Xul-Banu Post is a Mine-Burner watch post on the basin's north-west edge, where the basin's water meets the Naka-Desh channels. It has grown with the river trade from Gul-Tej, whose boats pay it a toll.
A message for Jarecai's elders, a toll quarrel with Gul-Tej's traders or a watch party that went out and has not come back.
A stilt post on the basin's north-west edge, a gate-tower facing Nha Enasa and a trading float tied beside the landing. Hides and baskets lie stacked on the float.
Xul-Banu Post is a stilt post with a gate-tower and a trading float tied beside the landing. Six Mine-Burners stand the watch.
Six Mine-Burner Argonians: a post-captain, two watchers, a trader and two youths. They are on good terms with the Naka-Desh of Sakeepa Station.
A few Mine-Burner tribesmen hold the post and watch the border with Nha Enasa. They trade with the Naka-Desh across the water but admit travellers to the basin only with leave.
Basin crocodiles, giant snakes on the dry ground and the Mine-Burners' suspicion of outsiders. The reeds are easy to get lost in.
They hunt and dry fish on the rack and sell it to the Mine-Burner watch posts. They send egg-gifts to Helstrom once a year.
They keep a clutch hearth in the egg-hut and carry hatchlings to a Hist when the eggs come. Their dead go back by boat to the tree they came from.

Olaxa Station is a Root-Folk stilt post in the northern reeds of the Banujha Basin, near the Mine-Burners' land. The interior tribes never left these reeds, and the Root-Folk have kept a post here as long as they have traded fish for the Mine-Burners' metal.
A clutch at risk, an intruder to turn back or a sap-run to escort.
A stilt platform in the northern reeds with a long drying rack, an egg-hut with a thatch roof and a boat landing hidden in the grass. Smoke from the fish-rack hangs over it.
Olaxa Station is a stilt platform with a long drying rack, a thatched egg-hut and a landing hidden in the grass. Four Saxhleel hold it.
Four Root-Folk: an egg-tender, two hunters and a rack-keeper. They are watchful of the Mine-Burner tribes, who think of the basin as theirs.
Four Saxhleel keep the post and trade quietly with the basin tribes. They tend a clutch of eggs in the egg-hut and say little to anyone.
Crocodiles and snakes lurk under the landing. Unfamiliar boats are watched, and a hostile one is turned away by arrow.
The five Naka-Desh fish for gar and run a small ferry for Gul-Tej's boats.
At the landing stands a chime-post hung in memory of the Kothringi, who were friends of the river-folk. For hatching and burial they travel to the Naka-Desh tree upriver.

Sakeepa Station stands at a bend of the channel east of Gideon, where the river-folk meet the boats from Gul-Tej. It is older than the Archwardens, and the same few families have rebuilt it many times.
A trade in gar-leather, a Paatru dispute or a Kothringi ruin the river-folk watch.
A reed-thatched platform on stilts at the channel's edge, a long boat-landing, a fish-rack and a chime-post with a signal lamp. Poled barges lie moored beneath.
Sakeepa Station is a reed-thatched platform on stilts at a bend of the Nha Enasa channel, with a long boat-landing and poled barges moored beneath. Five Naka-Desh keep it.
Five Naka-Desh: a trader, a ferryman, two net-menders and a young one learning the channels. They talk with Gul-Tej's merchants in riddles and remember every debt without writing one down.
A few Naka-Desh keep the station through the year and ferry goods to and from Gul-Tej. They exchange news with every boat and know who has gone up and down the channel.
Watchers with bows cover the road. Bandits sometimes test the post at night, and giant snakes cross the causeway at dusk.
The Mine-Burners watch the road toward Soulrest and take a small toll on the carts that use it.
These watchers belong to Jarecai's Hist; a death at the post means a long carry inland for the body. A fang-charm is nailed over the toll gate.
Deshaa Post is a Mine-Burner watch post at the basin's south-west edge, covering the road toward Soulrest and Chasepoint. The tribes set it there to decide who uses the road out of their basin.
A road-warden needs a witness, a smuggler's crate or a Soulrest agent.
A stilt post at the basin's edge where the road turns toward the coast, with a toll gate, a lookout and a wagon yard. The road runs in a raised causeway beside it.
Deshaa Post is a stilt post with a toll gate, a lookout and a wagon yard beside a raised causeway. Six Mine-Burners man it.
Six Mine-Burner Argonians: a toll-keeper, three watchers, a smith who mends axles and a boy with a horn. They know the carters of the road by name.
A few Mine-Burner tribesmen hold the post, watching the road and taking toll from carts. They are known on the road for fair, hard bargaining.
Naga raiders from the south-west camp and swamp predators; the watch is the city's first warning of anyone coming up from the south.
Eggs, fish and a small toll for rafts passing between the south fork and Helstrom.
The rise has no Hist; hatchlings are carried the short way to Helstrom's own tree. A small totem-post with a lamp-niche stands on the crest, and the keepers speak to it at dusk.
A watch has been kept here since the Third Era settlements on Helstrom's approaches. It is now a Root-Folk station.
A signal went up at night with no visitor in sight; an egg-tender claims the Hist spoke to her in the mud.
Stilt huts around a clay nest-pit on a low rise, a signal pole and a rope bridge to the next hummock.
Five Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom keep stilt huts round a clay nest-pit, with a signal pole on the crest.
About five Saxhleel, egg-tenders and night watchers, live on the rise south of Helstrom around the clay nest-pit.
Five Saxhleel keep a night watch on the rise and tend a clutch of eggs. They light a lamp for travellers on the south road and report each dawn to a tree-minder in Helstrom.
Giant snakes and crocodiles near the landing. A Paatru hunter who takes offence is dangerous, and so is the open north reach beyond the lamp.
The Naka-Desh fish for gar and barter salt and iron with the Paatru camps for hides.
The Naka-Desh hung the landing's chime-post for the Kothringi. The nearby Paatru camps follow another Hist, and the two peoples avoid talk of it.

Nahk-Zeel Station stands at the northern edge of the Nha Enasa, where the channels thin out toward Gul-Tej. The Naka-Desh keep it as the place where Paatru hunters bring hides down to the river trade.
A message to Gul-Tej, a lost net or a riddle contest with a stranger.
A reed platform on stilts at the channel's northern edge, with a lamp-post, a fish-rack and a boat landing. Hides hang drying on a frame beside the landing.
Nahk-Zeel Station is a reed platform on stilts with a lamp-post, a fish-rack and a boat landing. Five Naka-Desh keep a lamp lit there for boats.
Five Naka-Desh: a salt-trader, two fishers, a lamp-keeper and a girl who runs messages to the Paatru camps. They are friendly to hunters and wary of anyone who comes with a blade drawn.
A few Naka-Desh river-folk hold it and trade with the Paatru camps nearby, giving salt and iron for hides. They keep a lamp lit at night so boats can find the landing.
The guards say beasts follow anyone who disturbs a totem, so the outpost is dangerous to anyone who meddles with its runes.

Its people earn their living on the far-west border road: guiding, selling meat to Nahk-Zeel Station and bargaining at the palisade gate with Cyrodiilic traders. The outpost lives on a toll paid in salt.
The guards carve their totems with runes that outsiders cannot read.
Another link in the Hutan-Tzel chain of river outposts, standing on the far-west edge by the Cyrodiil border.
A traveller disappeared from the far side of the camp. He has not been found.
A dark palisade stands above a landing at the far-west edge of the marsh.
Hutan-Veel is the Hutan-Tzel post closest to the Cyrodiil border, where the tribe deals with Cyrodiilic traders at its gate rather than let them into the marsh.
Hutan-Tzel guards live at the outpost under the elder styled naheesh.
A palisade of dark posts holds a rune-carved totem on the Cyrodiil border.
The Naka-Desh let a stranger pass if he trades them a good riddle. They are hostile to those who will not.
The station lives by fishing the osheeja gar from the weir and the river.
The Naka-Desh hold to the roots of their own Hist and tell riddles as part of their worship.
The Naka-Desh have kept the station since they spread south, and it has passed down through their river families.
A good riddle gains passage past the station. A message for Gideon needs carrying on.
A small group of huts stands on a river bank, with fishing weirs running out into the water.
Reek-Anu is a river station of the Naka-Desh near Naxan, on a bank at the northwest edge of the cape.
Five Naka-Desh live here, wide-webbed river-folk who love a good riddle.
A group of huts stands on the bank beside a fishing weir that traps gar in the river.
The reeds hide crocodiles and snakes, and the keepers shoot at anyone who touches the sapling. Few outsiders can find the post.
They hunt the reeds for birds and eels, and send sap and egg-gifts to Helstrom. Little leaves the station except by the tree-minders' own boat.
The Hist sapling at the post's heart is sacred, and its whispers guide the keepers' choices. They hatch eggs under it and bury their dead in the reed-beds beside it.

Sarth-Hul Station is a stilt post deep in the Nha Enasa's reeds, where the Root-Folk of Helstrom tend a Hist sapling grown from a cutting of their forest trees. They planted it here so that hunters far from the great forest still have a tree to hatch under.
An egg to protect, a Hist whisper to follow or a hunter lost in the reeds.
A stilt platform in the reed-beds, with a drying rack, an egg-hut and a young Hist sapling with a ring of stones round it. The reeds are tall enough to hide the whole post.
Sarth-Hul Station is a stilt platform in the reed-beds with an egg-hut and a young Hist sapling ringed with stones. Four Saxhleel hold it.
Four Root-Folk: a sapling-tender, two hunters and an egg-sitter. They speak the root-talk of the great trees, and hold that visitors who lie to them are seen by the Hist.
Four Saxhleel hold the post. They hunt and tend the sapling, and the tree-minders' boat comes from Helstrom to fetch sap and bring news.
Mangrove crocodiles, snakes and mudcrabs lie along every channel and the channels look so alike that strangers lose their way among them.
The Naka-Desh fish for gar and gather mangrove bark, selling fish and rope to Gideon's boats.
The river-folk set a chime-post at the landing for the Kothringi dead who lie in the mangroves nearby. The river-folk make the long trip to their tree for hatching and burial.

Teth-Kasa Station is the Naka-Desh's western-most post, among the mangrove channels south of Gideon. It gives the river-folk a landing on Gideon's delta trade, and Gideon's boatmen buy their fish and rope there.
A boat-hand needed, a riddle for passage or a smuggler's cache in the mangroves.
A platform on stilts among mangrove roots, a rope-walk, a fish-rack and a hidden boat landing. Reed bundles and coils of rope are piled under the thatch.
Teth-Kasa Station is a platform on stilts among mangrove roots, with a rope-walk and a hidden landing. Five Naka-Desh keep it out of sight of the sea.
Five Naka-Desh: a rope-maker, two fishers, a pilot who guides boats through the mangroves and a boy who cuts reed. They are cautious with strangers from the coast.
A few Naka-Desh hold it and sell fish and reed rope to Gideon's boats. The mangroves hide it from the sea, and only people who know the channels find it.
Far from the guards; crocodiles in the channels and the odd Naga raider.
Cut reed is bundled at the camp and carried by flat boat to Jal-Veesa and on to Stormhold's mat-makers.
A Hist-shoot is set on a post at the centre of the camp, the cutters' shrine for the season.
The reed beds of the northern plain beyond Jal-Veesa have been cut for as long as there have been mats to sell.
Cutters report a stranger who is paying for reed to be burned; a child has gone missing near the old Imperial waystation to the south.
Reed-thatched lean-tos on a mud bank, bundled reed stacked like haystacks, flat boats pulled up.

Sedge-Kal Camp is where Veesa-Teeleel crews cut the northern plain's reed for Stormhold's mat-makers. Jal-Veesa lives on reed mats sold to the city, and the reed beds beyond it on the northern road are the nearest wide stand; the name is in the wardens' tongue.
Veesa-Teeleel cutters and their families, with a watcher from Jal-Veesa.
A cluster of lean-to huts and boat landings, where a crew of cutters lives until the reed is bound and then another crew takes its place.
Deep swamp predators and Naga hunters; the hummock is the only dry ground for hours.
Hides, herbs and guide fees for those crossing the marsh toward Nacydes and the ridge.
There is no Hist on the hummock; the keepers walk the long route to the nearest village tree for hatching and burial. A totem-post at the path-head is hung with hunters' bone-charms.
A hunters' camp that became permanent because the marsh to the south-west has no other dry ground.
A guide lost a party at the last crossing; the post's fire was lit three nights running without a keeper.
A single hummock with two huts, a firepit and a signal post, with open reed all round.
Four Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom hold two huts, a firepit and a signal post, with open reed on every side.
About four Saxhleel live on the lone hummock south-west of Helstrom: hunters, and a guide who takes travellers toward Nacydes.
Four Saxhleel hold the hummock, hunting in the marsh and feeding the hunters who pass to Nacydes. Any hunter going on to Helstrom carries their news.
Crocodiles and giant snakes gather under the log boom. The camp is safe; the Nenria marsh south of it is not.
Eels and gar from the traps are sold up river. The catch goes to Urvyn Farm's cart every other day.
A Hist-shoot post stands at the weir, where the wardens keep their shrine.
The weirs here belong to the Sedge-Wardens, the Veesa-Teeleel who keep the traps for Jal-Veesa.
Strangers come asking the way to Gandranen. The wardens wonder what they want there.
Pale stilt huts stand on a small platform beside a woven weir across the creek.
Teel-Fen Weir is the Veesa-Teeleel weir closest to Jal-Veesa on the Gandranen creek; its catch goes to Urvyn Farm's cart on the northern road, the nearest way to market.
Veesa-Teeleel families live at the weir on the creek north-east of Gandranen, five wardens and their kin.
Five wardens and their families live on a small stilt platform at the weir, with a landing and a drying rack of fish. They hand off the catch to Urvyn Farm's cart every other day.
Totem rules; Naga parties from the south-west camp; Murkwood's medusas just across the bend.
A toll on river boats, guide fees and a share of what the go-betweens carry between Helstrom's Root-Folk and the Gideon country.
A rune-carved totem stands at the Murkwood edge of the post, and the keepers leave a bowl of river water at its foot. They say it keeps the wood's beasts from the landing.
The Hutan-Tzel sit between Helstrom and the Gideon country and act as go-betweens.
A go-between's canoe came back to the landing with his carved message-stick in it and no one aboard; the naheesh wants a bargain struck with the Root-Folk over the river toll.
A palisade of reed on the bank, totem posts with runes only the tribe reads and a long canoe shed.
Six Hutan-Tzel keep a reed palisade on the bank, totem posts and a long canoe shed.
About six Hutan-Tzel hold the post at the Murkwood edge, with a messenger who carries their naheesh's words to Helstrom.
Six Hutan-Tzel keep the post on the Murkwood edge and carry word by mouth between Helstrom and the west. They house the go-betweens overnight and answer to their own naheesh.
Giant snakes hunt round the post, and the smugglers at Meris-Keth shoot at anyone who comes too near.
They hunt along the basin edge, tend a clutch of eggs and trade fish to the Mine-Burners for iron.
The post has a clutch hearth but no Hist of its own; its keepers carry hatchlings to a village tree. They leave a share of the first catch at the village's old shrine.

Zul-Meeka Station stands on the south-east edge of the Banujha Basin, near an empty Lilmothiit den and the abandoned village of Meris-Keth. The Root-Folk keep it so the Mine-Burners' sap-gatherers have somewhere to rest near the dead village's sick Hist.
A hunter guarding a clutch, a Mine-Burner dispute or a missing sap-gatherer.
A stilt platform on the basin's dry south-east edge, an egg-hut, a lookout post and a boat landing. The abandoned village's roofs show through the reeds nearby.
Zul-Meeka Station is a stilt platform on dry ground with an egg-hut and a lookout post. Four Saxhleel hold it.
Four Root-Folk: two hunters, an egg-tender and a lookout who watches the path to Meris-Keth. They are quick to tell strangers which paths are safe.
Four Saxhleel hold the post and keep watch on the empty den and the abandoned village. They warn anyone heading for Meris-Keth about the smugglers who use it.
Ghosts of the flu-dead walk the market square and the towers. Slaughterfish fill the water over the drowned quay, and the sunken boats lie where a swimmer must hold breath to reach them.
Once a river quay and market; now it holds old Velothi goods and boat fittings for the taking.
The Velothi followed Mephala by their own tradition; Guxal's people call the ground sick and lay their eggs far from it.
One of the Dunmer dissident settlements of the east coast, killed by the Knahaten Flu in 2E 560-603 and never reoccupied.

A Thorn ferryman who wants his father's boat found; it sank at the old quay with the old man's harpoon still in it. Behind the market a cellar door carved with Mephala's spider stays barred from the inside.
Curved Dunmer stonework with root-split walls, a stone quay going under water, moss and bright fungus.
A Cantemiric Velothi ruin on the water's edge, one of the Velothi settlements of this coast.
The ruin has no living inhabitants. Guxal's hunters and Thorn's fishers pass by day and keep their boats off the quay.
A drowned quay, fallen towers and a market square with a tree growing through it; Guxal's people hunt round it but do not enter.
Sarpa raiders from the south-west are the risk at Oxayo. The watch-elder's horn gives warning of them.
Oxayo lives on stone cut at the Xanuc Diggings, river fish and the mending of tools for the quarry hands.
A cairn replaces a tree; the elder passes dreams to Tsonac's tree-minder.
Founded over an old foundation as Tsonac's people spread south onto the mesa.
The horn blown at night when every family in Oxayo denies blowing it, and a bundle of Sarpa feathers tied to the quarry gate, a warning the watch-elder knows from her own youth.
Stone houses with reed roofs on a riverbank, a signal horn on a pole, mesa cliffs beyond.
The Stone-Sleepers' hamlet nearest the Sarpa, on the river at the mesa's north-west. Its quarrymen work the Xanuc Diggings, and its horn warns the hamlets east of it when the Sarpa come.
Stone-Sleeper families, quarry hands and a watch-elder who keeps the signal horn and has lost an eye to a Sarpa arrow.
Eight live there; they quarry the Xanuc Diggings and watch for Sarpa raiders.
Steep cliffs, loose rock and nesting hackwings, plus a pirate lookout who shoots at strangers.
Nothing is made here. It serves as the lookout for both camps and the mark that boats on the Okuwun coast steer by.
Sailors leave a pebble on the cairn for luck. The Argonians tell that the stone is a Hist's old bone.
Seamen of every age have used it as a landmark. The Imperial keep on the shore was built in sight of it, and was held until the secession.
Both camps believe the captain of the Stormwidow buried his share under the cairn, and both have dug around it and found only stones. Pirates tell of a shaman's bones in a cave on the north face.
A dark grey-green tooth of rock with sea-birds nesting in its cracks, thin salt-grass on the lower slopes, wind-bent shrubs.
A bare grey-green peak of dark, sea-worn rock at the island's centre, called the Grey Tooth for its look. Its stone is dark green-grey like the rest of the island.
No residents. A lookout from Marque Landing climbs it in the day.
It serves as a seamark. A rough cairn stands at the top and a goat-path climbs the south face. The pirates keep a lookout post on it in clear weather.
The summit of Nacydes Watch lies open to Paatru and Naga raiders, and giant snakes den in the crevices below it.
Nothing is made on Nacydes Watch; it is a lookout post kept by the hamlet below, with no trade of its own.
A small chime hangs at the top of Nacydes Watch the same kind the hamlet below hangs from its huts.
A lookout kept by the people of Nacydes, who keep one sentry on it at all times.
The sentry saw a light in the Paatru camp that is not a fire; a lost scout's pack lies in a crevice beside a giant snake den.
A rocky summit with a hut and a chime, with wide views over reed and mere.
Nacydes Watch is a peak on the west of the Aunike Ridge, above Nacydes. A hut and a small chime stand on its rocky summit, where one sentry from Nacydes keeps watch.
The peak has no residents; a sentry from Nacydes sits in the hut at all times.
Nacydes keeps one sentry in the summit hut, who rings the chime when Paatru or Naga come near the ridge.
On the summit path of Aunike Crown there are giant snakes and Naga parties out of the northern camps.
Nothing is made here; the watchfire basket is the only work.
The fire-basket on Aunike Crown is kept burning as a small offering to the Hist, tended by the keeper from Tydeos.
A lookout for the Chime-Keepers of Tydeos, whose watchfire burns on its top.
A Kothringi cairn of beads stands on the summit, and giant snakes den below it; a stranger was found dead beside the fire-basket.
A bare rock summit above the marsh with a fire-basket, a few stunted trees and a view of lakes.
Aunike Crown is a peak above Tydeos on the Aunike Ridge. Tydeos' watchfire-keeper climbs its bare rock summit each dusk to tend a fire-basket.
The summit of Aunike Crown has no residents. Passing hunters cross it, on the path from Tydeos.
Tydeos' watchfire-keeper climbs it each dusk and comes down at dawn; otherwise it is empty.
Gas pools in the hollows, fire vents flare from the glassy crust where a foot falls and fire-undead walk the vents.
Sulphur and alchemical reagents are gathered from the vents and the burned soil of the scar.
Argonians avoid the scar as a place of Sithis's anger and will not camp on it.
The Great Burn (1E 2828) spread by an underground peat network from Stormhold to Soulrest.
A vent shaft leads down to the burn network. Reagent harvesters work the scar's edge.
Black ground and white ash stretch away, with dead snags standing among the gas vents.
A named landmark: the scar where the Great Burn's underground network reached the cape.
The scar has no residents. Sulphur-gatherers and scavengers go onto it, and few stay.
The scar is still dead ground. Smoke hangs low over it in damp weather.
Rockfalls come down on the quarry face. Bandits watch the Percar road for the stone carts.
It sells cut stone to Soulrest's builders and road-menders and gives the merchant council a share of its blocks for its protection on the road. Carts leave twice a week for Chasepoint and the port.
The crew keeps a small Sithis niche in the cutting shed and leaves a rock chip on its ledge for each month without a death.
Stonecut Quarry was opened in the Third Era to supply stone for the buildings of Soulrest, and has worked on since.
A builder at Soulrest wants a large order of cut stone hauled quickly. A find in the strata has stopped work at the face.
A terraced cut climbs the hillside, with a stone sled track running down to the Percar road.
Stonecut Quarry is a terraced cut with a stone sled track beside the Percar road. Its grey blocks go to Soulrest's harbour works and the coast road.
Five Argonian quarrymen work the Stonecut face, living in a shed by the Percar road.
A crew of five, kin to one Soulrest-quarter family, works the Percar road face for the merchant council, cutting grey blocks for the harbour works and the coast road.
Rockfalls come down on the quarry face. Bandits watch the track to the shore for the barge loads.

It sends red facing stone by barge to Soulrest's coast wall and its warehouses, and a share of the blocks goes to the merchant council for its protection of the shore track. Redbank blocks are prized for their colour.
The crew keeps a Sithis shrine in a niche cut into the face itself, and the foreman marks the first block from each new bench with red for it.
Redbank Quarry was opened to cut red stone for Soulrest's builders on the south side of the cape.
A rival stone crew is breaking Redbank's sleds and cut blocks at night to drive it off the red face.
A red-stained cut opens in the hillside, with a sled track running down to the shore.
Redbank Quarry is a red-stained cut with a sled track and a short track to the shore. Its blocks are prized for their colour.
Four Argonian quarrymen cut the Redbank face and live in a shed beside the sled track.
A crew of four works the red-stone face on the south side of the cape, for Soulrest's merchant council, with a short track to the shore.
Pirates, a locked strong room, trapped stairs and wet lower cells where the pirates keep a pen of slaughterfish.
A strong room for prize cargoes and ransom. Captives are kept for ransom or sold to buyers on the Okuwun coast.
The Imperial shrine to Akatosh in the chapel was left standing and is now stacked with crates; the pirates swear by their figureheads.

Built by the Empire to watch the Archon coast and break the pirate trade, and kept as a signal tower until the secession, when the garrison left. No Warden family took the keys, and the keep stood empty until pirates moved in.
A captive in the cells knows how to reach the Resolute Crest's chest. The quartermaster knows which wardens took the pirates' money.
A squat square keep of grey stone with a signal tower, weather-pitted, a sea-wall and a stone jetty, hung with fishing nets and ships' lanterns.
A stone keep on a rise by the shore of Skeith Isle, built by the Empire and now held by pirates.
Twelve of the Marque Landing pirates live here under the quartermaster, with up to a dozen captives in the cells at a time.
Pirates took it in recent years. They hold the upper hall as their moot-room and the lower vault as a strong room; the undercroft, once the garrison's cells, is the pirates' prison.
Coastal crocodiles, mudcrabs on the inlet shore and smuggler landings after dark.
Estuary fish, eels and rice. The guesthouse earns from travellers on the Seafalls road.
Renhu sends its eggs inland to the Hist at Aroxhu. Grave-stakes of drowned netters stand along the mound edge, carved by the elder's family, who also carve a clay fish for each good catch.
People of Inoja settled it as a late daughter-village when the mounds filled. Seafalls-bound carts stop there because it lies on the road.
A boat sold to a stranger has turned up in Skeith's camp with the elder's mark burned into the keel. A signal light shows on the bluff at night.
Reed-thatched stilt houses on three low mounds by a muddy inlet, nets draped over poles, boats at a clay landing and gulls overhead.
A village between the inlet and the road to Seafalls, with a view of Skeith Isle on clear days.
About twelve Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel, farmers and netters. A few Seafalls pilots lodge here.
A tidy village with a small guesthouse and good fish. The elders watch for Skeith smugglers who sometimes buy their boats.
The village sits by the fort road and is safe in daylight. Drunk soldiers cause trouble after dark, and deserters hide in the reeds.
Fish, rice, laundry and labour for the fort; boat hire for the Archon crossing.
Hatching families go to Lilmoth's tree; the fort families keep a few Imperial habits but go to Lilmoth's tree to hatch their young.
Grew beside the Imperial fort; the villagers kept their houses after the secession, when the Legion left and the Archwardens' families took the fort in their name.
A soldier who owes a village family a debt; a net that brought up something strange; a deserter hiding among the stilt houses.
Stilt houses on a low rise by the road, fish racks, a landing and the fort's tower visible to the east.
A village on the north shore of the northern island, by the road from Uluo to Fort Reedmoth.
Argonians of the Lilmoth coast, some married into fort families of Archein descent.
Ten households trade with the fort, the ferrymen and passing boats.
Sea-drakes patrol the shallows, pirates work the Sea of Mists offshore and the deep creeks behind the village hold slaughterfish.
Salaxul earns landing fees from the boats that put in, and sells salt, shellfish and coastal freight.
A Sithis shrine of piled conch shells stands at the top of the beach. Salaxul's eggs go inland to be hatched under a Banujha tree.
Salaxul began as a Third Era timber landing and kept its trade as a coastal boat stop after the mines burned.
A smuggler's boat lands by night on the Salaxul beach. A shipment of salt has gone missing on its way to the jetty.
A wooden jetty runs out from the shore, with drying racks above the beach, low stilt houses and a salt pan behind them.
Salaxul is a village on the south coast of the cape, below Mir-Xal, where the road from the interior reaches the sea.
Salaxul's villagers are Argonian boatmen, joined by a few Khajiit coasters who put in at the jetty.
Under the Soulrest merchant council; its reeve collects landing fees.
Falls from the wet rocks and rope-bridges, slaughterfish in the sea-pool and Skeith pirate boats in the dark.

The portage, which charges cargo-carriers by weight; piloting; pearl-shell and sea-salt; and driftwood and wreck-salvage. Seafalls is the transfer point on the north-east link between Thorn, Branchmont and Archon.

They hold that the memories the Hist let fall are kept in the sea that the Hist let fall. They leave painted shells and knotted cords at the falls, keep death-dancers for burials and nest on the shoals. Hatching and naming mean a long journey inland.
The Spray-Folk came here from the Archon shore, beyond any Hist tree. Under the East Empire Company they ran the portage for Company boats. Since the secession the portage is theirs alone.
The pilot-elder needs a successor and has chosen a hatchling who cannot swim. A ship has come in whose cargo does not match its master's story, and Archon's chartered privateer wants it quietly held.
White falls dropping into a sea-pool, stilt houses and nest-platforms on the cliff and shoals, rope-bridges over the spray, salt-crusted decks, the lighthouse beyond the point, gulls and surf.
A coastal village at the falls where a river reaches the Padomaic, the reason cargo changes boats here. It lies north-north-east of Archon and is a falls-and-portage settlement.
About fourteen Argonians of the Spray-Folk: pilots, portage-men and net-menders. The pilot-elder, an old woman who has taken a hundred ships through the surf, is the village's voice.
A small, self-contained village. Its pilots take ships into Archon and off the Thorn road. The Archwardens charge the village nothing because no other crew will do the job.
Falls from the gallery, slippery rocks and Skeith pirates who take the tower in the dark.
The pilots of Seafalls give the keeper a share of the salvage from every wreck on the shoals.
The keeper keeps a clay lamp for the lost dead and lights it with the beacon.
Built by the East Empire Company for its Archon-Thorn run. The Spray-Folk have kept it alight since the secession.
The lamp is dark and a boat crew from Skeith Isle holds the gallery. The keeper's hatchling saw them land and hides in the hut.
A white-lime tower of stone on the point, a gallery with a great brass lamp, a keeper's hut, a boat-slip and surf below.
A tall beacon house on the point south-east of the falls, to warn ships off the shoals.
Three Argonians, a keeper and his two hatchlings. One hatchling is a trained watcher with a long glass.
Lit every night by the keeper, who burns fish-oil bought from Archon and sells directions to the lost.
Mud-crabs and slaughterfish off the flats, deep water past the shell banks where breath runs out and the occasional patrol from the fort; risky ground.
Shellfish, dried fish and salt, sold toward Truowa; rice and tools come back by raft.
Sithis and the Hist as the tribe holds them; the sea-edge families say a prayer to the sea at each net-laying.
Founded by Three Waters families seeking clams and cockles on the western mudflats, then drawn into Truowa's trade when the city grew.
A trader needing safe passage between the fort and Truowa; a shell midden older than the hamlet with Cantemiric Velothi beads in it, from before the Flu.
Pole houses over grey mudflats, shell middens like low white hills, nets spread to dry on frames and salt pans.
A coastal hamlet at the far west of the Nushara waters, nearest to Truowa and the fort that watches the water-road.
Three Waters Argonians with some Truowa-bound rice traders; the families are kin to Tapauo and Uluo.
Eight raft-families net, gather shellfish and sell to Truowa's lighters; they pay the garrison at Fort Gysilla the toll and nothing more.
Sea-drakes hunt the shallows over the wreck, divers can drown in the hull and broken timbers are sharp.
The Salt Heron carried Senchal cloth, brass lamps and casks of salt; Natai's divers still bring pieces of it up.
Natai's divers lay a fish on the bow before they go in, so the drowned Khajiit let them take from the hold.

The Salt Heron was running to Soulrest when she struck the shoals off Natai in a night fog and broke up where she struck. Her crew were Khajiit, as most Southern Sea crews are and two came ashore alive.
A locked captain's chest lies in the stern, and moon sugar is packed in a false bottom of the salt casks.
A broken hull on a sand bar, its ribs standing up through green water.
The Salt Heron is a Khajiit coaster from Senchal lying off the south shore of the washes, a short boat ride from Natai.
The wreck has no residents. The Natai salvagers who dive it are its only visitors.
Natai's salvagers dive the Salt Heron by turns, each taking a share of what they bring up.
A slaughterfish shoal circles the wreck. Inside, the sphere is a sealed shell with no air and a diver's breath runs out fast once he squeezes through the hatch.
It was a Company tool for stripping the spires of bronze; now the sphere itself is the salvage, brass fittings and whatever its crew left aboard.
