Argonian divers tap the sphere's brass three times for luck as they pass, the way they touch the bell-cord at Bell Station.

The East Empire Company had it built to reach the drowned xanmeer spires without a bell, and lowered it from a barge in the years before the secession. Its cable parted and the Company's crew left when the Company did.
A locked brass hatch whose key a Company salvage master carried; a cable end to follow across the sand to the spires.
A brass ball with portholes and rivets, a broken cable trailing from its crown, wrapped in kelp and lit from within.
A sunken brass diving sphere lying on the sea floor near Echo Deep, reached by swimming down to it.
The sphere holds no living crew. Divers tell of the sphere's pilot tapping on the glass from inside.
It lies on its side half buried in silt, its ports cracked and its glass still glowing under the kelp. Bell Station's divers know it as a landmark and a salvage prize they have not yet opened.
Crabs swarm the hull, and the rotten decks hide holes down to the hold.
She was bringing Elsweyr cloth and moon sugar for the Archon trade. Now people strip timber, nails and brass.
Sailors leave bits of cord on the stern post for the drowned.

In the years Naarifin's army held Leyawiin and the Blackwood Road was shut, so Cyrodiil's and Elsweyr's goods came by sea to Archon. The Tidewarden, out of Senchal, missed the channel and went onto the bar; the crew lived.
A sealed strongbox in the hold; the Khajiit captain's logbook, which names the Archon pilot who ran her onto the bar.
A grey broken hull with the masts down, barnacled, gulls on the rail, half buried in white sand.
A wrecked trading ship on the shore a short walk from Archon.
No one lives there. Beachcombers from Archon come to the hull and a hermit crab-catcher camps near.
The hull lies on its side half sunk in sand, stripped of cargo and rigging by locals long ago.
Drowned crew and shackled dead in the hold, slaughterfish around the hull and a captain who keeps his strongbox. The wreck is a short swim from shore, .
Nothing is made here. Divers from Thorn go down for the captain's strongbox and the brass fittings, and Dunmer relic-hunters pay for anything marked with Dres colours.
Thorn's coast Argonians do not pray at the Silt Bride, because she carried their kin in chains. They leave a painted shell on the nearest shore for the captives and spit on the water over the hull.

A brig of the kind that carried Argonian captives out of Thorn for House Dres, and ran Arnesia's coast after the Arnesian War. She went down with captives chained in the hold in the late Third Era, before the Red Year ended the Dunmer slavers' trade here.
The captain's log, still in the stern cabin, names the Dunmer families who bought captives from Thorn; some of them still trade there. The Thorn Vicecanon wants it, and so do the families it names.
A black-oaked hull furred with weed, rusted shackles trailing from the hatch, fish in the cabin windows.
The Silt Bride lies on her side on the shelf off Thorn, a short swim from shore. She was a Dres-chartered slaver of the Arnesian trade.
The wreck has no living residents. The slaver crew drowned in the hold with their captives, and the shackled dead still move in the cabin and along the lower deck.
The brig lies on her side on the shelf, hull split amidships, the stern cabin whole. Fish have taken the cabin windows.
Slaughterfish in the shallows and drowned dead in the hold; the lower deck is narrow and the water is cold.
A strongbox of Company coin is the draw, with the bills of lading that name the cargo's buyer. Salvagers from Ysan and Arorha have picked at the hull but not reached the hold.
Local Argonians leave a knotted cord on the nearest shore for sailors lost at sea, as the Spray-Folk do at Seafalls.
One of the Company's saltrice runs from Thorn to Archon in the last years before the secession; it ran onto a sandbar at the bight's mouth and settled where it lies.
Ysan's boatmen will pay a share to anyone who clears the drowned dead from the hold and brings up the captain's strongbox.
A listing timber hull on grey silt, barnacled ribs, rotten sacks heaped in the hold, ropes drifting in the green light.
The Pale Harvest, a sunken Company saltrice freighter, lies on the seabed of Hatandros Bight, a short swim from the shore near Ysan.
The wreck has no residents. The crew drowned with the ship and remain aboard as drowned dead.
Barnacled and half-buried in silt. The hull is intact enough to enter; the cargo has long since turned to black sludge.
Slaughterfish and the drowned captain who guards the strongbox. The water is shallow, but the shoal bottom is jagged and the hull is crowded with weed.
Her cargo, moon-sugar casks gone to rot and a strongbox of Skeith coin, is the draw. Skeith crews dive for it and keep quiet about it.
Skeith smugglers drop a coin in the water above the Brindle Gull before a night run, for luck against the privateers. Arorha's fishers leave a knotted cord on the shore for the crew.

A fast sloop running untaxed goods from Skeith Isle to the Arorha shore. In recent years she ran onto the Kornakim shoals at night while a chartered Archon privateer, or a rival Skeith crew, chased her without lights.

The Hollow Tide crew says the sloop was theirs and the strongbox is owed to them; the Marque Landing captain says his privateers sank her and the strongbox is a prize. Whoever brings it up has both camps asking after it.
A small clinker hull with a painted gull on the bow, soft with weed, with spars and lines floating above it.
The Brindle Gull was a fast sloop on the Skeith Isle run to the Arorha shore. She rests upright in shallow green water on the Kornakim shoals.
The wreck has no living residents. The smuggler crew died on the shoals, and the captain stands guard over the strongbox as a drowned dead man.
The hull rests upright in shallow green water, mast broken at the step, the deckhouse hatch still shut.
Rotten decks, mudcrabs in the hold and scavengers who attack anyone they catch at the wreck.
Timber, copper sheathing and cordage are stripped for the camps. The captain's strongbox is the real prize.
None; the pirates say the figurehead is bad luck and have turned it to face the sea.
A chartered privateer of the Archon coast that ran onto the beach in the dark and was abandoned by her crew, who joined the Marque Landing camp.
The captain's strongbox is still sealed in the stern, and the pirates believe its brass key opens the cache under the cairn on the Grey Tooth. Both camps search for it and neither has found it.
A listing hull half-buried in grey sand, ribs open to the sky, ropes and sails rotting, a figurehead of a veiled woman.
The Stormwidow lies beached on the south-west shore of Skeith Isle, where both island camps can reach her.
The wreck has no living residents. Scavengers from both camps sneak in at night.
Her upper hull is picked clean; the lower hold is full of sand and rarely entered.
A long swim down to a deep hull, drowned Imperial marines on the decks and slaughterfish in the dark below the quarterdeck. A diver swims a long way down through dark water.
Nothing is made here. A chest of Akaviri tribute and the ship's brass would fetch a great price from a collector at Archon, and the long swim is what has kept it down.
Skeith's crews tie a knotted cord at their camp for the Navy dead. The coast Argonians call the wreck a drowned Imperial's grave and do not touch the figurehead.
One of the Septim ships that crossed the Padomaic Ocean with Uriel V in 3E 288. She was lost off Black Marsh in the years of that campaign, long before the secession.
Two Skeith divers have not come back from it, and Marque Landing pays for anyone who returns with the chest. A captive in the cells of Rainbreaker Keep says he knows the way down to it.
A tall black-oaked hull ringed with weed, a bronze figurehead of a crest worn smooth, ballistae on a sunken deck, shoals of fish.
The Resolute Crest sailed in Uriel Septim V's fleet against Akavir in 3E 288 and went down off the east coast. She rests upright on the deep shelf east of Skeith Isle.
The wreck has no living residents. The marines went down with the ship, and their drowned dead still stand on the quarterdeck.
The great hull rests on the deep shelf east of Skeith Isle, upright, weedgrown, the quarterdeck still above the silt.
Sea-drakes hunt over the wreck. Divers can drown inside the hull.
The Brine Gull carried Valenwood silk and bundled bows, and Soulrest salvagers still bring up what the sea has spared.
Acra-Tiin's fishermen will not set nets over the Brine Gull; they say the Bosmer dead keep to their own rites and resent Argonian hands.
The Brine Gull was bound for Soulrest when she struck a reef off the cape in the dark and sank with her hull mostly whole. Her Bosmer crew drowned with her.
A Bosmer captain's chest lies in the stern, and a Soulrest buyer pays for any silk raised dry in its oilcloth.
A dark hull lies on the sea floor in blue water, with weed trailing from her ribs.
The Brine Gull is a Bosmer coaster from Valenwood lying on the sea floor off the south-west of the cape, near Acra-Tiin's islands.
The wreck has no residents. The salvagers who dive her are its only visitors.
Soulrest salvagers dive the Brine Gull on calm, clear days.
Slaughterfish nest in the hold, and a diver caught among the fallen beams runs out of breath before finding the way back up.
Its hold still holds Cyrodiilic wine casks and iron bars, and the divers bring them up a few at a time.
A Nibenese sailor's Dibella charm of shell and copper is tied to the stern post, where the last of the crew left it.

The Grey Heron carried wine and iron across Topal Bay from Leyawiin to Gideon in the last years of Imperial shipping before the secession. It struck the sand-bar off the estuary in a gale and went down with most of its cargo.
The captain's chest still in the stern cabin, the iron Olvani's divers cannot lift or a Gideon family's wine that never arrived.
A broken hull lies on the sand under green water, its ribs hung with weed and its stern post still standing. Small fish move among the beams.
The Grey Heron is a Leyawiin merchantman that sank off Gideon's estuary and now lies on the floor of Topal Bay.
It is uninhabited. Two of Olvani's divers come out by punt, and the fishers mark the spot with a float.
Olvani's divers work the wreck and haul up what they can reach. Part of the cargo is still in the hold, behind beams too heavy to shift.
Slaughterfish rest in the shade of the cleft, and the way into the hold is long enough to drown in.
Its hold carried moon sugar, skooma flasks and bolts of Valenwood silk, some of it still wrapped in oilcloth.
A tin cup of offering-coins for Jone and Jode is wedged below the helm, where the Khajiit crew left it.

The Sallow Anne was a sloop bought in Leyawiin by a Khajiit crew from Senchal, running moon sugar and Valenwood silk into Topal Bay. A rival crew chased it onto the rocks off Aphon some years ago, and none of its crew came ashore.
The captain's strongbox is wedged somewhere in the cleft; the rival crew who sank the sloop, still on the bay; or the Kelp-Mouth smugglers who want the cargo first.
A narrow hull jammed into a rock cleft, its mast snapped short and kelp netted over the open deck. Silver fish flicker in the shadow beneath.
The Sallow Anne is a Khajiit smuggler's sloop that was wrecked on the rocks off Aphon Isle.
It is uninhabited. Aphon fishers dive for what they can sell, and a smuggler from the bay comes now and then to search.
Divers from Aphon and Soulrest come out to the wreck, and the Kelp-Mouth crew search it for the captain's strongbox, that has never been found.
Slaughterfish, slaughterfish and crocodiles in the reeds; no bandits.
Thatch, mat-reed and eel traps sold at Uluo; they buy salt, iron hooks and cloth.
Reed-cutters leave the first bundle of each cutting on a stump for the Hist; otherwise they go to Uluo for hatching and burial.
Settled by Three Waters reed-cutters who followed the best beds; the houses stand on the one firm hummock nearest them.
A cutter who found something metal in the mud of the bed; a trapper's request to clear a nest of slaughterfish.
Low reed-thatch houses on stilts above hummocks, tall drying racks of pale reed and eel traps hung like baskets over the water.
A small hamlet on a ridge of firm ground in the reed beds south of Inoio, off the road and reached by punt.
Three Waters Argonians; a reed-master leads and answers to Uluo's elder.
Six households cut, dry and bundle reed and trap eels and crabs. The hamlet is quiet and few outsiders come.
A guarded crossing; hackwings in clouds, crocodiles in the river, the odd smuggler.
Road trade to Gideon and Leyawiin, the ferry fare, a market of smugglers and herb-sellers.
Dibella shrine in the old customs house, as in Gideon; no Hist, a foreign foundation. Argonian residents go home to a village tree to hatch and bury.
The Empire built the post, bridge and customs house to tax the Blackwood Road. The Legion left at the secession; the families who served the post stayed on.
A smuggler who wants the ferry rope cut on the night he crosses; a Gideon trader who will not pay a toll to the successor state and is held at the fort.
A long white bridge broken in the middle over a black river; a stone customs house with weathered Imperial eagles; mud-and-timber houses on stilts and a few Cyrodiilic gables; hackwing-chewed guards.

Slough Point was an Imperial census-and-excise post with a Commission-built white bridge over a black tidal river, its guards chewed by hackwings. It stands inside Black Marsh, beside Fort Rustmoth, close to the Blackwood border.
Lukiul Argonians and Nibenese-descended families of the Gideon frontier; Khajiit and Imperial traders pass through; the garrison are Archwarden soldiers.

A village around the old customs house and the bridge. The bridge's low middle span lies under the black water, and a rope ferry carries the road across. The toll is kept by the garrison of Fort Rustmoth next door.

Inside the gates guards keep order; threats are theft, smugglers' feuds and a visitor carrying the wrong cargo. The landward burn-scar is gas and dead timber; the inland tribes are hostile to coast officials.

Southern Sea trade, salvage from wrecks off the cape and Bramman's river, the concealed channel from Topal Bay to the Blackrose lakes. Gold and timber are no longer exported at scale; the old workings behind the city are derelict.

Sithis and the Hist through the interior tribes' trees; Imperial-descended families keep the Nine in small shrines; Khajiit sailors keep the moons. A Brotherhood of Seth presence is known and stays hidden.

Argonians lived here since the wraxu birds were alive. Red Bramman ran pirates from a mangrove river nearby in 1E; the Great Burn (1E 2828) reached its edge; the tribes burned its plantations and mines in 3E 427, ending gold and timber exports. The Legion and the Company sailed away at the secession (4E 5-10).

A faction contest for the council, a hidden mangrove landing to find, derelict Imperial mines to enter, the hatching-ground leverage that the Banujha tribes hold over the city and control of smuggling through Bramman's river.

A port behind its gates: stone Imperial quarter at the peninsula's neck, timber and stilt wharves below, mangrove creeks to the south, xanmeers etched with wraxu and burn-scarred dead ground and gas vents on its landward edge.

The southwest coast port on a peninsula wrapping Topal Bay, capital of Black Marsh in the Third Era. In 4E 201 it is an administrative city with nothing left to administer, and the most mixed and contested city in the province.
About 60% Argonian, a large Khajiit share among seafarers, Imperial-descended administrators' families, Bosmer and other maritime minorities. A few dozen named residents at Skyrim's scale.

A merchant council, the ex-Imperial civil apparatus with no sovereign and the mangrove-river interests contest the city, in the unexplained 'struggle for regional hegemony', while the interior mine-burning tribes hold the hatching grounds. The government quarter is half empty and repurposed. The city has no Hist, so its Argonians hatch, name and bury inland in Banujha country.
Slaughterfish in the shallows below the landing, wreckers in a sea-cave on the shore and reef rocks that tear hulls.
The keep takes a toll on ships that anchor below it and buys its provisions from the fishermen of Karketa. Spare fish is sold at the gate.
There is no Hist at the keep; the garrison hatches its young and buries its dead at Lilmoth.
An Imperial coast fort. The Legion left at the secession, 4E 5-10 and the Archwardens took the keep over soon after.
The beacon lamp is found put out by hand, and the watch blames wreckers. A ship's captain swears he paid the toll and will not pay twice.
A squat stone keep with a beacon tower, a landing below and the sea open to the south.
A coastal fort at the south-west tip of the island, facing the sea road to Lilmoth.
Argonian garrison of Archein-line officers, with fishermen from Karketa as neighbours.
Eight garrison men keep the beacon lit, check the ships that anchor below and pay little attention to Lilmoth's politics.
Safe inside the walls, where guards keep order. Outside the gate are crocodile-infested ravines and sunken marsh; below the city the Silyanorn tunnels and a sunken Ayleid ruin are an outlaws' refuge.

River traffic to Morrowind and to Alten Corimont down the northern trunk road, the customs on that traffic and the Stormhold Crystals dug in the tunnels below. Sedge mats, dried fish and reed goods arrive daily from Jal-Veesa and the weirs; the trading halls sit in the repurposed Ayleid compound.

The Hist tree stands in the town square in the middle of a pond, ringed by ancient pillars and a low stone wall, public and defended. Dunmer households keep their ancestors and a quiet Tribunal-shaped habit; the grave-stake tradition of the Argonians and the Ayleid-compound mortuary sit side by side.

Barsaebic Ayleids founded Silyanorn here after 1E 198; the Hist later conquered them, by legend. The Dunmer used the site as the foothold of their slave trade, adding stone roads, light posts and bridges and the city invented the Vicecanon office to try slavers. It was the Pact's capital of Black Marsh in 2E, held a prison under Warden Quintus Varus in the late 3E and was overrun but lightly damaged by Umbriel's undead in 4E 48.

Below the city, the Silyanorn tunnels hold crystal galleries and an Ayleid well-room that outlaws use as a hideout. The old quarrel between the Argonian west quarter and the Dunmer families flares over a stolen clutch of eggs from the square's Hist pond, and the Vicecanons want the thief found before the quarters settle it themselves.

A city on a mountainside: Dunmer ornate stone, stone roads, light posts and long wooden bridges over ravines, with large Argonian mud huts on the mounds between and a waterfall running down through the old Ayleid compound.

Stormhold is the largest settlement of Shadowfen and a major city of Black Marsh, near the banks of the river that forms the border with Morrowind. It is the city of the Valley of Storms and the likeliest first sight of the province for a newcomer.

Argonians beside the largest and oldest Dunmer minority in Argonia, descended from a colonial population, about a fifth of the city. The western quarter was where the Argonians who worked for the Dunmer lived, and the memory is still live. Townsfolk meet outsiders with pragmatism; they have always had to live with them. Several Vicecanons sit at once, one for each people.

The waterfall, the ravine-severed mounds, the Hist in its pond and the Silyanorn substructure all survived 4E 48. The rest has been rebuilt in the 153 years since. Only the population has not recovered. The Vicecanons keep the river customs and the frontier screen's offices here.
A diver can drown on the long spiral stair when the breath gives out, and the mudcrab's claws hold fast. Reef slaughterfish dart out of the lower windows.
The upper floors gave bronze, vakka stones and bone to Bell Station, which sells them on to Lilmoth's merchants. What remains lies behind the sealed door and in the mudcrab's gallery.
Divers say it belonged to Sithis and the water-spirits, and they pray before going in. The Hist-glyph cut into its sealed door marks the chamber where a tree once grew.

Argonians raised it in the Stone-Nest age, before the land sank: legend says the Southern Sea swallowed Murkmire and the Padomaic took most of the Hist's first domain. Its Hist chamber was sealed when the tree died.
A salvage chest left half-opened in the mudcrab's gallery; the sealed door with its Hist-glyph that Bell Station's divers cannot force.
A broken spire furred with weed, round windows and a stair spiralling down inside.
A drowned xanmeer tower standing on the sea floor, reached by diving. It is the spire nearest Lilmoth.
A giant mudcrab has taken one gallery. Divers say a drowned priest walks the stair and never speaks.
Silted and furred with kelp and coral, it stands close enough for a day's dive from Lilmoth. Bell Station's divers have stripped its upper floors bare.
Slaughterfish fill the flooded hall and one old fish is far larger than the rest. A salvager who lost his breath in a dead-end gallery has no way out but up.
Once a temple-tower, now a salvage ground of bronze, vakka stones and bone that Bell Station sells to Lilmoth. The rooms left are the hard ones, at the deep edge.
Divers say the tower belonged to Sithis and the water-spirits and pray before entering. They read the curling stone arms as an offering held out to the deep.
It was a temple-tower of the Nisswo priest-kings' age, and its stone arms were carved to hold offerings to the deep. It sank with the land around it, and its tribe is long gone.
A drowned diver in a gallery still wears the key to a locked grate; behind the grate stands the salvage chest that no diver has reached.
A tall spire with curling stone arms and a flooded inner hall.
A drowned xanmeer tower standing on the sea floor near Echo Deep, reached by diving.
The spire is uninhabited. A slaughterfish school holds the hall, and divers tell of a diver still caught in one gallery.
Weed furs the spire and Bell Station's divers have cleared half of it. They work the rest in short dives, because slaughterfish school in the flooded hall.
The dreugh attacks at once on sight, and a diver deep in the galleries has only the breath he took. Young dreugh swim in its upper rooms.
The bronze and bone of a temple-tower lie where few can reach. The dreugh's hoard in the nest draws the bravest divers.
Argonian divers say it belonged to Sithis and the water-spirits and pray before going in. Many read the dreugh as the water-spirits' answer to those who come to strip it.
Argonians raised it as a temple-tower in the Stone-Nest age, and no tribe has held it since the sea came. Its leaning shows how deep the old land fell.
A dreugh's hoard lies in the nests; the dead diver's kit at the foot of the stair carries a brass bell-cord token from Bell Station.
A leaning spire, dark with weed, with nests in its upper galleries.
A drowned xanmeer tower leaning on the sea floor near Echo Deep, reached by deep diving.
A dreugh and its brood live in it and defend the nests. A dead diver's kit lies at the foot of the stair.
Dark with weed, it carries a dreugh's nests in its upper galleries. Bell Station's divers enter rarely and never alone.
Dreugh scouts strike from the dark, and silt hides their approach until they are on the diver. A carved prize in a dreugh's grip is bait.
A salvage ground of bronze, vakka stones and bone, fought over with the dreugh. Bell Station sends divers only in numbers, and few come back with a full haul.
Argonian divers say it belonged to Sithis and the water-spirits and pray before going down. The dreugh's coral wrap marks it as theirs now.
It was a temple-tower of the Stone-Nest age, taken long after the sea came by the dreugh who now watch the water from it.
A dreugh keeps a carved prize in the spire's crown; a cut bell-chain hangs beside it, and the bell below still holds what the scouts left of its crew.
A spire half buried in silt, its top wrapped in coral.
A drowned xanmeer tower half buried in silt, north of Bell Station, reached by diving.
Dreugh scouts live in the upper rooms, watch the water and keep carved prizes taken from divers. Bell Station's divers tell of a bell-chain cut from below.
Capped with coral and half buried in silt, it is held by dreugh scouts. Bell Station's divers give it a wide berth.
Slaughterfish strike at the foot of the spire, and the dive is long: a diver who goes down the full height has used most of his breath before reaching the shrine.
A salvage ground of bone and bronze on the sand plain, though the summit shrine is left alone by custom. Few boats make the sail for what it gives.
The shrine on the summit holds a basin of Hist-sap that Bell Station's divers refill from the tree at Uluo, and they pray there before going in. The old faith is practised at this spire.
Argonians raised it as a temple-tower in the Stone-Nest age, and its summit shrine is older than the sea over it. Divers have kept the shrine untouched since they first came here.
The dead salvager's lamp marks his grave on the sand, and his crew's kin pay for it to be re-lit; a diver who leaves a worthy offering and touches the sap at the summit shrine receives its blessing.
A lone spire on a sand plain, with a shrine on its summit and a lamp glowing at its foot.
A lone drowned xanmeer tower on a sand plain, the furthest north-east of the spires, reached by a long dive.
Slaughterfish live at the foot of the spire. Divers who come leave offerings of shell and bronze at the summit shrine.
Bell Station's crews come rarely, because the sail from the station is long. A dead salvager's lamp still burns on the sand.
Divers drown in the lower gallery where the crew died, and slaughterfish shelter in the grave-rooms. The cache's lock is trapped and holds a poison needle.
Bell Station has worked it since its founding and takes what the upper floors still give. The crew's cache below stays shut out of respect.
Divers touch the platform's bell-cord before going down and pray to Sithis and the water-spirits. The crew's grave is left unstripped by the station's custom.
Argonians raised it in the Stone-Nest age, and the station was built over it for that reason. The first bell hung from a platform at its foot.
A failed crew's cache lies in the lower gallery under its trapped lock; the station's first bell hangs by the spire.
A spire beside Bell Station's anchor chains, a platform of old salvage at its foot.
A drowned xanmeer tower beside Bell Station, the nearest spire to the platform and the easiest to reach.
Nothing lives in it but fish, and a failed salvage crew lies in the lower gallery. Their names are carved on a grave-stake on the station and the crews do not speak them.
A platform of old salvage is built around its foot, in the shadow of the station's anchor chains. Little of value remains above the grave.
The ghost strikes at anyone who nears the sealed door, and the depth leaves a diver little breath for a fight. Divers must not touch the door's lock.
Its bronze is known but untouched, kept sealed by the ghost. Divers have not stripped it, and the hoard behind the door draws only the bold.
Argonian divers say it belonged to Sithis and the water-spirits, and that the ghost is its last priest. They pray before approaching and do not linger.
It was a temple-tower of the Stone-Nest age, and its Hist chamber was shut when the sea came. The ghost is taken for its last priest.
Thul-Kesh is the outermost spire, and its sealed Hist-chamber door opens only when the ghost is put to rest.
A tall pale spire on the edge of the deep, bright in the water where the ghost walks.
It is the outermost drowned xanmeer tower, standing on the edge of the deep and reached only by a long dive.
A drowned sea-priest's ghost keeps the sealed door. Divers who have seen it describe a figure bright in the water.
Tall and pale, it stands where the water is dark and the light is poor. Bell Station's divers go rarely.
Wildlife on the causeway; crocodiles lie in the drowned stretch and take the odd goat.
Saltrice, marsh greens and eels carried to Stormhold's market; a ferry stage on the river branch below the village.
A small Hist-shoot shrine at the causeway head; Dunmer ancestor stones in the farmyards.
The causeway farmsteads grew up under the Dunmer colonial period, when Stormhold needed food from raised ground and kept their stone footings through the generations since.
A family on the far mound whose causeway stones were pulled out by someone in the night, so their saltrice cannot reach market; a feud between the Argonian and Dunmer farm-holders over a water-right.
Low stone-footed houses with mud-plaster walls and reed roofs on raised platforms; stone causeways between the mounds and drying frames in the yards.
Surkina is a village in the Stormhold manner, a few miles south-east of the city, living on the city's farm trade.
Mixed Argonian and Dunmer farm families; a headman who is also the Vicecanon's reeve.
A dozen households of Argonians and Dunmer on stone mounds, linked to Stormhold by a causeway whose lower stretch lies under shallow black water that carts wade through.
Slaughterfish, slaughterfish and mud-crabs in the channels between the beds; risky outside the hamlet.
Saltrice, the main food crop of the bayou, with surplus sold to Archon and Lilmoth by raft.
Planting and harvest are marked by chanting to the Hist; the first sheaf is set on the water.
The tribe's rice grounds are older than the town; Tapauo's founders moved up the channel to find fresh silt.
The rice-warden distrusts seed bought from an outsider and wants the seller found. Two families wager over who may plant the last bed.
Rafts of rice-bed in neat rows beside stilt storehouses, with drying racks, sacks and a long landing of poles.
A hamlet of rice-growers between two channels, a half-day's raft north of Uluo.
Three Waters Argonians; a rice-warden decides when to plant and what the elder is owed.
Eight households plant, tend and harvest, loading rice onto rafts for Uluo and the Archon market.
Feather-serpents, undead of the old assault and deep water around the halls.
Once a tribal stronghold; now salvage for passers-by and an Argonian grave-place.

Nothing is worshipped at Tarak Shan now. Amalaja's minder leaves a reed offering at the old gate for the defenders whom the Third Legion killed. People in the washes hold that the water here is a grave.
Stormed by the Empire in the time of Tiber Septim (2E 857 to 861), where the soldier Attrebus was wounded; abandoned since, with a feather-serpent legend attached.
A pile of Imperial arms from the storming; a feather-serpent's den; a Legion banner.
Tarak Shan is a ring of tiered halls standing on the water, broken by the old assault and covered in lichen.
Tarak Shan is a ring of broken tiered halls on the water, covered in lichen, with a flooded stockade and a sunken landing. A feather-serpent legend clings to it.
Tarak Shan is uninhabited. Scavengers come by boat for Legion brass and the occasional skull. Hunters from Amalaja will not stay a night.
Collapsed stilt halls, a flooded stockade, a sunken landing.
Marsh predators haunt the paddy edges and the channels. Bandits from the delta come by water at night.
Tei-Kur grows rice and cuts reed, sets fish traps in the channels and sends its rice on to Delta Ferry by the ferry connection.
The Hist at Lilmoth, regrown since the city was rebuilt, serves them; they carry their dead to its tender.
A delta farming village cleared and rebuilt in the generations after 4E 48.
A paddy blight, a landlord's feud and a chance to carry rice to Blackrose.
Paddies in shallow terraces, stilt houses with rice stores, a boardwalk road.
A village in the farmed land east of Blackrose, within Lilmoth's trade.
Tei-Kur's people are Argonian rice farmers who live with their households among the paddies east of Blackrose.
Part of Lilmoth's trade network and hostile to the Archwardens.
Wildlife threatens travellers on the river road east of Stormhold, and the crystal pits above the village are worse, with rockfall traps and whatever lives in the old workings.
Wayhouse trade on the road east, river landing fees and Stormhold Crystals dug in the nearby pits.
A Hist-shoot shrine and Dunmer ancestor stones; the villagers avoid the old shrine ground on the hill.
The name echoes Ten-Maur-Wolk, a Boethiah-worshipping Dunmer settlement after 1E 700 turned slave camp; the villagers do not speak of it.
A pit-boss who has found a vein that hums; a traveller who came by river with a sack of Dres slave-irons and has not left his room since.
Stone-footed stilt houses along the bank, a landing of timber stages, a long wayhouse with a stone chimney.

Tenmal is a village in the Stormhold manner on the road east of the city. Its name is close to Ten-Maur-Wolk (Tenmar Wall), the road hinge that neighbours Stormhold and the village grew up along the same road.
Argonian and Dunmer families of the river road; a ferryman and a pit-boss.
A river-side village with a landing and a wayhouse, and a crystal pit above it worked by a few households.

Inside the walls it is safe by law, but purse-cutters and bribed guards are the real risk. At the door the paddies and the coast road are mostly safe; the saltrice workers bear grudges against the field-owners.

Saltrice, the crop the East Empire Company once exported, is the city's wealth, with the Tear road, border tolls and smuggling beside it. Timber and stone come in from the Arnesian jungle to the west; Tsonac sells to Thorn and buys its rice.

The Argonians worship at a Hist tree on the field edge outside the walls; the Dunmer minority keeps the old Temple saints, among them Roris, the trader whose death began the Arnesian War. The Nine have a few shrines in the old Imperial quarter.

The Barsaebic Ayleids founded it. House Dres raided it in the mid-First Era and rose to a Great House on the slaves taken; Dres ruled it in the Second Era until Heita-Meen, once a slave in its saltrice fields, killed Councilor Glathis Dres in 2E 572. In the Third Era it was a city-state under King Tibus and rival to Archon, and the Arnesian War of 3E 396 was fought on its border.

Two field-holding families who each say their grandmothers stood in the same saltrice field when Dres fell, a smuggling ring that moves moon sugar through Fort Thornmoth's gate, a Dunmer family hunting a runaway slave's grandchildren and the Velothi pieces scavengers sell in the market from Kharraluhl and Ovezza.

A walled city of Ayleid-founded stone under Dunmer and Imperial rebuilding, with Argonian timber and reed quarters round it, set on flat grassland that runs to green saltrice paddies in every direction. Thorn Palace, the Conclave of Riana and the Conclave of the One still stand; the old Mages Guild hall has been shut since the guild dissolved before 4E 48 and is now a saltrice store.

Thorn is one of the eight major cities of Black Marsh, in the grassland of Thornmarsh in the north-east, with Morrowind and the road to Tear to its north. Its epithet is the Jewel of the East: as deadly as it is beautiful, a city where vagabonds eye purses and the guards turn a blind eye.

About three in four are Argonian, with a large Dunmer minority of mixed families whose ancestors stood on both sides of the coffles and a few Imperial-descended traders. The people who matter are the Vicecanons (one to three, chosen locally), the field-holding families, the saltrice gangs and the smugglers who work the quays.

In 4E 201 Thorn is intact and the most prosperous place in the north-east. With Dres gone the saltrice fields passed to whoever stood in them: freed labourers' descendants and the ex-Archein families who managed them. Who holds title to which field is the city's standing quarrel, settled by Vicecanons.
Safe inside; the surrounding washes hold large predators, and the roads east are watched by outlaws from the Rose.
Tin and copper chimes, metal-woven rope, shallow-draft sail-and-paddle boats and fees from river traffic.
Sithis and the Hist, with a quiet regard for Z'en and Dibella beside them.
A Kothringi town before 2E 560; resettled by flu-immune Argonians, who kept the name; nativists in the generations since called its people half-foreign.
Kothringi treasure rumours, a chime-maker's commission, a dispute over a wreck and the old foundations beneath the stone footings.
Stilt houses on stone footings, chimes of tin and copper hanging from every eave, boardwalks, neat rope-walks and a boatyard on the channel.
A market town named by the Kothringi, kept by Argonians who settled the empty Kothringi towns after the Knahaten Flu.
Argonians of the oxblood towns with a few mixed families: metalworkers, boatwrights, traders.
A craft-masters' council governs and deals coldly with the Archwardens and warmly with Gideon. It is the best-ordered place for days around.
Sarpa archers on the shelf and spear-bearers at the tents attack outsiders on sight. The shelf ends in a sheer drop to the gorge.
They hunt, raid and take what they need; they trade nothing.
They keep the Hist of High-Flower, the Sarpa tree and mark their ground with feathers.
The Sarpa have hunted the mesa's western edge as long as Oxayo's grave-singers remember; this warband's camp has stood on the shelf for three generations of Stone-Sleepers.
A Tsonac stone caravan lost three guards on the road below the shelf, and their bodies hang on the feather poles; a Sarpa elder who will parley for a gift of fresh fish.
Hide tents on a flat shelf, feather-hung poles and drying racks, with the cave beside it.
Hanaxi Roost is a Sarpa camp on the western mesa edge. The Sarpa are winged Argonians found in Middle Argonia alone. They are hostile to outsiders.
A dozen Sarpa live on the shelf: a warband of hunters and a few elders.
A permanent camp of a warband, watching the mesa and raiding the road to Tsonac.
Sarpa archers on the high perches shoot at anyone on the bank, and the wing-chief's guard rushes the path.
Feathers, eggs and raided goods; they trade fish for clay beads.
They read omens in the wind and speak of the Hist as the sky's roots.
The Sarpa are winged and hostile to outsiders and live only in Middle Argonia; this camp stands on the edge of Oxhu country, where the confederacy clashes with them often.
The wing-chief wants a stolen perch-pole returned from Aroxhu. An Aroxhu spear-captain wants peace and needs an envoy.
Tall perches and streamers over a mud-bank, tents of reed and hide, rope nets, droppings white on stones.
A permanent Sarpa camp on a high mud-bank west of Aroxhu. The winged hunters roost in reed shelters on the bank's crown, where they can watch the clay-mound country around them.
About eight Sarpa live on the roost, led by a wing-chief with a scarred crest.
A camp of perches and tents; Aroxhu's spears and the Sarpa trade blows now and then and trade fish for clay beads between fights.
Sarpa archers shoot intruders from the perches; the camp's boundary poles are marked in feathers and bones.
Feathers, bird-eggs and fish; they trade for salt and clay beads at the edge of their ground. Ash-glass picked from Virtluush is their one valuable good.
The Sarpa hold the wind to be a messenger of the Hist and read omens in flight patterns. They keep a rack of old Velothi ancestor-bones on a post as a boundary mark.
The Sarpa came out to the eastern edge to roost on the towers and walls of the Virtluush ruin, and stayed beside it.
The Sarpa want a stolen Velothi bone-flute back from an Arorha potter. The old female will trade safe passage across the Virtluush ground for it.
Tents of woven reed and hide on a rise, tall poles with feathered streamers, nets slung between trees, droppings white on the stones.
A permanent camp of Sarpa, one of the winged interior breeds, on high ground behind the bight. A roost this far east is a long way from the Sarpa's home in the middle of the province.
About nine Sarpa, led by an old female who speaks Jel and a few words of Dunmeri. They are cautiously willing to trade for dye and salt if a visitor approaches openly.
A camp of tents and perches, with scouts on the high perches at dawn. The Sarpa watch the road to Arorha and drive off clay-diggers who come near.
Peaceable with those who come openly; dragon's-tongue beds around the camp can kill the careless.
Herbs including dragon's-tongue, pelts and fish; they trade with Korydon.
Sithis and the swamp; each hunter wears a tuft of swamp-moss for luck.
A swamp-hunters' ground near the dragon's-tongue beds, used by the Tumnatu since before Argonians resettled the Kothringi towns round it.
The herb-wife needs help to harvest dragon's-tongue; Korydon's elders accuse the camp of stealing a chime.
Reed shelters on a hummock among cattails, herb bundles on poles and a smoke fire.
Tumnatu Cattail Camp is a Tumnatu camp on the northern edge of Korydon's ring of water. The camp is the Tumnatu tribe's.
About eight Tumnatu: hunters, a herb-wife and a boy who knows the best channels.
Eight Tumnatu hunt the swamp and bargain with Korydon's guild elders for chimes.
Wary but not hostile to those who come openly; raiders if provoked.
The Tumnatu on the lake's north shore trade fish, eels and woven reed mats to the townsfolk of Marzai and Julo.
Sithis and the lake; the Tumnatu leave a bowl of eel-fat at the waterline.
The Tumnatu are a lake tribe and this is their fishing ground on the lake's north shore, older than Marzai. Their own songs say little more to outsiders.
A net-line has been cut, and the camp blames Marzai; the headwoman wants a go-between who speaks for neither side; a clay pot of Imperial coin came up in a fish-trap.
Reed shelters on a low bank, fish racks and drag-nets, dugout canoes drawn up.
Tumnatu Reed Camp lies near Marzai, in reed shelters on a low bank of the lake. The camp is the Tumnatu tribe's.
About eight Tumnatu: fishers, hunters and a headwoman who bargains openly.
Eight Tumnatu hold the camp and keep a cool peace with Marzai, trading eggs for pots.
Ambush on the river and the ferry; the Hutan-Tzel fight them on sight.
The band lives by raids on the Hutan-Tzel's boats, by hunting and by extorting payment from the ferry at Tzel-Haar.
Sithis, above all. This band keeps no village tree; it buries its dead at the water's edge on the western bank, each marked with a snake's fang pushed into the mud.
A band of the Naga who left the Panther River road after the plantations ended and settled on this dry rise.
The Hutan-Tzel pay a bounty for the seer; a stolen totem-stone is in the camp.
Lean-tos under a root arch, fish-bone racks and a bank trampled bare.
Hiss-Bank Camp is a Naga camp on the western river bank. About eight Naga live in lean-tos under a root arch on a trampled bank, with a seer who reads bones.
About eight Naga, a few young ones and a seer who reads bones.
Eight Naga hold a bend of the western river and raid the Hutan-Tzel's boats.
Paatru kill unwary outsiders on sight; their mere is deep and poisoned.
Hunting, frogspawn and mudpot herbs; they trade with the Chime-Keepers at Nacydes.
The Hist and Sithis, each in a mud-shrine; the Paatru believe the toad-forms of the dead stay in the pools.
The Paatru keep to the interior; this camp is one of their lasting grounds, used since before the Empire came.
The elder wants a chime tuned and will let one trusted visitor in; a hunter vanished at the mere's edge; a lost caravan's goods rest in the mud.
Domed mud huts at the edge of a mere, hung with strings of knuckle-bones. The Paatru croak at dusk.
Mud-Croak Camp is a Paatru camp on the western edge of Murkwood's reach. The Paatru are toad-like Argonians found only in Middle Argonia.
About twelve toad-like Paatru, led by a croaking elder; a hostile tribe.
About twelve Paatru hold it and kill outsiders on the spot, as the Paatru are known to do; they bargain only with Nacydes' chime-makers.
Hunters on the bank challenge strangers within bow-range. Swamp crocodiles and snakes use the same reeds.
They hunt along the reeds and cure the hides on the rack for sale at Gul-Tej. The riverbank gives them fish and reed-grubs between the hunts.
They honour Sithis and the Hist of Low-Crown, and hang feather and reed charms from the smoke-rack. A tiny totem-stone by the landing is turned to face the water at dawn.

The Paatru hunt the forest edge west of the Hist country, and this bank is one of their old hunting grounds, left to them because the Naka-Desh fish the channels below and never wanted the dry reeds above. The interior tribes were untouched by Umbriel, so the camp has stood on the same bank for as long as the hunters remember.
A stolen egg, a trade for skins or a hunter asking for a guide through the reeds.
Lean-tos of reed and hide among tall reeds, a smoke-rack by the bank and a boat drawn up on the mud. The ground is trampled flat around a hearth pit.
A Paatru hunters' camp on the western edge of the Hist country: reed lean-tos on a riverbank, a smoke-rack and a drawn-up boat.
Six Paatru: three hunters, an egg-tender, a hide-curer and a youth learning to net. They are wary of strangers who come by boat and warn them off by banging on a hollow log.
A handful of Paatru hunters and an egg-tender keep the bank. The lean-tos stand all year, and there is always a hide on the rack.
Hunters watch the camp from the reeds and Mine-Burner watchers are close. Basin crocodiles and giant snakes use the same ground.
They hunt the basin's edge for deer and marsh-birds, and trade skins and herbs to Hixinoag when they go north. They pay the Mine-Burners nothing but meat left at a boundary stone.
They keep the Paatru faith in Sithis and the Hist of Low-Crown, and bury their dead at the camp's edge under a mound of reeds. They do not speak of the Hist at Jarecai.

The Paatru and the Mine-Burners have shared the basin's north edge since before the mines burned in 3E 427: the hunters take game on the dry ground and leave meat at a boundary stone, and the Mine-Burners leave them alone.
A border quarrel with the Mine-Burners, a hunter's missing son or a hide-trade.
A ring of reed shelters on dry ground at the edge of the basin, a smoke-rack and a stack of drying hides. A boundary stone with a few bones on it stands at the south side.
A Paatru hunters' camp on dry ground at the Banujha Basin's north edge, close to Mine-Burner land.
Six Paatru, led by an old hunter who knows the basin trails. They are polite to Mine-Burner watchers and closed to everyone else.
A party of Paatru hunters stays on the dry ground for the drier months and leaves when the water rises. They keep a careful distance from the Mine-Burner watch posts.
Naga warbands raid from the camp and strike at travellers. The approaches to it are set with traps.
Highway robbery and ransom; some trade of stolen goods with Dunmer smugglers.
The Naga worship Sithis at a shrine of bones; no Hist tree stands in the camp.
The Naga highwaymen live off the road traffic from Stormhold to Helstrom. They come and go as the merchants do.
A captive merchant held for ransom; a Naga who wants to defect.
Reed-and-bone huts around a pit, a lookout on a dead tree and a pole of trophies.

Karsh-Naal Camp is a Naga brigands' camp in the marsh south of Stormhold. The Naga are the tribeless Argonians of canon who rob travellers on the roads; the busy road from Stormhold toward Helstrom is where such a band would live.
Tribeless Naga, tall and hard-eyed and they rob for a living.
A band of Naga lives in huts of woven reed and bone around a fire pit.
Naga ambush boats and lone travellers; needle fangs and poison; they flee from numbers.
They live on river raids, hunting and what they take from passing boats.
Sithis, above all. There is no village tree at the camp; its dead are laid in the dry ground north of Helstrom with a snake's fang as marker.
The Naga were road-robbers on Imperial plantation routes and retreated to the inner swamps when the roads failed; this camp is where one band settled.
A Root-Folk sap-gatherer is held here for ransom; the camp hides the sap-skins stolen from Tseli-Oon; the old leader will bargain for a boat.
Hide-covered lean-tos on a dry mound, bones strung on lines, a fire pit and a slit-trench latrine.
Dry-Fang Camp is a Naga camp north of Helstrom. About nine tribeless Naga live in hide-covered lean-tos on a dry mound, led by a scarred old female.
About nine tribeless Naga, adder-featured, seven to eight feet tall, led by a scarred old female.
About nine Naga hold it in 4E 201, beyond the reach of Helstrom's assembly and prey on the north river arm.
The ruin is haunted by the Kothringi dead, and the hunters shoot at trespassers. Swamp beasts come to the hide-racks at night.
They hunt and cure hides and sell them to traders from Gideon. The ruin's dry rooms let them keep a stock of hides through the heaviest rain.
They honour Sithis and the Hist of Low-Crown. They make a point of leaving a bowl of salt at the ruin's door since, the Paatru say, the Kothringi dead want it.

The Paatru roofed the standing walls of a Kothringi ruin with hide and reed long ago, when the ruin had been empty since the Knahaten Flu. The hunters keep away from its inner rooms, where the Kothringi dead still walk.
A Kothringi relic the hunters found, a claim on the ruin or a boat for hire.
Hide and reed shelters built up against a broken Kothringi wall, a hearth pit in the open and a smoke-rack in the lee. Chimes hang from the ruin's lintel.
A Paatru hunters' camp on the western edge of the Hist country, built against the walls of a Kothringi ruin.
Six Paatru, who tell newcomers the ruin is haunted and say they keep to the camp for that reason. One of them speaks a little Cyrodilic from trading with Gideon's boats.
A small party of Paatru hunters winters in the old ruin's best-preserved room and hunts in the reeds outside. The ruin holds their stores of dried meat and bundled hides.
Ambushes near Nacydes and the marsh crossing; Murkwood's medusas nearby are a danger to them too.
The band lives by hunting and raiding, and sells stolen fellrunner feathers taken from the edge of Murkwood.
Sithis, above all. The band has no tree; its dead are sunk in the marsh south-west of Helstrom with a salt-crusted fang to mark the place.
A band of Naga who retreated into the deep swamp when the Imperial roads ended and made their fires here.
A feather armband lies in the leader's tent; Nacydes would pay to see the band gone; the one-eyed leader seeks a boat.
Hide tents on a salt-crusted mound, bones and feather bundles on poles, smoke from a hidden fire.
Salt-Tooth Camp is a Naga camp in the marsh south-west of Helstrom. Ten Naga live in hide tents on a salt-crusted mound, led by a one-eyed male with a feather armband.
About ten Naga, led by a one-eyed male with a feather armband.
Ten Naga hunt the marsh toward Nacydes and Murkwood's edge, and sell Murkwood feathers that they should not have.
Naga warbands hold the camp and strike travellers on the road. The marsh around it is dangerous ground.
The band lives by highway robbery on the road past Gandranen.
The Naga worship Sithis at a shrine made of bones beside the fire pit, with no Hist tree.
Naga bands follow road traffic, and this camp south of Gandranen lives off the travellers of the road.
The band holds a Khajiit trader for ransom; one of the Naga wants out of the camp and will open the stockade at night for a price.
Huts of reed and bone stand around the fire, and a pole hung with trophies marks the camp.
Ushaan Camp is a second Naga band's camp, in the marsh south of Gandranen on the road toward Slough Point. Naga rob road traffic, and the Blackwood Road trade passes close by.
Tribeless Naga, a band of brigands who belong to no clan, hold the camp.
Huts of reed and bone ring a fire pit in the marsh south of Gandranen.
Safe inside the harbour watch. Smuggling and tolls start quarrels on the quay; out on the lake there are slaughterfish in the deep water and rival boatmen.
Rice, fish, sap, feathers and clay come down the lake; cloth, tin, tools and salt go back up. The harbour master charges a mooring toll and the council holds the deep-water quay on the lake.
The Hist grows in a small city tree. Sithis is kept privately. The foreign factors keep a shrine to Zenithar.

No song names Truowa before its rise. It grew from a lake landing where interior goods met coast-bound boats; in the generations after Umbriel destroyed Lilmoth, traders who would not live under the successor state came here.

A cargo of cloth has gone missing from the quay and each side blames the other; the council refuses Fort Gysilla's toll and the garrison has begun stopping Truowa boats; a Lilmoth trader wants a guard on the boat road to Helstrom.
Stilt quays and warehouses on reed piles, rose-washed plaster on the merchants' houses in the Lilmoth manner, rafts and canoes at every landing and the lake spread flat and grey-green to the west.

Truowa is a small city, on the scale of Falkreath, at the south-east edge of Lake Ulaish where the water runs out toward Lilmoth. It belongs to Lilmoth's trade: goods from the delta and the coast arrive here and go up the lake to the Helstrom country.

About 38 residents, mostly Argonian, with a few Imperial, Khajiit and Bosmer traders on the quay, come up the river from Lilmoth's coast. Council merchants, harbour watchmen, ferrymen, rice buyers and a tree-minder everyone knows.

In 4E 201 a merchant council, copying Lilmoth's, runs the city, takes a toll on lake boats and keeps a harbour watch. It trades openly with the delta and the Lilmoth coast and is cool toward the Warden fort at Gysilla.
Tselan sits in settled country and its people keep the paths clear. Giant snakes still hunt the jungle edge round the quarry.
Quarried stone, fish, jungle fruit; it buys cloth and tools from Tsonac.
The Stone-Sleepers believe their Hist sleeps; at Tselan a stone cairn takes the place of a tree, and dreams are reported to Tsonac's tree-minder.
Founded over an old foundation as the Stone-Sleepers spread west along the river.
The quarry gang has broken into a sealed Velothi chamber under the hamlet's oldest foundation, and the elder wants Tsonac's tree-minder to come before anyone goes in. One of the gang went in anyway.
Square stone houses with reed roofs, terraced vegetable plots and a riverside quay for stone barges.
A Stone-Sleeper hamlet on a river that runs down to the bay, the westernmost of their quarry hamlets. Its people cut stone from the hill above and raft it to Tsonac.
Stone-Sleeper families: a quarry gang of four and an elder who learned the Hist's dreams from Tsonac's tree-minder in her youth and still walks there to hear them.
Eight Argonians cut stone from a quarry on the hill above and send it down by raft.
The elders keep order inside Tsonac's terraces. The jungle around the city is dangerous.
Quarried stone, hardwood, hides and carved goods sold to Thorn; it buys saltrice, cloth and iron.

The Hist at the city's centre is held to be asleep. The tree-minder hears its dreams in the sap and in what the town's hatchlings dream, and the town treats the tree as a living elder that must never be woken.

Barsaebic Ayleids and Cantemiric Velothi once held this country; the Argonians built over their foundations after the Flu emptied it. The name echoes Tsono-Xuhil, the mad Hist of the Xit-Xaht that its neighbours put to sleep and the grave-singers say Tsonac's tree is a sapling of that line, asleep since it was planted.

A tree-minder who says the Hist's dreams have turned bad since a mason cut too deep under the mound, a Thorn buyer who wants an Ayleid welkynd stone cut from the foundations and two mason families quarrelling over a seam of good stone.
Terraces of squared stone with timber upper storeys climbing a slope from the river quay, a central mound with the Hist and a ring of carved stone steps, sunlit and clean.

The one city of the Stone-Sleepers (Tsona-Kaleel), who, unusually among Argonians, build in stone. Like the Xit-Xaht of Shadowfen they kept the old craft; unlike them they never raided for labour, and their Hist sleeps rather than raves.
About forty named townsfolk: masons, timber-cutters, hunters, the tree-minder who hears the Hist's dreams, its pupils and buyers from Thorn who lodge by the quay.
Tsonac is peaceful, dry and proud and run by elders and a tree-minder. It is the Stone-Sleepers' one city and watches the road to Thorn.
Naga hunters from the north camps, giant snakes, bad footing at night.
Hunting, herb-gathering, lizard-hides and chime-mending for Korydon.
The families honour Sithis; the watchfire on the peak above the hamlet doubles as a small offering to the Hist.
A Kothringi settlement before 2E 560; Argonian chime-keepers moved in, and its watchfire on the peak has burned ever since.
The watchfire went dark one night and a stranger was found beside it; a giant spider nest guards a Kothringi cache along the ridge path.
Stilt-and-stone houses against a rock rise, a signal fire basket on the peak, chimes in the wind.
Tydeos is a hamlet of about six at the foot of the ridge's southern peak, a Kothringi-named place kept by Argonians.
About six Argonians: chime-menders, a watchfire-keeper and young hunters.
Six people tend the peak's watchfire, keep goods for passing parties and trade with Korydon.
Safe in the town. The channels around it hold slaughterfish, slaughterfish and the odd smuggler who has not paid the elder's share.
Net-fish, shellfish, saltrice, reed mats and bundles and the back-water freight that moves between Archon and the Lilmoth delta without passing customs. The elder takes a share of every raft.
Argonian Sithis and Hist devotion; a small Hist pool lies in the town, tended by a tree-minder and hatching families come in from the hamlets. Rafts are blessed at launching.

The tribe's Elder Nuetepa is remembered in Archon from long ago. Each family tells the tribe's first settlement on the islands differently; the town grew where the bayou channels meet the open strait, and the Flu that emptied the coast of other peoples left the Argonians alive.

The elder wants a cargo of saltrice carried to Archon past the customs post. A raft-master offers a back channel the customs officers do not use, for a favour. Two families dispute who tends the Hist pool.
A pentagon of raft-mounted halls and reed houses around a landing, with a long communal hall for the elder's moot, drying frames of fish and rafts lashed in rings beside the landing.

The one town of the Three Waters Tribe, and the place the bayou hamlets send their catch, rice and reed. It matters as the tribe's seat and as a crossing point between Archon, Lilmoth and the Nushara waters.
Three Waters Argonians: the elder, a council of raft-masters who know the channel routes, a handful of Archon and Lilmoth traders and traders from Aroxhu.

A market town of raft-houses and stilt halls, never taken by any power and untouched by Umbriel. The tribe is wary of the An-Xileel's successors and sends its own to sit with Archon's merchants, so it is both neutral ground and a smuggler's door.
Umpholo stands in wild country at the far west. Its people fear Sul-Xan raiders from the Blackwood frontier.
River fish, clay pots and reed, carried to Slough Point.
The chapel to Mara is empty; the river folk have a Hist-shoot shrine beside it and say Dibella's name in the Gideon way.
The Maran mission's temple was built about 3E 378 and abandoned within a month; the Agaceph looted its books by about 3E 399.
A silver Mara amulet the villagers found under the chapel floor; a visiting Agaceph who wants it; a Sul-Xan scout in the reeds.
A stone chapel with a fallen roof, vine-covered and stilt houses along the bank.

Umpholo is the site of a Temple of Mara built about 3E 378. The missionaries died of swamp rot within a month and the library was picked clean by about 3E 399. The story is told in The Argonian Account, Book 4. The site lies in the far west.
Lukiul and Naka-Desh Argonians of the Blackwood frontier; Agaceph come now and then to trade.
A hamlet of river Argonians living in and around the stripped stone chapel, which the swamp has been overgrowing for two centuries. A fish-and-reed trade with Slough Point.
The flu-dead of the old Velothi household are unquiet in the deep, dark halls. Sarpa hunters roost nearby and shoot at anyone whom they take for a robber.
Once a river-quay market; now a ruin with uncollected goods and no trade.
The Velothi followed Mephala; the Hist-guarded land beyond is held to be worse than the ruin itself.
A Velothi town of the east, emptied by the Knahaten Flu in 2E 560-603; too far from any road to have been scavenged.
A Noota Nara scout went into the outer yard and was found dead with a key of Velothi bronze in his hand, and the hunters of Noota Nara will pay for the bell that hangs silent in the high tower.
Deeper, darker Dunmer stonework than the northern ruins, half sunk into a mesa slope and thick with fungus.
Vorannuhl is the deepest Cantemiric Velothi ruin of the east, half sunk into the mesa's south slope. The name is the one Noota Nara's hunters give it, in the Velothi style of the other ruins.
The ruin has no living inhabitants. A Sarpa warband sometimes shelters in its outer yard and leaves bones there.
Fallen towers and undisturbed halls; the nearest living people are the Sarpa camp to the north-west and Noota Nara's hunters.
Ancestor ghosts and undead guards walk the lower rooms, and the fallen side of the dome walls off the south hall.
It once served as a shrine to the Velothi's ancestors. Treasure hunters and grave-robbers from Archon are drawn to its grave-goods.
Ancestor worship of the Velothi dissidents, probably with a Mephala tie from Chimeri myth.
The Cantemiric Velothi settled the seaboard between Archon, Arnesia and Thorn. The Knahaten Flu, 2E 560-603, killed all of them and left their shrines and graves.
A ghost by the east niche that will not move until its ashes are carried to the sea. Smugglers digging in the mound for grave-goods.
A stepped dome of grey stone overgrown with vine, carved ash-grey doors, shrine niches and ash-bowls.
A ruin of the Cantemiric Velothi, a stepped dome shrine near Archon's marshes.
No one lives there, though a few of Archon's Dunmer families carry offerings to the east niche. The people of Archon say the Velothi dead walk its lower rooms.
Overgrown and half buried; the dome has fallen in at one side. The Argonians call it sick ground.
Ancestor ghosts, skeletal guards and crocodiles in the drowned halls.
Once a river-fort. Now a draw for scavengers after Velothi bronze, ash-glass and carved tablets.

The Cantemiric household kept altar niches in each room and carved a tablet for each family dead. It served a Daedric power in the lower hall, now under water. The Oxhu say the tablets still answer the right voice.
Cantemiric Velothi settled the eastern seaboard; the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560 ended them, and Anvadas was empty within a generation.
A sealed vault door opens only to the right family tablet, and the Oxhu tell of a tablet carried off into the marsh. A Yulca elder will pay for any carved Velothi tablet that survives.
Dark Velothi stonework in heavy courses, tilted and sunk, reeds in the courtyard, a leaning tower, still black pools within.
Anvadas sits on a mud-ridge in the marsh south of Gaweja, with a leaning tower and a courtyard drowned in black water. Its name is in Velothi style.
Anvadas has no residents. The Oxhu and Agaceph keep clear of the mud-ridge. The household's ghosts stay in the drowned courtyard and the tower.
The ruin is half sunk in the marsh. The Oxhu and Agaceph alike avoid it.
Ancestor ghosts in the lower halls, a humming sealed door and river crocodiles at the landing.
Once a river-fort. The Agaceph take ash-glass shards from its upper halls and trade them.

The household's ancestor tablets and altar niches survive in the upper halls, where Yina's Agaceph leave them untouched. The lower hall's Daedric shrine is shut, and the Agaceph say that it should stay shut.
The Cantemiric Velothi built it and the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560 killed them; the Agaceph moved in at its foot soon after.
The sealed door hums at night. Yina's eldest will pay anyone who can open it without waking what lies behind.
A black stone keep with a broken tower on a river bank, ivy, vines, reed rafts moored under the wall.
Sethiral is a black stone keep with a broken tower and reed rafts moored under its wall. Yina's Agaceph use the upper halls and the lower halls are shut. Its name is in Velothi style.
Sethiral's halls have no residents. Yina's Agaceph sit in the upper rooms and leave at dusk. The household's ghosts keep to the lower halls, behind the humming door.
The upper halls are used by Yina's Agaceph as a sitting and reading place; the lower halls are shut behind a humming door.
Ghosts, rotten floors over a drop in the upper tier and a sea-cave the smugglers hold, reached by swimming.
Once a coastal watch-hold. Now a draw for scavengers and for a smuggling crew's cache.

Its Velothi families kept the Velothi ancestor rites, with a niche and tablet for each family dead. The shrine in the lower hall served a Daedric power, and the spell-fire on the upper tier still burns.
Cantemiric Velothi built this coastal hold. The Knahaten Flu of 2E 560 ended them, and the headland has been unoccupied since.
A Khiar fisherman is held captive on the upper tier by the smugglers. Their cache lies in the sea-cave below.
Black stone on a cliff edge, a broken sea-tower, salt crust, sea-birds nesting in the roof, surf below.
Mazurath crowns a sea-cliff above the surf, with a broken sea-tower that glows faintly after dark. Its name is in Velothi style.
Mazurath's headland has no residents. Khiar's villagers will not go up after dark. The household's ghosts are blamed for the glow on the sea-cliff, and a smuggling crew uses the lower cave.
A ruin on a sea-cliff, glowing faintly after dark, which the village of Khiar blames on its ghosts.
Rock-fall traps in the old galleries, a crocodile nest in the flooded drift and smugglers who use the sealed lower galleries as a store.
Ochre for dye and alum for fixing it. Both go to Aroxhu's dyers, and any surplus is sold to Archon.
The miners leave a pot of ochre at the mouth. Their dead are carried to Aroxhu and staked there.

The Company worked this ochre and alum mine in the last years of the Third Era and left at the secession. Aroxhu's clay-diggers and Seafalls families reopened the upper galleries in the generations after.
The sealed galleries hold the Company's last strongbox. The gallery-boss wants someone to swim the flooded drift past the crocodiles to reach the locked lower door from below.
A hillside cut in rust and yellow bands with a plank-lined adit, a Company-era timber headframe, ore carts and yellow-stained pools.
A mine on the road between Renhu and Seafalls whose Imperial-sounding name marks an old East Empire Company working.
About six miners, Oxhu clay-diggers and Seafalls families, led by a gallery-boss who keeps the key.
The upper galleries are worked. The lower ones are plugged with clay behind a locked timber door after a roof fall killed two men.
Ancestor ghosts, skeletal guards and a Sarpa lookout who will shoot anyone who approaches by air or reed-path.
Once a river-fort that took tolls from boat traffic. Now a scavenger's draw: Velothi bronze, ash-glass, ancestor tablets and a locked vault of dye-stuffs.
Mephala-influenced Velothi ancestor worship: altar niches to a Daedric lord and carved family tablets in every room.
Cantemiric Velothi held it until the Knahaten Flu (2E 560-603) ended them. It stood on a river bend with a boat road to the coast.
The steward's ghost still wears a ring of the lord's house; the Dunmer relic-seller in Thorn will pay for it. The cistern joins the bight by a drowned tunnel that a swimmer can follow.
Black stone courts and a tall broken tower in heavy Velothi courses, ivy and vines over the walls, a cistern with dark water in the heart.
A bigger Velothi ruin on a river bend behind the bight, with a Sarpa camp at its flank. It is one of the Cantemiric Velothi settlements of this seaboard.
No living folk inside. Velothi ancestor ghosts haunt the lower halls, and the ghost of the household's steward still guards them.
Collapsed courts, a standing tower and a deep cistern, haunted. The Sarpa live beside it and take ash-glass and tablets from the edges but will not go into the lower halls.
Slaughterfish run the channel below the landing. Drunk sailors and smugglers put in at the quay by night.
Rice, fish and reed sold on the water and a quiet trade in cargo that never goes through Archon's quay.
Sailors drive a scrap of net into a mud post on the bank for the drowned of the estuary, as kin drive grave-stakes.
Grew with Archon's trade: the Three Waters wanted a landing to sell from without entering the harbour and paying its customs.
A boat to hire into the bayou; a pilot's family owes a raft-master's family a debt; a raft that left for Archon and did not arrive.
Stilt houses on the bank, a long plank landing, lanterns and boats; the hamlet's lights show from the harbour.
A hamlet on the west bank of the estuary just above Archon, where bayou rafts and harbour boats meet.
Three Waters Argonians, with Archon pilots as regular visitors; one old pilot's widow keeps a lantern house.
Ten people hold the landing under the raft-master's family, sell to passing Archon boatmen and hear all that moves in the estuary.
Illusion-casting guards on the approach, marsh crocodiles and giant snakes.
Books, copied pages, illusion-work and eels. Prices are steep but fair.
They honour the Hist from a distance and read the missionary's tracts as comedy.
The hamlet grew round a chest of books that its people carried off from a dead Maran outstation in the Third Era.
A mission lamp-glass from the old outstation has been sold to a trader at Seafalls, and the eldest will pay in books to have it back.
Raft-houses and stilts on a marsh pond, books drying on lines in the sun, rafts hauled onto reed beds.
A raft-and-stilt hamlet in the marsh between Gaweja and Renhu.
About seven Agaceph, led by a literate eldest who knows every book on the shelf by its cover.
A hamlet that guards its shelf of books and sells a few to those who bargain well.
Safe by day. Smugglers land on the south bank at night, and mudcrabs come up into the paddies.
Rice, fish and ferry hire. The garrison buys at a fixed low price, which the farmers resent.
Sithis and a small village tree, with an Archein household still keeping a Divines-style roadside shrine.
No stake tells of its founding. It is read as a farm set up in the generations after 4E 48 to feed the traders and the Warden garrison on the lake's south side.
The farmers are close to refusing the garrison their grain; a stranger hired a boat for one night and left a pouch of uncut stones behind; smugglers landing on the south bank want a dry store.
Stone-footed reed houses along a low shore, paddies fenced with reed, a small plank quay and the fort's lamp visible across the water at dusk.
Yalugo is a hamlet of about six on the south lake shore between Truowa and the waters toward Korydon. It follows the Stormhold manner of raised stone footings.
About six residents: Argonian farmers and a retired cook of Archein descent who once fed the Gysilla garrison.
Two farm families sell grain and smoked fish to Fort Gysilla and wayfarers, and keep a spare boat for anyone crossing to Luntoc or south toward Korydon.
Ancestor ghosts in the lower halls, illusions on the approach and river crocodiles.
Illusion-work, tomes and ash-glass shards from the upper halls; they trade a little with Renhu.
The Agaceph keep a respectful distance from the ruin's lower halls where the Velothi dead lie.
The Agaceph moved in at the foot of a Velothi stronghold soon after the Flu emptied it. They use its upper halls and are not afraid of ghosts.
A sealed door in the ruin hums by night, and the eldest needs help opening it without waking the dead behind it.
Raft-houses on the river, tied to the black Velothi wall, painted reed screens, books drying on the stone.
A hamlet on the river bank where a Cantemiric Velothi ruin stands, the two sharing the same stretch of country.
About six Agaceph, among them an eldest who knows every stair of the upper halls.
A hamlet of stilt-houses leaning against the ruin's wall. They defend it against Skeith raiders and tribal bands alike.
Crocodiles in the river mouth and skeevers among the stone stacks. The Tsonac men turn away any trader who asks after labour.
Cut stone, hewn timber and lime go out to Thorn; salt, rope and cloth come in. Tsonac keeps the price of stone high. Thorn's buyers complain of it.
They carry small tokens of Tsonac's sleeping Hist and a tree-minder's charm of resin for sleeping. They do not pray to it in public.
Founded as a coast landing by Tsonac in the settled generations after 4E 48, when Thorn's builders began buying stone again. The freight path down from the jungle uplands is older than the hamlet.
A load of carved lintel stones for a Thorn client has gone missing between Tsonac and the jetty. The quarry-men suspect the smugglers on Skeith.
The landing has a neat dry-stone jetty with stacked blocks sorted by size, lime-white dust on the reeds and a few terraced stilt-houses with stone footings on the shore.
A hamlet at the bight's northern shore where the stone and timber of the Tsonac-Kaleel reach the sea. Its culture is that of Tsonac.
About six Argonians of Tsonac who move between the uplands and the shore, with a Thorn broker who lodges here while he buys.
A busy river-mouth landing with a stone jetty, a lime kiln and loading sheds. Thorn boats call whenever stone is ready.
Illusion and paralysis spells on strangers; otherwise the town is calm. The lake has crocodiles, and a pirate raft that works its far shore.
Books, ink, illusion-work and spell-teaching, sold for coin, fish and rice. Yulca's teachers charge outsiders; its illusions are cheap.
No Hist grows here. The Agaceph find the Hist loud and prefer their books. They keep a hall of the Maran mission's tracts, which they read for sport.
The Agaceph gathered here after the Maran missions died in the Third Era. They looted the Maran mission at Umpholo for its library, and Yulca holds the most books of any place in the east.

The founding elders' carved raft-prow, kept in the hall, has been stolen and the elders will not say why they want it back so badly. A visiting Dunmer scholar wants to buy the secret of the Agaceph's freezing spell.
A town of lashed rafts and stilted pavilions on a broad lake, reed screens in bright scale-colours, a book hall under a tall roof, books drying on lines, rafts like blades on the water.
A raft-town on a wide lake in the west, the only Agaceph place of any size. The Agaceph belong to Middle Argonia and live nowhere else.
About twenty-two Agaceph in rainbow colours, ruled by five elders who sit together in the book hall. A few visitors from Gaweja and Aroxhu live on a guest raft.
Yulca is a lake town of rafts with a hall of books open to guests. Its people are polite and wary, and will freeze an intruder with a spell before deciding what to do.
Surf, crabs and hackwings on the shore and Skeith outlaws who beach a boat in the cove. The station's folk do not like uninvited visitors and send word of them to Helstrom.
Dried sea-salt, sea-kelp for dyeing, shore-wrack and eggs of sea-birds; they trade news and goods for clay and pottery from Arorha.
Without a Hist near, they keep a stoppered sap-jar from Helstrom on a shrine and read it as their counsel; they do not speak of the sea.
Founded in the generations after 4E 48, to keep watch on the sea; its people came from the Lake Ulaish country by canoe.
The sap-jar has gone cloudy and the elder fears the Hist is ill. A fresh jar must be carried from Helstrom, or the foulness in this one must be found.
A cluster of reed-and-root stilt houses above the shore line, drying racks of kelp, canoes drawn up on mud, nets in a line.
A hamlet of Helstrom's people, set on the open coast far from any Hist tree. The Root-Folk's hunting and egg-tending stations spread through the inner swamp. This is their outlier on the sea.
About five Saxhleel. The eldest has the status of a mid-ranked tree-minder and speaks to Helstrom through a sap-jar sent twice a year.
Five Root-Folk keep the station and go home in turns. They watch ships and trade quietly with Arorha.
